evidence.explanation: Supports the inverse edge: restoring mitophagy reduces amyloid-beta species and neuroinflammation, so impaired mitophagy is curated as a plausible contributor to amyloid accumulation.

edges/24.description: Impaired mitochondrial quality control is modeled as a contributor to amyloid-beta accumulation through reduced mitophagy-linked microglial plaque clearance and increased neuroinflammatory stress.

evidence.snippet: Mitophagy enhancement abolishes AD-related tau hyperphosphorylation in human neuronal cells
evidence.explanation: Supports the inverse edge from enhanced mitophagy to reduced Alzheimer-related tau hyperphosphorylation in human neuronal cells.

evidence.snippet: reverses memory impairment in transgenic tau nematodes and mice.
evidence.explanation: Supports the model-organism functional arm of the same mitophagy-enhanced tau-model finding; this item is partial for the tau pathology edge because the snippet reports memory impairment rather than tangle burden.

edges/25.description: Impaired mitophagy is modeled as a contributor to tau hyperphosphorylation and tau pathology, but its position relative to amyloid and glial activation remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: In both amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau Caenorhabditis elegans models of AD, mitophagy stimulation (through NAD+ supplementation, urolithin A, and actinonin) reverses memory impairment through PINK-1 (PTEN-induced kinase-1)-, PDR-1 (Parkinson's disease-related-1; parkin)-, or DCT-1 (DAF-16/FOXO-controlled germline-tumor affecting-1)-dependent pathways.
evidence.explanation: Supports a causal link from mitophagy stimulation to improved memory in amyloid-beta and tau model systems, motivating impaired mitophagy as a potential upstream contributor to cognitive decline.

edges/26.description: Mitochondrial quality-control failure is modeled as one upstream stressor that can worsen cognitive outcomes, but cognitive resilience may decouple pathology burden from symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Depletion of autophagic proteins promoted the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria and cytosolic translocation of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and ATP in macrophages.
evidence.explanation: General macrophage mechanism for autophagy/mitochondrial-quality-control failure licensing inflammasome activation; not microglia-specific or Alzheimer-specific, hence indirect.

evidence.snippet: Mitophagy diminishes insoluble Aβ1-42 and Aβ1-40 and prevents cognitive impairment in an APP/PS1 mouse model through microglial phagocytosis of extracellular Aβ plaques and suppression of neuroinflammation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the inverse edge in an Alzheimer mouse model: restoring mitophagy suppresses neuroinflammation, so impaired mitophagy is curated as a plausible contributor to it.

edges/27.description: Impaired mitochondrial quality control is modeled as licensing NLRP3 inflammasome activation through cytosolic mitochondrial DNA release, in addition to reduced mitophagy-mediated resolution of glial activation.

evidence.snippet: Thus, current evidence suggests that BBB dysfunction may causatively and consequently contribute to AD pathogenesis, forming a vicious cycle between brain Abeta accumulation and neurovascular unit impairments during disease progression.
evidence.explanation: Supports a causal and consequential cycle between BBB dysfunction, amyloid-beta accumulation, and neurovascular-unit impairment.

edges/28.description: Blood-brain barrier dysfunction and neurovascular-unit impairment are modeled as contributors to brain amyloid-beta accumulation and impaired clearance.

evidence.snippet: Aberrant remodeling of microvesselsis associated with blood-brain barrier breakdown, development of neuroinflammation, inadequate microcirculation in active brain regions, and leads to the dysfunction of the neurovascular unit and progressive neurological deficits.
evidence.explanation: Supports neurovascular-unit dysfunction and inadequate microcirculation as contributors to neurological deficits.

edges/29.description: Reduced perfusion and neurovascular-unit injury are modeled as contributors to neuronal and synaptic dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Specific disruption of slow wave activity correlated with an increase in amyloid-β40
evidence.explanation: Interventional human evidence that removing the sleep drive for glymphatic clearance raises amyloid-beta levels.

evidence.snippet: one night of sleep deprivation, relative to baseline, resulted in a significant increase in Aβ burden in the right hippocampus and thalamus
evidence.explanation: Human PET evidence that a single night of sleep deprivation increases measured brain amyloid burden.

edges/30.description: Reduced perivascular clearance raises the steady-state interstitial amyloid-beta concentration, favoring aggregation and plaque deposition.

edges/31.description: Impaired autophagy and lysosomal degradation are modeled as contributors to amyloid-beta accumulation through reduced aggregate clearance.

edges/32.description: Impaired autophagy and lysosomal degradation are modeled as contributors to tau aggregate accumulation through reduced proteostatic clearance.

evidence.snippet: Integrative single-nucleus analyses resolve direct evidence of HSV-1 expression in RORB+ glutamatergic neurons, implicating viral reactivation in a neuronal population progressively lost during dementia.
evidence.explanation: Supports HSV-1 reactivation in a vulnerable neuronal population, while the synaptic dysfunction edge remains an inferred downstream consequence.

edges/33.description: HSV-1 reactivation in selectively vulnerable cortical neurons is modeled as a possible upstream contributor to loss of synaptic integrity and cognitive-network failure.

evidence.snippet: These results show that Arc is critical for the packaging of tau in EVs, which plays a significant role in intercellular tau transmission.
evidence.explanation: Arc-dependent EV packaging of tau is required for intercellular tau transmission, the basis for the seeding edge back onto tangle pathology in recipient neurons.

edges/34.description: EV-delivered seed-competent tau is taken up by recipient neurons and seeds aggregation of endogenous tau, propagating tangle pathology along connected circuits.

evidence.snippet: NF-κB-induced neuroinflammation, dysregulation of mitophagy, and disruption of the neuroprotective SIRT1 signaling pathway
evidence.explanation: PARP1 overactivity is modeled as driving NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation through NAD+ depletion and parthanatos-driven inflammatory amplification.

edges/35.description: PARP1 overactivation amplifies NF-κB-dependent neuroinflammatory responses and promotes microglial activation.

evidence.snippet: dysregulation of mitophagy, and disruption of the neuroprotective SIRT1 signaling pathway
evidence.explanation: Links PARP1-driven NAD+ depletion to SIRT1 loss and mitophagy dysregulation, sustaining oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.

edges/36.description: PARP1 hyperactivation and NAD+ depletion impair mitochondrial redox homeostasis, sustaining oxidative stress through disruption of antioxidant SIRT1 and mitophagy.

evidence.snippet: precursors of NAD+ such as nicotinamide and NMN attenuate Aβ deposition, normalize metabolism, and ameliorate cognitive decline
evidence.explanation: Supports PARP1-driven NAD+ depletion and mitophagy dysregulation as contributors to mitochondrial failure and therapeutic intervention targets.

edges/37.description: PARP1 hyperactivity and NAD+ depletion impair mitochondrial dynamics, mitophagy, and ATP production, contributing to quality-control collapse.

evidence.snippet: Inhibition of interferon-γ and PDCD1 signalling both significantly ameliorated brain atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Blocking IFN-gamma or PD-1 signaling reduces brain atrophy, supporting a causal edge from the T cell response to neurodegeneration/synaptic failure.

edges/38.description: T cell-derived IFN-gamma and cytotoxic activity, engaged downstream of tau pathology, amplify neuronal and synaptic loss; IFN-gamma/PD-1 blockade reduces brain atrophy.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism underlying the effect on the Abeta pathology was caused by the selective activation of ADAM17, thereby shifting APP processing toward the nonamyloidogenic pathway, whereas the reduction in tau pathology is mediated by decreased GSK3beta activity.
evidence.explanation: Identifies ADAM17 as the effector coupling M1 signaling to non-amyloidogenic APP processing, so loss of M1 signaling is the directional inverse of this rescue.

evidence.snippet: Ablating the M(1)R increased plaque and tangle levels in the brains of 3xTgAD mice
evidence.explanation: Genetic removal of M1 increases plaque burden in an AD model, the loss-of-signaling direction this edge asserts.

edges/39.description: Withdrawal of M1 signaling shifts APP processing away from the ADAM17/alpha-secretase route toward amyloidogenic cleavage, increasing amyloid-beta available for deposition.

evidence.snippet: tau hyperphosphorylation and potentiation of amyloidogenic processing in the mice with AD lacking M(1)R were attributed to changes in the glycogen synthase kinase 3β and protein kinase C activities
evidence.explanation: Names GSK3-beta and PKC as the kinases mediating tau hyperphosphorylation downstream of M1 loss.

edges/40.description: Loss of M1 signaling de-represses GSK3-beta and alters protein kinase C activity, promoting tau hyperphosphorylation and tangle formation.

evidence.snippet: Here we show in mouse models that complement and microglia mediate synaptic loss early in AD.
evidence.explanation: States the causal edge from the complement-microglia axis to synapse loss.

edges/41.description: Complement tagging and microglial engulfment remove intact synapses, producing the synapse loss that underlies impaired plasticity and neurotransmission.

evidence.snippet: Quantitative analyses confirm that individual neurons exhibiting PANTHOS are the principal source of senile plaques in amyloid precursor protein AD models.
evidence.explanation: The causal edge from the intraneuronal lesion to the plaque, established in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mouse models.

edges/42.description: Amyloid-beta accumulated within de-acidified autolysosomes of individual neurons is released when those neurons rupture, so the plaque is modeled as originating from a dying neuron rather than from secreted peptide.

evidence.snippet: Elevated APP-βCTF Tyr682 phosphorylation in two mouse AD models similarly disrupts v-ATPase function.
evidence.explanation: Extends the fibroblast mechanism to Alzheimer mouse brain, supporting the edge onto the general autophagy-lysosomal node.

edges/43.description: APP-βCTF inhibition of the v-ATPase is modeled as one upstream cause of the broader autophagic-flux failure curated in that node.

evidence.snippet: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the selective vulnerability of specific neuronal populations, the molecular signatures of which are largely unknown.
evidence.explanation: States the selectivity premise while making explicit that the molecular basis is unknown, which is why this edge is curated with unknown intermediates.

edges/44.description: Cell-intrinsic vulnerability of RORB+ entorhinal excitatory neurons is modeled as determining where neurofibrillary inclusions first form, giving tau pathology its characteristic anatomical starting point.

evidence.snippet: In addition, we found that the set of genes regulated by RIPK1 overlapped significantly with multiple independent AD transcriptomic signatures, indicating that RIPK1 activity could explain a substantial portion of transcriptomic changes in AD.
evidence.explanation: Supports RIPK1 activity shaping the broader Alzheimer transcriptional state, of which the inflammatory response is a major component. The specific edge to glial activation remains inferred, hence unknown intermediates.

edges/45.description: Necroptosis is lytic: unlike apoptosis it releases intracellular contents, so necroptotic neuronal death is modeled as feeding the glial inflammatory response rather than being silently cleared.

evidence.snippet: Collectively, these results show that senescent cells have a role in the initiation and progression of tau-mediated disease, and suggest that targeting senescent cells may provide a therapeutic avenue for the treatment of these pathologies.
evidence.explanation: States the causal role of senescent cells in initiating and progressing tau-mediated disease.

edges/46.description: Senescent cells are modeled as promoting tau hyperphosphorylation and tangle deposition; the direction is established by the inverse experiment, in which clearing them prevents both.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest a role for Aβ-induced OPC cell senescence in neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits in AD, and a potential therapeutic benefit of senolytic treatments.
evidence.explanation: States the modeled edge from amyloid-induced progenitor senescence to neuroinflammation and cognitive deficit.

edges/47.description: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype is modeled as a chronic proinflammatory input to glial activation; senolytic clearance reduces neuroinflammation.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, myelin dysfunction causes the accumulation of the Aβ-producing machinery within axonal swellings and increases the cleavage of cortical amyloid precursor protein.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the subcellular mechanism for the edge from myelin damage to increased amyloid production.

edges/48.description: Myelin dysfunction is modeled as increasing amyloid deposition both directly, by concentrating amyloidogenic processing in axonal swellings, and indirectly, by diverting plaque-clearing microglia to myelin damage.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, conditioned media from lipid droplet-containing microglia lead to Tau phosphorylation and neurotoxicity in an APOE-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: Conditioned-media transfer establishes that the effect on tau is mediated by secreted factors rather than contact.

edges/49.description: Factors secreted by lipid-droplet-containing microglia drive tau phosphorylation and neurotoxicity in an APOE-dependent manner, linking the glial lipid state to tau pathology.

evidence.snippet: RNA-sequencing analysis of LDAM revealed a transcriptional profile driven by innate inflammation that is distinct from previously reported microglial states.
evidence.explanation: Supports the state being transcriptionally inflammatory and distinct from other described microglial states, in the aging rather than Alzheimer brain.

edges/50.description: Lipid-droplet-accumulating microglia are a proinflammatory, phagocytically defective state, so their accumulation is modeled as amplifying neuroinflammation while reducing amyloid clearance capacity.

evidence.snippet: Restoring Nav1.1 levels in hAPP mice by Nav1.1-BAC expression increased inhibitory synaptic activity and gamma oscillations and reduced hypersynchrony, memory deficits, and premature mortality.
evidence.explanation: Gain-of-function rescue of a single interneuron channel subunit corrects oscillations, hypersynchrony and memory, establishing the edge as causal in this model.

evidence.snippet: However, patients with subclinical epileptiform activity showed faster declines in global cognition, determined by the Mini-Mental State Examination (3.9 points/year in patients with epileptiform activity vs 1.6 points/year in patients without; p = 0.006), and in executive function (p = 0.01).
evidence.explanation: Human correlate of the same edge: hyperexcitability is associated with more than twice the annual rate of cognitive decline.

edges/51.description: Loss of inhibitory control and network hypersynchrony are modeled as direct contributors to cognitive impairment; restoring Nav1.1 in a model reverses both the hypersynchrony and the memory deficit.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, the nucleoporin Nup98 accumulates in the cell bodies of some tangle-bearing neurons and can facilitate tau aggregation in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Supports the feed-forward edge from mislocalized Nup98 back onto tau aggregation.

edges/52.description: Nup98 mislocalized into the neuronal cytoplasm facilitates tau aggregation, closing a feed-forward loop in which tau-driven transport failure promotes further tau aggregation.

evidence.snippet: Notably, shPGM3-treated 5xFAD as well as PS19 mice exhibited significant improvement in social memory interaction patterns when compared with the shScr-treated mice
evidence.explanation: Knocking down PGM3, the hexosamine-pathway enzyme upstream of UDP-GlcNAc, lowers brain N-glycans and improves memory in both an amyloid and a tau model.

evidence.snippet: These data reinforce that lowering excessive N-glycosylation is sufficient to enhance cognitive outcomes and highlight hyperglycosylation as an actionable target for dementia-related memory decline in mice.
evidence.explanation: A mechanistically different intervention, the oligosaccharyltransferase inhibitor NGI-1, reaches the same endpoint. The authors describe the NGI-1 behavioural rescue as partial.

evidence.snippet: By contrast, glucosamine-treated 5xFAD mice exhibited a further exacerbation of social memory deficits, showing no recognition of previously encountered conspecifics across trials
evidence.explanation: The opposite perturbation: raising glycan precursor supply worsens the same memory readout, so the relationship is bidirectional.

evidence.snippet: Notably, our data indicate that neither OST inhibition nor shRNA-mediated inhibition of PGM3 significantly impacted neuroinflammatory markers such as astrocytosis or GFAP levels, nor did they substantially alter amyloid-beta formation in the mouse model.
evidence.explanation: Places the memory effect outside the amyloid and astrocytic pathways, which is why this edge goes directly to the phenotype rather than through Amyloid Plaque Formation or Neuroinflammation.

edges/53.description: Reducing N-glycan biosynthesis restores social recognition memory in 5xFAD and PS19 mice, and increasing it with oral glucosamine worsens memory in 5xFAD mice, without changes in amyloid-beta or astrocytic GFAP. The intermediate steps between excess glycosylation and impaired memory are not identified; the glycoproteomic data point to neuronal membrane proteins but no specific glycoprotein has been shown to carry the effect.

evidence.snippet: A 10-year cumulative dose-response relationship was observed for dementia and Alzheimer disease
evidence.explanation: Cumulative-dose dependence is the signature expected if sustained receptor blockade, rather than transient pharmacologic effect, is what matters.

evidence.snippet: aCH+ participants had increased risk of progression to MCI
evidence.explanation: Anticholinergic exposure predicts incident MCI in cognitively normal adults, with the effect amplified by APOE4 and CSF AD pathology — interaction with AD biology rather than an independent cognitive effect.

edges/54.description: Chronic anticholinergic exposure is the pharmacologic route by which M1 muscarinic signaling is persistently withdrawn, the state the mouse work links to accelerated amyloid and tau pathology. PREDISPOSES rather than TRIGGERS: the human evidence is observational, dose-dependent, and does not establish that the exposure initiates disease.

evidence.snippet: Conversely, glucosamine supplementation significantly increased glycosylation across the brain, as shown by global heat map analysis
evidence.explanation: Oral glucosamine for two weeks raises brain N-glycans in 5xFAD mice, at a dose scaled from a human intake of about 2.5 g per day.

evidence.snippet: Strikingly, glucosamine supplementation did not result in hyperglycosylation in WT mouse brains
evidence.explanation: The same regimen has no effect on wild-type brains, which is why the effect is curated as exacerbation of an existing state.

edges/55.description: Glucosamine bypasses the rate-limiting step of the hexosamine pathway and supplies precursor for N-glycan biosynthesis. EXACERBATES rather than TRIGGERS: in mice it raises brain N-glycans only on an AD background and leaves wild-type brains unchanged.

evidence.snippet: Four mutations involving amino acid substitutions in exons 16 and 17 of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene, have been identified which co-segregate with the disease in some families multiply affected by early onset Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the association of APP genetic mutations with early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: This is the first case demonstrating that a low-degree APP gene-dose increase suffices to cause EOAD with prominent amyloid-beta/tau pathology.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the role of APP gene mutations in causing early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Numerous mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP) and presenilin 1 and 2 (PSEN1 and PSEN2) have been identified for EOAD, but they can only account for a small proportion of EOAD cases.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the association of APP genetic mutations with early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: In this study, a novel mutation in APP gene, Val669Leu ('Seoul APP'), was reported in a Korean female patient with Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the association of APP genetic mutations with early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: It is thought that this risk is conferred by the presence of three copies of the gene encoding amyloid precursor protein (APP)--an Alzheimer disease risk factor.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the association of APP genetic mutations with early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: APP mutations cause Alzheimer disease (AD) with virtually complete penetrance.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the association of APP genetic mutations with early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Presenilin 1 (PSEN1) gene mutations are the major known genetic cause of early-onset Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: The study reports a novel PSEN1 mutation associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, supporting the genetic association.

evidence.snippet: At present, three early-onset AD genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) and one late-onset AD susceptibility gene apolipoprotein E (APOE) have been determined.
evidence.explanation: The reference confirms that PSEN1 is one of the genes associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: A genetic association study was conducted to examine ADAD AAO in 340 individuals with the PSEN1 E280A mutation.
evidence.explanation: The study discusses a large cohort with a specific PSEN1 mutation associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, reinforcing the genetic link.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset AD represents about 5.5% of the total cases and occurs in patients under age 65. The EOAD progresses more aggressively and has a shorter life expectancy due to a greater pathogenic load.
evidence.explanation: The reference discusses early-onset Alzheimer's disease and mentions PSEN1 mutations, supporting the genetic association.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) is commonly diagnosed with an onset age of earlier than 65 years and accounts for 5-10% of all Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases.
evidence.explanation: The study highlights the occurrence of early-onset Alzheimer's disease and mentions PSEN1 mutations, supporting the genetic link.

evidence.snippet: The gene mutations in the amyloid precursor protein (APP), presenilin 1 (PSEN1), and presenilin 2 (PSEN2) are the frequent causes of AD.
evidence.explanation: The reference confirms that PSEN1 mutations are a frequent cause of early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: The established causative mutations in the APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 can explain less than 1%, Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. Of the identified variants, the PSEN2 mutations are even less common.
evidence.explanation: The reference confirms that PSEN2 mutations are among the causative factors for early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset AD (EOAD) was defined as AD occurring before age 65. Although it has a high genetic risk, EOAD due to PSEN2 variation is very rare.
evidence.explanation: The reference supports the association of PSEN2 with early-onset Alzheimer's disease, although it notes that such cases are rare.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset familial Alzheimer disease (EOFAD) is caused by heterozygous variants in the presenilin 1 (PSEN1), presenilin 2 (PSEN2), and APP genes.
evidence.explanation: The reference explicitly states that early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease can be caused by PSEN2 mutations.

evidence.snippet: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer disease.
evidence.explanation: Establishes APOE4 as the leading genetic risk factor for late-onset AD.

evidence.snippet: The individual had two copies of the APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) mutation, unusually high brain amyloid levels and limited tau and neurodegenerative measurements.
evidence.explanation: The homozygous APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) variant is associated with resistance to autosomal-dominant AD despite high amyloid, evidence for a protective APOE variant acting on tau/neurodegeneration.

evidence.snippet: Mice expressing APOE3-Jac have reduced amyloid pathology, plaque-associated immune responses, and neuritic dystrophy.
evidence.explanation: The APOE3-Jacksonville (V236E) variant reduces APOE aggregation and amyloid pathology, a second protective APOE variant supporting APOE aggregation as a therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that reducing ApoE4 levels should be explored further as a therapeutic approach for APOE4 carriers with tauopathy including Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: APOE4-lowering antisense oligonucleotides reduce tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation, supporting APOE as an actionable therapeutic node.

genes/3.notes: APOE is the strongest common-variant genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease. The APOE4 allele increases risk and accelerates onset in a gene-dose-dependent manner (relative to the common APOE3), while APOE2 is protective. Beyond amyloid, APOE4 exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, glial lipid/cholesterol accumulation, and dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier. Rare protective coding variants illuminate mechanism and are therapeutic templates: APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) reduces receptor-binding avidity and limits tau seeding/spreading (a homozygous carrier resisted autosomal-dominant AD for ~3 decades despite heavy amyloid), and APOE3 Jacksonville (V236E) reduces APOE self-aggregation and amyloid pathology. Preclinically, lowering APOE4 (e.g., with antisense oligonucleotides) reduces tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation, motivating APOE-directed therapeutics. See the apoe_risk_modulation_model mechanistic hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: eQTLGen tested 16,875 genes for AD risk and identiﬁed 204 FDR-signiﬁcant genes, led by BIN1.
evidence.explanation: eQTLGen blood eQTL analysis identified BIN1 as the lead AD-risk gene among 204 FDR-significant hits, establishing it as a primary genetic risk factor distinct from amyloid-burden genetics.

evidence.snippet: CEACAM16-AS1 led cortex, frontal cortex BA9, anterior cingulate BA24, and hippocampus, whereas BIN1 led cerebellum
evidence.explanation: Multi-region eQTL analysis (cortex, frontal cortex BA9, anterior cingulate BA24, hippocampus, cerebellum) confirms BIN1 as the lead gene in cerebellum, establishing brain-region-specific eQTL support.

evidence.snippet: BIN1 is the strongest broad AD-risk anchor and has external disease-state expression support.
evidence.explanation: Integrated analysis across eQTL, colocalization, MetaBrain, and disease-state expression layers converges on BIN1 as the primary non-APOE AD-risk architecture anchor.

evidence.snippet: BIN1 was testable in 10 region-dataset pairs across GSE5281 and GSE48350 and showed four nominally signiﬁcant AD–control differences, all of which survived FDR correction.
evidence.explanation: Disease-state expression analysis supports altered BIN1 expression in Alzheimer disease post-mortem brain tissue, validating the genetic risk association with disease-relevant molecular change.

evidence.snippet: the already known, GWAS-defined genes (ABCA7, BIN1, CD33, CLU, CR1, CD2AP, EPHA1
evidence.explanation: The IGAP genome-wide association meta-analysis (74,046 individuals) lists BIN1 among the established GWAS-defined late-onset Alzheimer disease susceptibility genes, providing peer-reviewed foundational support for the BIN1 risk association beyond the eQTL preprint.

genes/4.notes: BIN1 encodes bridging integrator 1, a phosphoinositide-binding adaptor protein involved in membrane dynamics, endocytosis, and synaptic function. Identified as the strongest broad AD-risk anchor across blood and brain-region eQTL layers (whole blood, cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum). The locus shows distinct causal variants (H3-dominated colocalization) across tissues, indicating region-specific regulatory mechanisms rather than a single shared causal variant. Disease-state brain-expression support shows reduced BIN1 expression in Alzheimer disease versus control tissue.

genes/5.notes: Microglial receptor that influences disease-associated microglial phenotypes, phagocytosis, and immune responses to Aβ pathology.

genes/6.notes: Encodes the NLRP3 inflammasome sensor in microglia that drives IL-1β production, pyroptosis, and neuroinflammation in response to Aβ and tau aggregates.

genes/7.notes: Encodes ASC (apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD), the inflammasome adaptor required for NLRP3 signaling and IL-1β maturation.

genes/8.notes: Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1, mediates Aβ clearance across the blood-brain barrier. Variants and reduced expression impair Aβ efflux.

evidence.snippet: Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are commonly used AChEIs in pharmacotherapy for AD, slowing the progression and controlling the symptoms of AD.
evidence.explanation: The literature supports that cholinesterase inhibitors, including donepezil and rivastigmine, are used to help with symptoms of Alzheimer's disease by slowing the progression and controlling cognitive symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, and a combination of a cholinesterase inhibitor and memantine have produced statistically significant but clinically small delays in various domains of cognitive and functional decline in select patients with Alzheimer disease.
evidence.explanation: The literature supports the use of cholinesterase inhibitors in delaying cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Two classes of drug - cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine) and memantine - are widely licensed for dementia due to Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: The literature confirms that cholinesterase inhibitors are licensed for use in Alzheimer's disease to alleviate symptoms and delay disease progression.

evidence.snippet: Currently approved medications are symptomatic and include two classes: cholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil, and NMDA receptor antagonist memantine.
evidence.explanation: The literature supports that cholinesterase inhibitors are approved symptomatic treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Donepezil is a specific and potent acetylcholinesterase inhibitor... Donepezil 5 or 10 mg/day was associated with significant improvements in cognitive function.
evidence.explanation: The literature supports that donepezil, a cholinesterase inhibitor, helps improve cognitive function in Alzheimer's disease.

treatments/0.description: Medications that slow the breakdown of acetylcholine to help with memory and cognitive function (e.g., donepezil, rivastigmine).

evidence.snippet: Lecanemab, a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity to Aβ soluble protofibrils, is being tested in persons with early Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: Identifies lecanemab as an amyloid-beta protofibril-directed monoclonal antibody developed for early Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events.
evidence.explanation: Phase 3 CLARITY-AD trial (NCT03887455) shows lecanemab lowers amyloid burden and modestly slows cognitive/functional decline versus placebo, supporting the disease-modifying anti-amyloid immunotherapy class.

evidence.snippet: Among participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer disease and amyloid and tau pathology, donanemab significantly slowed clinical progression at 76 weeks in those with low/medium tau and in the combined low/medium and high tau pathology population.
evidence.explanation: Phase 3 TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial (NCT04437511) demonstrates that donanemab significantly slows clinical progression in early symptomatic Alzheimer disease, anchoring the second FDA-reviewed anti-amyloid immunotherapy in this class.

evidence.snippet: Lecanemab is an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody, recently approved in the UK as a treatment for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease (AD)
evidence.explanation: UK appropriate use recommendations position lecanemab as an approved anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody for mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia due to Alzheimer disease.

treatments/1.description: Amyloid-beta-directed monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) are disease-modifying immunotherapies for early Alzheimer disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia with confirmed amyloid pathology). They clear brain amyloid-beta and produce a modest slowing of cognitive and functional decline; use is limited by amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) and infusion reactions, and requires amyloid confirmation plus MRI monitoring.

evidence.snippet: We sought to inhibit MAPT expression with a tau-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (MAPTRx) and reduce tau levels in patients with mild AD.
evidence.explanation: Phase 1b MAPTRx trial establishes diranersen as an antisense oligonucleotide that lowers tau by inhibiting MAPT expression in mild Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: Dose-dependent reduction in the CSF total-tau concentration was observed with greater than 50% mean reduction from baseline at 24 weeks post-last dose in the 60 mg (four doses) and 115 mg (two doses) MAPTRx groups.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates dose-dependent CSF total-tau lowering (target engagement) with MAPTRx, the pharmacodynamic basis for the tau-directed ASO approach.

evidence.snippet: randomized 3:1 to intrathecal bolus administrations of MAPTRx or placebo every 4 or 12 weeks during the 13-week treatment period
evidence.explanation: Documents the intrathecal (CSF) route of administration required for CNS delivery of the unconjugated ASO.

treatments/2.description: Diranersen (BIIB080 / IONIS-MAPTRx) is an investigational, intrathecally administered antisense oligonucleotide that binds MAPT mRNA and recruits RNase H1 to degrade it, lowering production of both intracellular and extracellular tau. It is the first tau-lowering strategy to demonstrate target engagement in Alzheimer disease and represents a mechanistically distinct disease-modifying approach from the anti-amyloid antibodies: rather than clearing extracellular amyloid-beta, it reduces the tau substrate that hyperphosphorylates and aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles, the pathology most tightly correlated with cognitive decline. The phase 1b MAPTRx trial (NCT03186989) showed dose-dependent >50% mean reductions in CSF total-tau, and the phase 2 CELIA study (NCT05399888) in mild cognitive impairment / mild AD dementia used the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) as its primary endpoint. Per Biogen/Ionis topline results reported at AAIC 2026, CELIA reduced CSF total-tau by ~50-65% across doses and showed a slowing of clinical decline versus placebo, although it did not meet its primary endpoint; the FDA granted diranersen Fast Track designation in 2025.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Diranersen indirectly inhibits this mechanism upstream rather than blocking aggregate assembly directly: RNase H1-mediated MAPT mRNA knockdown lowers the total tau available to become hyperphosphorylated and aggregate into neurofibrillary tangles.

evidence.snippet: Memantine, an antagonist of the glutamatergic NMDA receptor, has been recently approved for the treatment of advanced AD. Due to its action mechanism, memantine is considered a neuroprotective drug, whose utility has been demonstrated in preclinical studies, and a useful symptomatic treatment for AD and vascular dementia.
evidence.explanation: The abstract confirms that memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is used to treat Alzheimer's Disease by regulating glutamate activity.

evidence.snippet: Studies indicate that the distinct outcomes of NMDAR-mediated responses are induced by regionalized receptor activities, followed by different downstream signaling pathways. The activation of synaptic NMDARs initiates plasticity and stimulates cell survival. In contrast, the activation of extrasynaptic NMDARs promotes cell death and thus contributes to the etiology of AD, which can be blocked by an AD drug, memantine, an NMDAR antagonist that selectively blocks the function of extrasynaptic NMDARs.
evidence.explanation: This abstract highlights that memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, helps in blocking the negative effects of excessive NMDAR activity in Alzheimer's Disease.

evidence.snippet: The hypothesis proposed is restoration of medium spiny neurons in Huntington's disease using neural progenitor cell implantation and attenuation of glutamate mediated excitotoxicity using a partial glutamate antagonist - Memantine. Memantine can block the NMDA receptors and will prevent excess calcium influx into the neurons decreases the vulnerability of medium spiny neurons to glutamate mediated excitotoxicity.
evidence.explanation: Although primarily discussing Huntington's Disease, this abstract supports the idea that memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, regulates glutamate activity, which is relevant to Alzheimer's Disease treatment.

treatments/3.description: Medication that regulates glutamate activity to improve symptoms (e.g., memantine).

evidence.snippet: Cognitive stimulation was found to be an effective intervention for people with moderate Alzheimer's disease because it helped to maintain memory function, executive functions, and attention.
evidence.explanation: This study specifically highlights the effectiveness of cognitive stimulation in maintaining cognitive functions in patients with moderate Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Cognitive stimulation programs show benefit in maintenance of cognitive function and improved self-reported quality of life in patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer disease.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the statement by indicating that cognitive stimulation programs help maintain cognitive function in patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: CS confers temporary, nonspecific benefits and might slightly reduce dementia risk for neurologically healthy individuals.
evidence.explanation: This reference indicates that cognitive stimulation offers temporary benefits and might reduce dementia risk, but it is less clear about long-term maintenance of cognitive function specifically in Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Mental training and cognitive stimulation interventions in AD have been shown to be useful in increasing patients' ability in performing activities of daily living (ADL), allowing them to maintain relative independence.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the utility of cognitive interventions in maintaining daily functioning, which is related to cognitive function, but does not directly address cognitive maintenance alone.

evidence.snippet: Interventions involving physical exercise and cognitive training have consistently shown positive effects on cognition in older adults.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the statement by indicating that cognitive training, a form of cognitive therapy, has positive effects on cognition in older adults, including those with Alzheimer's disease.

treatments/4.description: Non-pharmacological interventions to maintain cognitive function.

evidence.snippet: Occupational therapy practitioners play a significant role in supporting adults with Alzheimer's disease and related major neurocognitive disorders, as well as their caregivers, through all phases of the disease process.
evidence.explanation: The reference highlights the role of occupational therapy in supporting individuals with Alzheimer's disease, which aligns with the statement that includes occupational therapy as part of supportive care.

evidence.snippet: The telephone hotline is a useful component of dementia care in Germany and an important contribution to the National Dementia Strategy.
evidence.explanation: The reference discusses the importance of caregiver support through telephone counseling, aligning with the statement that includes caregiver support as part of supportive care.

evidence.snippet: This article first describes the educational, information, and support needs of individuals living dementia and their family caregivers across all stages of Alzheimer's.
evidence.explanation: The reference discusses the support needs of individuals with Alzheimer's disease and their caregivers, which aligns with the statement that includes caregiver support as part of supportive care.

evidence.snippet: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are used from 15 years, in Alzheimer's disease. Benefits have been demonstrated according to cognition, activities of daily living, affective symptoms and behavior, and global impression of change.
evidence.explanation: The reference primarily discusses pharmacological treatments, with some mention of activities of daily living, but does not specifically address occupational therapy or speech therapy.

treatments/5.description: Includes occupational therapy, speech therapy, and caregiver support.

evidence.snippet: The aim of this review is to emphasize the importance of mental activity and aerobic physical exercise as one of the most important health-related activities which may delay the onset or slow down the progression of Alzheimer's dementia.
evidence.explanation: The review highlights the importance of mental and physical exercise in potentially slowing the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

evidence.snippet: Combined with the prevention of AD risk factors such as heart disease, diabetes, and with more recent evidence, microbiome dysfunction, there is a substantial foundation for diet as a modifiable risk factor and preventative measure for AD.
evidence.explanation: The review suggests that a healthy diet can be a preventative measure for Alzheimer's disease, supporting the role of lifestyle modifications.

evidence.snippet: Results showed that eating a healthy diet with plenty of fruits and vegetables, and participation in leisure and physical activities may protect against cognitive decline and cognitive impairment among oldest-old regardless of the APOE genotype.
evidence.explanation: The systematic review indicates that lifestyle factors such as diet and physical activities may protect against cognitive decline, supporting the statement.

evidence.snippet: Rehabilitation approaches to support memory and behavioral/lifestyle interventions are recognized as promising strategies for preserving or improving cognitive health.
evidence.explanation: The intervention described combines lifestyle modifications and memory support to improve cognitive health, supporting the statement.

treatments/6.description: Physical exercise, mental stimulation, and healthy diet to potentially slow disease progression.

evidence.snippet: The 'amyloid cascade hypothesis' posits that an extracellular build-up of amyloid-beta oligomers (Abeta-os) and polymers (fibrils) subsequently inducing toxic hyperphosphorylated (p)-Tau oligomers (p-Tau-os) and neurofibrillary tangles starts the sporadic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD)...
evidence.explanation: Supports amyloid-beta accumulation as an upstream causal model that induces downstream tau pathology.

evidence.snippet: Generation of amyloid peptide (Abeta) is at the beginning of a cascade that leads to Alzheimer's disease (AD)... soluble assembly states of Abeta peptides can cause cognitive problems by disrupting synaptic function...
evidence.explanation: Supports amyloid-beta generation as an initiating cascade event with synaptic consequences.

evidence.snippet: APP-A673T significantly downregulated β-cleavage and attenuated the production of Aβ and amyloid pathology in the brains of these animals.
evidence.explanation: In vivo arm of the bidirectional genetic argument: introducing the protective Icelandic APP variant into Swedish-mutation-free App knock-in mice reduces beta-cleavage and amyloid pathology, complementing the causal familial mutations at the other end of the dose range.

evidence.snippet: Donanemab reduced the risk of progression from MCI to mild AD by 33% (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.67; 95% CI 0.52-0.87; p = 0.003) and from mild to moderate AD by 50% (HR = 0.50; 95% CI 0.33-0.78; p = 0.002).
evidence.explanation: Partial pharmacological validation of the amyloid target: removing plaque amyloid slows clinical stage transition. Note this identifier is a clinical-meaningfulness analysis of TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 combining prespecified and post hoc analyses, not the primary trial report.

evidence.snippet: Successful removal of amyloid from the brain does not seem to be associated with clinically meaningful effects in people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease.
evidence.explanation: Cochrane review of 17 randomized trials in 20,342 participants; the effect on cognition and dementia severity at 18 months is graded trivial. Removing the proposed causal species does not produce a clinically meaningful benefit, which is the strongest available qualification of the cascade's sufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Gantenerumab significantly reduced brain amyloid load. Tau positron emission tomography showed no treatment effect in a small subset of participants.
evidence.explanation: Human interventional evidence bearing on the amyloid-to-tau step: 116 weeks of amyloid removal moved amyloid PET and multiple fluid biomarkers but did not move tau PET, constraining a simple unidirectional amyloid-drives-tau reading. The tau PET substudy was small, so this bounds rather than excludes the link.

evidence.snippet: In the amyloid-first subtype, extensive neocortical amyloid-β precedes the spread of tau beyond the medial temporal lobe, while in the tau-first subtype, mild tau accumulates in medial temporal and neocortical areas prior to interacting with amyloid-β.
evidence.explanation: Data-driven subtyping of ADNI tau/amyloid PET and ROSMAP neuropathology recovers a tau-first subtype in both, so amyloid does not initiate the sequence in every case. Refutes universality, not the cascade itself — the source paper is explicit that the hypothesis does not require amyloid to occur first in all cases, and tau-first APOE e4 non-carriers largely recapitulate primary age-related tauopathy rather than Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: Unfortunately, this compound showed to accelerate cognitive decline in both asymptomatic and symptomatic trial participants, and this failure of solanezumab further questioned the Aβ cascade hypothesis of AD.
evidence.explanation: Targeting soluble monomeric amyloid-beta did not help and was judged to worsen decline. Graded OTHER deliberately: this sentence is the authors' expert-opinion summary of the solanezumab programme in a narrative case history, not a trial result, and the underlying EXPEDITION, A4 or DIAN-TU reports should be cited for any quantitative claim.

evidence.snippet: Among 235 participants (mean age at death = 98 years, 70% women), 33% maintained normal cognition.
evidence.explanation: Amyloid pathology is not deterministic for clinical disease: a third of oldest-old people with intermediate or high Alzheimer neuropathologic change died cognitively normal. The fraction falls to 22% in the high-change subgroup, so the headline number depends on including intermediate change.

evidence.snippet: In this study, the presence of neurodegenerative neuropathologic changes other than ADNC and the absence of hypertension distinguish oldest old individuals with dementia from those with normal cognition.
evidence.explanation: Carries the study's own explanation for the resilience above: co-pathology (LATE-NC, Lewy body disease, hippocampal sclerosis, a high count of non-Alzheimer changes), not tolerance of amyloid, separates the demented from the cognitively normal. Curated alongside the 33% figure so the number is not read as evidence for a synaptic or metabolic resilience mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The modest elevation of endogenous APP-βCTF needed to disrupt lysosomal function in DS is relevant to sporadic AD where APP-βCTF, but not APP, is also elevated.
evidence.explanation: An APP-dependent but amyloid-beta-independent pathogenic arm: the beta-cleaved C-terminal fragment C99, not amyloid-beta, mediates the lysosomal acidification failure, and C99 rather than APP is what is elevated in sporadic disease. Scoped to lysosomal acidification in a Down syndrome model (fibroblasts, cultured Ts2 neurons, and Bace1 allele deletion in vivo), not to Alzheimer pathogenesis generally.

hypotheses/0.description: Amyloid-beta production, oligomerization, and plaque deposition are modeled as upstream drivers of tau pathology, synaptic toxicity, glial activation, and progressive cognitive decline, especially in APP/PSEN-associated familial Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: Extracellular accumulations of Abeta, hyperphosphorylation of tau and intracellular neurofibrillary tangle formation have been the hallmarks of Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
evidence.explanation: Supports tau hyperphosphorylation and tangle formation as central Alzheimer disease pathology.

evidence.snippet: Tau protein is the principal component of the neurofibrillary tangles found in Alzheimer's disease (AD), where it is hyperphosphorylated on serine and threonine residues.
evidence.explanation: Identifies hyperphosphorylated tau as the principal neurofibrillary tangle component in Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: Our findings indicate that tau seeding is an early event that occurs well before the appearance of AT8-positive NFT.
evidence.explanation: Places seed-competent soluble tau upstream of the tangles the model names, and the same study shows that blocking Ser214 phosphorylation reduces propagation in mouse primary neurons and seeding in a Drosophila tauopathy, supplying a perturbation arm. Two mouse models plus Drosophila only.

evidence.snippet: Brains of 5×FAD mice deficient for hnRNP R contained less phospho-tau aggregates and amyloid-β plaques in the cortex and hippocampus.
evidence.explanation: Lowering axonal tau — genetically, or with a MAPT antisense oligonucleotide that blocks hnRNP R binding to Mapt — reduces both phospho-tau and amyloid plaque load and prevents neurodegeneration, so the tau-amyloid relation runs in both directions rather than only downstream of amyloid.

evidence.snippet: We found distinct glial responses with increased proinflammatory and decreased homeostatic markers, both in regions with tau tangles (temporal pole) and without overt tau deposits (visual cortex) in demented but not in resilient.
evidence.explanation: In 55 brains matched at Braak III-IV, tangle burden alone does not determine clinical expression: the demented and the cognitively resilient are separated by glial phenotype, including in visual cortex that carries no overt tau at those stages. Refutes tangle burden as a sufficient proximate driver. The design is cross-sectional post-mortem, so the co-factor is an association and its necessity is not established — see the toxic-species knowledge gap.

evidence.snippet: No significant effects were identified in cognitive and functional tests as no dose resulted in a favorable change from the baseline CDR-SB score at week 78 compared to placebo control
evidence.explanation: Lowering extracellular N-terminal tau in 654 participants with early Alzheimer disease did not slow cognitive or functional decline, despite significant target engagement in cerebrospinal fluid. A translational gap for a hypothesis curated as CANONICAL.

evidence.snippet: Based on the results of the prespecified coprimary endpoints, this study was negative. While semorinemab had a significant effect on cognition measured by the ADAS-Cog11, this effect did not extend to improved functional or global outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Second anti-tau antibody failure at a later disease stage; the ADAS-Cog11 signal (42.2% reduction in decline, p = 0.0008) did not carry to the ADCS-ADL coprimary endpoint, MMSE, or CDR-SB, so the trial is negative on its own prespecified terms.

hypotheses/1.description: Tau hyperphosphorylation and aggregation into neurofibrillary tangles are modeled as proximate drivers of neuronal dysfunction, microtubule disruption, neurodegeneration, and clinical progression.

evidence.snippet: Compelling evidence suggests that soluble amyloid-beta (Abeta) and hyperphosphorylated tau serve as toxins in the dysfunction of synaptic plasticity and aberrant neurotransmitter (NT) release at synapses consequently causing a cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence.explanation: Directly supports synaptic dysfunction as a convergence point downstream of amyloid-beta and tau toxicity.

evidence.snippet: Histological studies indicate loss of pyramidal neurones and their synapses in Alzheimer's disease (AD), this together with biochemical evidence suggests presynaptic (and postsynaptic) glutamatergic hypoactivity.
evidence.explanation: Supports loss of synapses and altered neurotransmission in Alzheimer disease.

evidence.snippet: CSF SV2A was lower in AD compared to CN participants. Within the AD group, CSF SV2A was highly correlated with SV2A PET.
evidence.explanation: Concordant fluid and imaging measurement of synaptic density itself rather than of its inferred consequences. Small: 21 participants with early Alzheimer disease and 7 cognitively normal controls, all scanned with carbon-11 UCB-J. Other cerebrospinal-fluid synaptic proteins were higher in Alzheimer disease and unrelated to SV2A PET, which sharpens the specificity of the SV2A measure.

evidence.snippet: Elevated plasma GAP-43 is associated with greater tau aggregation, faster brain atrophy, and accelerated cognitive decline, particularly among cognitively unimpaired individuals.
evidence.explanation: A blood-based marker of the convergence endpoint, in two Chinese cohorts totalling 785 participants with SV2A PET in 85, tau PET in 280 and MRI in 595. Ties synaptic degeneration to tau burden and to subsequent decline, and does so earliest in people who are still cognitively unimpaired.

evidence.snippet: Hp NFT burden strongly correlated with synaptic density, while the ERC showed weaker effects.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the tau-to-synapse arm in living people (94 older adults imaged with carbon-11 UCB-J, carbon-11 PiB and fluorine-18 MK-6240). The companion result — hippocampal synaptic density is similar in controls and in cognitively unimpaired people with biological Alzheimer disease — places synapse loss at the pathology-to-symptom step rather than at pathology onset.

evidence.snippet: A lower ALPS index, indicating greater glymphatic impairment, was significantly associated with reduced synaptic density.
evidence.explanation: First quantitative link in this entry between the separately curated glymphatic_clearance_model and synaptic convergence, in 182 participants. Curate as an association only: the design is cross-sectional with mediation modelling, and DTI-ALPS is an imaging surrogate for glymphatic function rather than a direct measure of it.

evidence.snippet: These bEVs activated microglial Piezo1, consequently precipitating an excessive synaptic pruning process mediated by the C1q-C3 complement pathway.
evidence.explanation: A mechanistically specific peripheral-to-central route into the complement arm of the convergence model: lipopolysaccharide-carrying bacterial extracellular vesicles, elevated in patient plasma, cross the blood-brain barrier and drive C1q-C3 pruning through microglial Piezo1. Single study, so an emerging edge rather than an established one; see the separate complement_synaptic_pruning_model block for the downstream pathway.

evidence.snippet: NDAN subjects displayed a higher spine density in regions distant from Aβ plaques versus AD patients.
evidence.explanation: Convergence on synaptic failure is not obligatory: people with Alzheimer neuropathology who remained non-demented preserve dendritic spine density away from plaques, with a predominance of immature spines and higher Pin1 than in Alzheimer dementia. Human post-mortem DiI labelling and descriptive, so it supports a resilience account rather than a causal edge.

hypotheses/2.description: Amyloid-beta, tau, inflammatory, vascular, oxidative, and infectious stressors converge on synaptic plasticity, neurotransmitter release, and network function, producing cognitive decline.

evidence.snippet: NOD-like receptor (NLR) family, pyrin domain containing 3 and 1 inflammasomes, present in myeloid cells and neurons, respectively, represent key components of the innate immune reaction observed in Alzheimer patient brains.
evidence.explanation: Supports inflammasome-mediated innate immune activation in Alzheimer disease brains.

evidence.snippet: A vicious cycle of inflammation has been formed between Abeta accumulation, activated microglia, and microglial inflammatory mediators, which enhance Abeta deposition and neuroinflammation.
evidence.explanation: Supports a self-reinforcing loop between amyloid-beta deposition and microglial inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Microglia work to reestablish efficiency and stop further degeneration in the early stages of AD but mainly fail in the illness's later phases.
evidence.explanation: Review-level support for treating microglial activation as stage-dependent rather than uniformly protective or uniformly damaging.

evidence.snippet: We show that both TREM2KO and microglial ablation dramatically enhance tau seeding and spreading around plaques.
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the amplification model by showing that TREM2-dependent activated microglia can restrain amyloid-associated tau propagation in mouse models.

evidence.snippet: Microglial INPP5D deficiency cell-autonomously promoted RIPK1-mediated transcriptional induction of diverse LOAD risk genes, proinflammatory cytokines, complements, and ROS mediators
evidence.explanation: Connects a late-onset Alzheimer risk gene to the inflammasome: the INPP5D SH2 domain binds RIPK1 at p-Y383 to suppress its kinase activation, and losing that restraint induces Nlrp3, gasdermin D, complement and Toll-like receptor signalling in microglia. The most mechanistically specific genetic entry point into this hypothesis in the entry.

evidence.snippet: HDAC6 deficiency in 5xFAD mice reduced BACE1 accumulation, Aβ deposition, ASC speck formation, and IL-1β levels, accompanied by improved cognitive performance.
evidence.explanation: A convergence node between amyloid production and inflammasome activation: HDAC6 both stabilises BACE1 by deacetylating K501 and facilitates NLRP3 activation, so removing it lowers amyloid and inflammasome readouts together.

evidence.snippet: transplantation of amyloid-β oligomer-activated microglia into the striatum of naïve mice was sufficient to generate all the features of Alzheimer's disease, including widespread tauopathy and synucleinopathy, gliosis, neuroinflammation, synapse loss, neuronal death, and cognitive and motor deficits
evidence.explanation: The strongest transfer-of-sufficiency result for microglia as an amplifier: the activated cells alone, moved into a naive brain, generate the downstream proteinopathies, and the pathology is abolished by microglial depletion or anti-inflammatory treatment. Mouse only.

evidence.snippet: PS19-TREM2R47H mice had significantly attenuated brain atrophy and synapse loss versus PS19-TREM2CV mice.
evidence.explanation: The mirror image of the Gratuze result above: the same TREM2 risk variant that worsens amyloid-associated tau spread is protective against tau-driven atrophy and synapse loss, with reduced microglial phagocytosis of postsynaptic elements seen in human Alzheimer brain as well. Direct evidence that the microglial contribution changes sign with the pathology present.

evidence.snippet: Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (sTREM2) were increased in preclinical AD.
evidence.explanation: Places glial reactivity in the preclinical phase in humans: 211 cognitively unimpaired participants, with CSF sTREM2 also influencing p-tau181 and neurogranin. Cross-sectional structural equation modelling, so it establishes early timing but not causal direction.

evidence.snippet: Once the Abeta deposition process has started, NSAIDs are no longer effective and may even be detrimental because of their inhibiting activity on activated microglia of the AD brain, which mediates Abeta clearance and activates compensatory hippocampal neurogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Records the failure of long-term NSAID and COX-2 trials, including the negative rofecoxib secondary-prevention and naproxen/celecoxib primary-prevention studies, which refutes a simple anti-inflammatory therapeutic reading of this hypothesis. Graded OTHER: this is a 2009 review, and the stage-dependence account in the quoted sentence is the author's hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result.

hypotheses/3.description: Microglia, astrocytes, complement, and inflammasome pathways are modeled as stage-dependent disease-modifying mechanisms that can respond to amyloid-beta and tau pathology, reinforce amyloid aggregation and inflammatory injury, or restrain amyloid-associated tau spread through protective phagocytic and plaque-barrier functions.

evidence.snippet: Thus, current evidence suggests that BBB dysfunction may causatively and consequently contribute to AD pathogenesis, forming a vicious cycle between brain Abeta accumulation and neurovascular unit impairments during disease progression.
evidence.explanation: Supports a bidirectional causal cycle between blood-brain barrier dysfunction, amyloid-beta accumulation, and neurovascular injury.

evidence.snippet: There is accumulating evidence suggesting that changes in brain perfusion are present long before the clinical symptoms of Alzheimer's disease (AD), perhaps even before amyloid-beta accumulation or brain atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Supports early cerebral perfusion changes as part of the vascular model.

evidence.snippet: we show accelerated pericyte degeneration in AD APOE4 carriers >AD APOE3 carriers >non-AD controls, which correlates with the magnitude of BBB breakdown to immunoglobulin G and fibrin
evidence.explanation: Human post-mortem molecular mechanism for the barrier arm, which this hypothesis otherwise stated only at review level. Cyclophilin A and MMP-9 accumulate in pericytes and endothelial cells in an APOE4-graded fashion; LRP1 was reduced similarly in APOE4 and APOE3 carriers, so the genotype effect runs through the CypA-MMP-9 route rather than through LRP1 abundance.

evidence.snippet: Late-onset AD risk factor Phosphatidylinositol binding clathrin assembly protein (PICALM) is associated with both ABCB1/P-gp and LRP1 representing a functional link and guiding both proteins through the brain endothelium.
evidence.explanation: Routes a common-variant risk locus directly into barrier amyloid-beta efflux by linking the two clearance proteins, which is what makes this model more than a physiological description. Molecular and in vitro, so curated as a mechanism rather than as human causal evidence.

evidence.snippet: A significant increase in soluble Aβ peptides (Aβ40/42) was detected after 1 month of hypoperfusion in the parenchyma in parallel with elevated APP and APP proteolytic products.
evidence.explanation: Interventional evidence that hypoperfusion is upstream of amyloid rather than downstream: bilateral carotid stenosis raises soluble amyloid within a month, with insoluble amyloid, microinfarcts and haemorrhage by three months. Tg-SwDI is a cerebral amyloid angiopathy model, which limits generalisation to parenchymal-predominant human disease.

evidence.snippet: In early stages, tau pathology is linked to hypoperfusion, whereas in established AD, elevated tau levels are paradoxically associated with increased CBF-potentially reflecting compensatory or neuroinflammatory mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: Constrains this hypothesis's assumption of monotonic perfusion decline: across 416 ADNI participants the tau-flow association inverts by stage, negative in mild cognitive impairment and positive in established disease. Cross-sectional, so the stage pattern is between-group rather than within-subject.

hypotheses/4.description: Cerebral blood flow changes, neurovascular-unit injury, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and impaired amyloid-beta clearance are modeled as causal or reinforcing contributors to Alzheimer disease progression.

evidence.snippet: When controlling for age, loss of perivascular AQP4 localization was associated with increased amyloid-β burden
evidence.explanation: Human postmortem dose-response between loss of the glymphatic conduit protein and amyloid burden, the core claim of this hypothesis group.

evidence.snippet: The glymphatic system, which clears the brain of protein waste products, is mostly active during sleep.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the sleep-gated clearance premise that distinguishes this hypothesis group from the other clearance models in this entry.

evidence.snippet: AppNL-F mice showed reductions in glymphatic influx and clearance at 6 months, preceding substantial Aβ plaque deposition.
evidence.explanation: Temporal ordering in a knock-in model that avoids overexpression artefacts: the clearance deficit appears before substantial plaque, and tracks loss of parenchymal border macrophages, which acute intracisternal amyloid-beta alone reproduces in wild-type mice.

evidence.snippet: Four weeks of systemic anti-Aβ antibody treatment efficiently reduced Aβ plaque load and rescued PBMs in some brain regions; however, the treatment did not restore glymphatic function in the AppNL-F model.
evidence.explanation: Curated alongside the item above because it breaks the return arm of the vicious cycle this hypothesis usually assumes: clearing plaque did not restore glymphatic function, and the authors conclude the deficit is not driven by parenchymal plaque load. The two directions of the loop are therefore not symmetric, and the same paper supplies both.

hypotheses/5.description: Failure of the sleep-dependent perivascular (glymphatic) clearance route is modeled as an upstream contributor to amyloid-beta accumulation, acting through reduced CSF-interstitial fluid exchange rather than through transcytotic blood-brain-barrier efflux (vascular_bbb_clearance_model) or intracellular degradation (autophagy_lysosomal_clearance_model). Held as EMERGING because the human evidence is dominated by imaging surrogates and small intrathecal-tracer cohorts, and because the microscopic transport mode underpinning the mechanism is itself contested; see the glymphatic_dysfunction module for the curated controversy.

evidence.snippet: In PS1 null blastocysts, neurons from mice hypomorphic for PS1 or conditionally depleted of PS1, substrate proteolysis and autophagosome clearance during macroautophagy are prevented as a result of a selective impairment of autolysosome acidification and cathepsin activation. These deficits are caused by failed PS1-dependent targeting of the v-ATPase V0a1 subunit to lysosomes.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that PS1 is required for v-ATPase V0a1 targeting to lysosomes; PSEN1 dysfunction therefore directly impairs lysosomal acidification and autophagosome clearance, anchoring the early-onset Alzheimer disease mechanism for this hypothesis group.

evidence.snippet: Mitophagy diminishes insoluble Aβ1-42 and Aβ1-40 and prevents cognitive impairment in an APP/PS1 mouse model through microglial phagocytosis of extracellular Aβ plaques and suppression of neuroinflammation.
evidence.explanation: Supports mitophagy as a mitochondrial quality-control mechanism that can alter amyloid burden, neuroinflammation, and cognitive impairment in an Alzheimer disease mouse model.

evidence.snippet: We found that both gene sets were enriched for genetic Alzheimer's associations: an enrichment score 3.67 standard deviations from the null model (P = 0.00012) was detected for AphagEndoLyso
evidence.explanation: Population-level genetic support for the pathway rather than for a single gene: an 891-gene autophagy and endolysosomal set is enriched for Alzheimer risk variants across three genome-wide association studies with a combined n of 62,415. Pathway-enrichment analysis over published summary statistics, hence COMPUTATIONAL.

evidence.snippet: The APOE locus explained most of the MenDisLyso signal (1.16 standard deviations after APOE removal, P = 0.12), but the AphagEndoLyso signal was less affected (3.35 standard deviations after APOE removal, P = 0.00040).
evidence.explanation: The contrast that makes the enrichment above evidence for this pathway rather than a restatement of APOE: removing the APOE locus collapses the Mendelian-lysosomal-disease subset's signal but leaves the broader autophagy and endolysosomal signal essentially intact.

evidence.snippet: Endosomal alterations were evident in most pyramidal neurons in Alzheimer brain, detectable at early stages of the disease but absent in several other neurodegenerative disorders examined.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that endosomal enlargement (up to 32-fold by individual endosome volume, 2.5-fold per neuron) is both early and disease-specific in human tissue. "Detectable at early stages" in cross-sectional post-mortem material means the change is present early, not that it precedes amyloid or tau.

evidence.snippet: alterations of the endosomal-lysosomal system in neurons of the Alzheimer disease brain, which preceded evident degenerative changes
evidence.explanation: Hydrolase-positive lysosomes accumulate in affected pyramidal neurons before visible degenerative change and far beyond normal aging. This is 1994 morphology in end-stage tissue, so "before overt degeneration" means before degeneration was visible in that neuron, not before disease onset.

evidence.snippet: This interaction impairs dynein recruitment to amphisomes through competitive interruption of dynein-Snapin motor-adaptor coupling, thus immobilizing them in distal axons.
evidence.explanation: A feedback route by which the aggregate impairs its own clearance: amyloid-beta oligomers bind dynein motors and displace the Snapin adaptor, stranding amphisomes in distal axons away from somatic lysosomes. Snapin deletion reproduces the axonal autophagic stress and Snapin overexpression relieves it, supplying the perturbation in both directions.

evidence.snippet: We report that presenilin loss leads to a lower total lysosomal calcium store despite the buildup of lysosomes found in these cells.
evidence.explanation: A second candidate mechanism for the presenilin lysosomal defect alongside the v-ATPase acidification route above, with altered two-pore calcium channel expression. Both come from presenilin-null or presenilin-depleted cells and neither has been weighed against the other in patient-derived cells carrying heterozygous PSEN1 mutations, so they are curated as complementary readings of one genetic lesion rather than as a settled dual mechanism.

hypotheses/6.description: Defective autophagic flux, lysosomal transport, mitophagy, and aggregate clearance are modeled as mechanisms that promote amyloid-beta accumulation, tau accumulation, mitochondrial stress, and downstream cognitive impairment.

evidence.snippet: Integrative single-nucleus analyses resolve direct evidence of HSV-1 expression in RORB+ glutamatergic neurons, implicating viral reactivation in a neuronal population progressively lost during dementia.
evidence.explanation: Supports HSV-1 reactivation in a selectively vulnerable Alzheimer-relevant neuronal population.

evidence.snippet: identifying recurrent herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) reactivation in healthy but not pathological post-mortem human brain tissue
evidence.explanation: Supports the temporal interpretation that HSV-1 reactivation may precede loss of vulnerable neurons rather than simply appear in end-stage pathological tissue.

hypotheses/7.description: Latent HSV-1 reactivation in selectively vulnerable RORB+ glutamatergic neurons is modeled as a possible upstream contributor to neuronal vulnerability and later synaptic-network failure.

evidence.snippet: Strikingly, intercellular tau transmission is almost absent in Arc KO mice.
evidence.explanation: Loss of Arc nearly abolishes neuron-to-neuron tau transmission in mice, supporting Arc-dependent EV packaging as a mechanism of prion-like tau spread.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, Arc levels in brain-derived EVs isolated from human Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains show a strong positive correlation with phosphorylated EV-tau levels.
evidence.explanation: Human AD brain-derived EVs link Arc levels to phosphorylated EV-tau, extending the EV-mediated propagation model to human disease.

evidence.snippet: Endogenous Arc protein is released from neurons in extracellular vesicles that mediate the transfer of Arc mRNA into new target cells
evidence.explanation: Arc self-assembles into virus-like capsids and is released from neurons in EVs that transfer cargo to recipient cells, establishing the biological plausibility for Arc packaging tau into EVs.

evidence.snippet: extracellular vesicles derived from transgenic mice were capable of seeding tau aggregation in a threshold-dependent manner
evidence.explanation: Brain-derived EVs from tau-transgenic mice seed aggregation of monomeric tau in recipient cells, supporting EVs as vehicles for seed-competent tau.

evidence.snippet: tau aggregation was only induced in cells that exhibited permeabilization
evidence.explanation: Endolysosomal permeabilization is the gating step by which internalized exosomal tau seeds escape into the cytosol to template aggregation, supplying the downstream seeding mechanism the model requires.

evidence.snippet: In each case, most tau was free-floating with a small component inside EVs.
evidence.explanation: Across iPSC-neuron media, CSF, and plasma most extracellular tau is free-floating rather than EV-encapsulated, qualifying the quantitative in vivo contribution of the EV-tau route.

evidence.snippet: reductions in both the number of Arc-activated neurons and the levels of Arc mRNA were seen in the neocortices of depositing mice from all transgenic lines (deficits ranging from 14 to 26%)
evidence.explanation: Amyloid-beta deposition suppresses activity-induced Arc expression, so the Arc-dependent EV-tau mechanism may be attenuated precisely in plaque-rich regions (the "Abeta-Arc paradox").

hypotheses/8.description: Cell-to-cell (prion-like) spread of tau pathology is modeled as being driven, in part, by packaging of pathological tau into neuronal extracellular vesicles (EVs). The activity-regulated, capsid-forming neuronal protein Arc binds tau directly and is required for efficient release of tau in EVs; Arc-tau co-packaging seeds tau aggregation in recipient neurons, propagating tangle pathology along connected circuits. In this model EV-tau release is partly protective for the donor neuron (eliminating toxic intracellular tau) but drives intercellular transmission of seed-competent tau.

evidence.snippet: P301S/E4 mice develop markedly more brain atrophy and neuroinflammation than P301S/E2 and P301S/E3 mice, whereas P301S/EKO mice are largely protected from these changes.
evidence.explanation: Isoform-dependent modulation of tau-driven neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation (E4 > E3/E2, and near-protection when APOE is absent) anchors APOE as a cross-pathology risk modifier acting beyond amyloid.

evidence.snippet: The individual had two copies of the APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) mutation, unusually high brain amyloid levels and limited tau and neurodegenerative measurements.
evidence.explanation: A homozygous APOE3 Christchurch carrier resisted autosomal-dominant AD for roughly three decades despite heavy amyloid, dissociating amyloid burden from tau and neurodegeneration and implicating APOE receptor-binding avidity as a protective lever.

hypotheses/9.description: Apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype is modeled as the strongest common-variant modifier of late-onset Alzheimer disease risk, acting upstream of and across multiple pathologies rather than through a single pathway. In proportion to APOE4 gene dose, APOE4 accelerates amyloid-beta seeding/aggregation and impairs its clearance, exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation, promotes glial lipid/cholesterol accumulation, and impairs blood-brain-barrier integrity, whereas APOE2 and the rare protective variants APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) and APOE3 Jacksonville (V236E) blunt these effects. The model predicts that lowering or structurally modifying APOE — especially APOE4 — should ameliorate several AD pathologies simultaneously, motivating APOE-directed therapeutics (ASO knockdown, AAV-APOE2, anti-aggregation small molecules).

evidence.snippet: We found that mice with tauopathy but not those with amyloid deposition developed a unique innate and adaptive immune response and that depletion of microglia or T cells blocked tau-mediated neurodegeneration.
evidence.explanation: Depletion of either microglia or T cells blocks tau-mediated neurodegeneration in a tauopathy model, establishing the adaptive T cell arm as functionally required rather than a bystander.

evidence.snippet: Inhibition of interferon-γ and PDCD1 signalling both significantly ameliorated brain atrophy.
evidence.explanation: IFN-gamma and PD-1 (PDCD1) blockade reduce brain atrophy, nominating specific, druggable nodes within the adaptive-immune neurodegeneration axis.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that tauopathy mice deficient in cDC1 are markedly protected against tau-mediated neurodegeneration and display a selective decrease in brain CD8+ T cell infiltration and glial reactivity.
