evidence.explanation: Provides the important nuance that increased TGF-beta signaling is not detectable in skin or end-stage vascular tissue, so the upregulation is stage-dependent; included to represent the mechanism faithfully.

steps/2.description: GLUT10 deficiency is associated with upregulation of the TGF-beta signaling pathway in the arterial wall, mirroring the dysregulated TGF-beta activity seen in Loeys-Dietz syndrome and the other heritable aortopathies. (Of note, one large series found that skin and end-stage diseased vascular tissue did not show increased TGF-beta signaling, so the upregulation is most evident earlier in the arterial-wall disease process.)

evidence.snippet: Skin and vascular biopsies show fragmented elastic fibers (EF) and increased collagen deposition.
evidence.explanation: This abstract directly supports abnormal elastic-fiber and collagen matrix organization in ATS tissues.

steps/3.description: Histologic studies of skin and vascular tissue show elastic-fiber fragmentation and increased collagen deposition, supporting a structural vessel-wall matrix mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Stenoses, tortuosity, and aneurysm formation are widespread occurrences.
evidence.explanation: This supports the structural vascular consequences downstream of the histologic matrix abnormality.

steps/4.description: Matrix disorganization compromises arterial-wall structure, producing tortuosity with associated stenosis and aneurysm formation across affected large and medium-sized arteries.

evidence.snippet: Arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) is an autosomal recessive connective tissue disease caused by biallelic variants in the SLC2A10 gene (NG_016284.1) and characterised by tortuosity and elongation of the aorta and medium-sized arteries.
evidence.explanation: The defining vascular phenotype is tortuosity and elongation of the aorta and medium-sized arteries.

steps/5.description: Elongation and tortuosity of the aorta and medium-sized arteries are defining vascular features.

evidence.snippet: Stenoses, tortuosity, and aneurysm formation are widespread occurrences.
evidence.explanation: The large review identifies stenosis as part of the widespread vascular phenotype.

steps/6.description: Stenosis can occur in affected arterial beds but appears variable across reported patients.

evidence.snippet: Stenoses, tortuosity, and aneurysm formation are widespread occurrences.
evidence.explanation: The abstract supports stenoses as widespread in ATS, although it does not isolate pulmonary artery stenosis in the quoted sentence.

steps/7.description: Pulmonary artery stenosis is a recognized vascular manifestation within the ATS stenosis spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Severe but rare vascular complications include early and aggressive aortic root aneurysms, neonatal intracranial bleeding, ischemic stroke, and gastric perforation.
evidence.explanation: This supports aortic root aneurysm as a severe ATS complication.

steps/8.description: Aortic root aneurysm is a severe vascular complication requiring early monitoring.

evidence.snippet: Of note, diaphragmatic hernia and infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS) are frequently observed.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports frequent respiratory distress syndrome in ATS.

steps/9.description: Infant respiratory distress syndrome is frequently observed in ATS and should be monitored early in life.

evidence.snippet: Of note, diaphragmatic hernia and infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS) are frequently observed.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports diaphragmatic hernia as a frequent ATS manifestation.

steps/10.description: Diaphragmatic hernia is a recurrent nonvascular ATS feature reported in cohort review.

evidence.snippet: Two patients initially presented with stroke, respectively at age 8 months and 23 years.
evidence.explanation: The clinical series directly documents stroke as an initial presentation at two distinct ages.

steps/11.description: Ischemic stroke is a severe but uncommon vascular complication and has been reported as an initial presentation in both infancy and adulthood.

evidence.snippet: GLUT10 deficiency is associated with upregulation of the TGFbeta pathway in the arterial wall
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery paper directly links GLUT10 loss to arterial-wall TGF-beta pathway upregulation on this edge.

edges/1.description: GLUT10 deficiency is associated with upregulation of the TGF-beta pathway in the arterial wall, the conserved aortopathy hub also seen in Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Skin and vascular biopsies show fragmented elastic fibers (EF) and increased collagen deposition.
evidence.explanation: SLC2A10-mutated ATS tissues show the fragmented elastic fiber and increased collagen matrix phenotype on this edge.

edges/2.description: SLC2A10/GLUT10 loss is linked to the abnormal elastic-fiber and collagen matrix phenotype.

evidence.snippet: owing to disruption of elastic fibers in the medial layer of the arterial wall
evidence.explanation: ATS features disruption of medial elastic fibers; the causal direction from TGF-beta dysregulation to elastic-fiber fragmentation is inferred by analogy to Loeys-Dietz, so the edge is PARTIAL.

A GJB3 variant alone is not a confirmed molecular diagnosis of hearing loss. Missense and truncating alleles have been reported, but variant-specific functional effects do not resolve the gene-disease dispute. The common screening allele p.Arg180* was classified VUS in the 2023 case-control paper. GJB2/SLC26A4 co-occurrence requires independent assessment of pathogenicity, zygosity and phase. open_questions/0.rationale: The cited cell studies measure selected variant effects, while the cited in-vivo study tests a homozygous null. open_questions/1.rationale: The null study reports normal adult skin and inner ear, but dominant EKV variants have diverse cellular effects. A null does not test every dominant variant mechanism in either organ. edges/2.description: Repeated avian antigen exposure initiates immune-mediated inflammation in the small airways, alveoli, and interstitium.

evidence.snippet: Both groups presented increases in resident monocytes, interstitial macrophages and type 2 dendritic cells (DCs), but also reductions in inflammatory monocytes, alveolar macrophages and tolerogenic DCs compared with their control groups.
evidence.explanation: The same pigeon-serum model places myeloid-cell remodeling in the immune-response branch.

edges/3.description: Monocyte, macrophage, and dendritic-cell remodeling is modeled upstream of the stage-dependent T-cell cytokine shift.

evidence.snippet: Both groups presented increases in resident monocytes, interstitial macrophages and type 2 dendritic cells (DCs), but also reductions in inflammatory monocytes, alveolar macrophages and tolerogenic DCs compared with their control groups. Group 1 had increased levels of eosinophils and T cells with reductions in neutrophils and B cells, while Group 2 showed high levels of B cells. Both groups exhibited increases in Th1 and Th2 cytokines. Group 2 also showed increased levels of IL-23, a Th17 cytokine.
evidence.explanation: The pigeon-serum model co-documents reduced myeloid and tolerogenic populations with Th1/Th2 cytokine increases and a later IL-23/Th17 signal. The indirect edge models this association, not a proven direct mechanism.

edges/4.description: Reduced inflammatory monocytes, alveolar macrophages, and tolerogenic dendritic cells are modeled as part of the myeloid-cell remodeling upstream of the stage-dependent cytokine shift.

evidence.snippet: Both groups exhibited increases in Th1 and Th2 cytokines. Group 2 also showed increased levels of IL-23, a Th17 cytokine. Increased levels of neutrophils, eosinophils and lymphocytes were observed in BAL samples of both groups compared with controls.
evidence.explanation: Cytokine and BAL inflammatory-cell changes co-occur in the bird-antigen model.

edges/5.description: The stage-dependent T-cell cytokine program participates in the inflammatory lung response measured in the pigeon-serum model.

evidence.snippet: A 57-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because of cough and low-grade fever for 2 months and shortness of breath for 2 weeks.
evidence.explanation: A biopsy-confirmed BFL case co-documents inflammatory lung disease and shortness of breath.

evidence.snippet: A 47-year-old woman, without significant past medical history, presented an acute dyspnea with hypoxia, marked pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and signs of right heart failure.

evidence.snippet: In sensitized individuals, the immune reaction after exposure to an antigen appears to consist of both humoral (i.e., antigen-specific IgG antibodies) and T-helper cell type 1 (Th1) cellular immune responses (83, 88). These responses lead to a predominantly lymphocytic inflammatory pattern and granulomatous inflammation (11, 75, 89).

edges/12.description: Antigen-specific humoral responses participate with T-cell responses in lymphocytic and granulomatous lung inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Trajectory analyses demonstrate that S100Ahi classical monocytes differentiate into SPP1hi lung macrophages associated with fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: The trajectory directly supports this transition in non-antigen-stratified fibrotic HP.

evidence.snippet: Compared with both control subjects and IPF, cells from patients with FHP are significantly enriched in GZMhi cytotoxic T cells. These cells exhibit TF activities indicative of TGFβ and TNFα and NFκB pathways.

evidence.snippet: immune-mediated interstitial lung disease (ILD) resulting from the repeated inhalation of avian proteins found in bird droppings, feathers, and serum.

edges/18.description: Keeping birds, or using feather products, delivers avian protein to the airway repeatedly over months to years, and it is the repetition rather than any single exposure that produces disease.

evidence.snippet: Complete antigen avoidance is the mainstay of treatment.

evidence.snippet: FVC% and DLCO% increased in nfHP patients after exposure avoidance, while a positive numerical trend was seen for FVC% after exposure avoidance in fHP patients (p = 0.15).
evidence.explanation: Retrospective data support lung-function improvement in nonfibrotic HP but leave benefit in fibrotic HP uncertain.

evidence.snippet: In our retrospective cohort, 136 patients met high or definite probability of HP and were included in the analysis. Median transplant-free survival was better in patients with antigen identified on clinical history alone than patients without identified antigen. Feather exposure was associated with improved TFS compared to patients without antigen identified; there was no difference in TFS between patients with feather exposure and either mold or live bird exposure.
evidence.explanation: The cohort supports systematic identification of live-bird and feather exposures but does not directly test avoidance.

treatments/0.description: Identify and remove the inciting avian source. Depending on the exposure, this can require removing birds, avoiding feather/down products, remediating contaminated material, and preventing indirect occupational or household exposure. Benefit is clearest in nonfibrotic HP; established fibrosis may continue to progress.

evidence.snippet: Complete antigen avoidance is the mainstay of treatment.

evidence.snippet: Although nfHP patients showed FVC% and DLCO% increase after corticosteroid initiation, no therapeutic effect was seen in fHP patients.

evidence.snippet: The patient was diagnosed with BFL and treated with a tapering regimen of oral corticosteroids, starting at 40 mg/day.

treatments/1.description: Systemic glucocorticoids such as prednisone are used for clinically significant inflammatory/nonfibrotic HP. Observational evidence does not establish a survival benefit, and the same cohort found no therapeutic effect in fibrotic HP.

evidence.snippet: Although nfHP patients showed FVC% and DLCO% increase after corticosteroid initiation, no therapeutic effect was seen in fHP patients.
evidence.explanation: Phenotype-stratified observational data support an anti-inflammatory benefit only in nonfibrotic HP.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with either MMF or AZA was not associated with improved FVC (0.5% at 1 year; P = .46) but was associated with a statistically significant improvement in Dlco of 4.2% (P < .001) after 1 year of treatment.
evidence.explanation: The retrospective study reports the limited lung-function outcome and calls for prospective trials.

treatments/2.description: Mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine may be used as steroid-sparing immunosuppression in chronic HP. Retrospective data found improved DLCO but no significant FVC improvement; prospective validation is lacking.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with either MMF or AZA was not associated with improved FVC (0.5% at 1 year; P = .46) but was associated with a statistically significant improvement in Dlco of 4.2% (P < .001) after 1 year of treatment.

evidence.snippet: The INBUILD trial was not designed or powered to provide evidence for a benefit of nintedanib in specific diagnostic subgroups. However, its results suggest that nintedanib reduces the rate of ILD progression, as measured by FVC decline, in patients who have a chronic fibrosing ILD and progressive phenotype, irrespective of the underlying ILD diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: The randomized trial supports the broader progressive-fibrosing-ILD indication while preserving subgroup uncertainty.

treatments/3.description: Nintedanib reduces FVC decline across progressive fibrosing ILDs. The INBUILD analysis included chronic HP, but it was not powered to prove benefit within the HP subgroup and did not stratify bird-related disease.

evidence.snippet: The trial was underpowered to detect a difference in the primary end point. Pirfenidone was found to be safe and improved PFS in patients with FHP.
evidence.explanation: The published trial reports a favorable secondary endpoint while explicitly acknowledging inadequate power for the primary endpoint.

evidence.snippet: The use of pirfenidone has not been approved for the treatment of FHP. It is considered experimental treatment in this study.
evidence.explanation: The trial registry explicitly identifies pirfenidone as experimental for fibrotic HP.

treatments/4.description: A small randomized trial in progressive fibrotic HP was interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic and underpowered for its primary FVC endpoint. Pirfenidone improved a secondary progression-free-survival endpoint but remains investigational for this indication.

evidence.snippet: It was emphasized that a positive serum IgG result does not mean that the exposure is the cause of the lung condition; it only indicates that the patient has likely been exposed to a potential cause of HP at some point in his or her life
evidence.explanation: The guideline directly separates exposure evidence from disease causation.

open_questions/0.rationale: Bird-specific antibodies document sensitization and likely exposure. They do not establish that the exposure caused the ILD, and test panels and thresholds are not standardized internationally. evidence.snippet: Single-cell 5' RNA sequencing was conducted on peripheral blood mononuclear cells and BAL cells obtained from 45 patients with FHP, 63 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), 4 patients with nonfibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and 36 healthy control subjects in the United States and Mexico.
evidence.explanation: The cohort is defined at HP phenotype level without an avian-antigen subgroup.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrated that suppressing toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) and nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) could attenuate MMP14 expression and exosome secretion in macrophages stimulation with SR-Ag.
evidence.explanation: The perturbation is performed in an SR-antigen rather than avian-antigen model.

open_questions/1.rationale: The single-cell cohorts are not stratified by inciting antigen, while the MMP14 perturbation study uses a non-avian SR-antigen mouse model. These results are retained as partial shared-HP evidence, not as established bird-specific mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: MUC5B rs35705950 and three neighboring TOLLIP variants (rs3750920, rs111521887, and rs5743894) were associated with increased susceptibility to fHP.

open_questions/2.rationale: The available association is for fibrotic HP and is non-causal. MUC5B and TOLLIP are therefore not represented as causal BFL genes; antigen-stratified replication and functional evidence would be needed.

evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the functional interdependence of COA3 and COX14 in the COX1-coupling assembly arm.

steps/1.description: Biallelic COA3 variants reduce the steady-state level of COA3, a small inner membrane Complex IV assembly factor. COA3 normally stabilizes the mtDNA-encoded core catalytic subunit COX1 and couples its synthesis with holoenzyme assembly. Loss of COA3 leaves COX1 destabilized and stalls an early COX assembly intermediate, so the mature enzyme fails to form and an isolated Complex IV biogenesis failure results. COA3 and COX14 are mutually interdependent — each is undetectable when the other is lost — situating this lesion within the COX1-coupling arm of the assembly pathway.

evidence.snippet: analysis showed an almost complete lack of COX assembly in subject fibroblasts, consistent with the very low enzymatic activity
evidence.explanation: Very low COX enzymatic activity establishes the functional terminal-electron-transfer deficit downstream of failed assembly.

steps/2.description: The near-absence of assembled Complex IV blocks electron transfer from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen and the coupled proton pumping, collapsing oxidative ATP synthesis. In COA3-deficient patient fibroblasts the COX enzymatic activity is very low, consistent with the assembly defect.

evidence.snippet: CODAS and CDH variants are hypothesized to cause loss-of-function effects, while NDD variants may act through dominant-negative mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: The cross-phenotype analysis proposes different mechanisms; it does not functionally establish a uniform null mechanism for CODAS.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that in CODAS syndrome, Lon-mediated degradation of some but not all protein substrates is impaired.

steps/1.description: Biallelic LONP1 variants impair selected functions of the mitochondrial Lon protease. The four initial CODAS missense proteins retain substrate-dependent residual activity, and the p.Arg721Gly founder variant has impaired oligomer assembly and ATP-dependent proteolysis. These findings do not imply complete loss of Lon protein or identical biochemical defects for every allele.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that in CODAS syndrome, Lon-mediated degradation of some but not all protein substrates is impaired.
evidence.explanation: Purified-protein assays compare StAR and TFAM, demonstrating substrate-selective impairment.

steps/2.description: CODAS-associated Lon proteins show substrate-specific proteolytic defects. Recombinant p.Pro676Ser and p.Arg721Gly degrade StAR less effectively while retaining TFAM degradation. Patient-derived p.Arg721Gly lymphoblastoid cells have altered handling of MT-CO2 and PDK4; degradation and chaperone contributions need to be distinguished.

evidence.snippet: In CODAS cells, we observed insolubility and aggregation of MT-CO2 (Figure 7A) but not MT-CO1, which is similarly hydrophobic.
evidence.explanation: MT-CO2 insolubility was measured in EBV-transformed patient lymphoblastoid cells. Direct proteolysis of purified MT-CO2 was not tested; defective degradation and defective assembly remain alternatives.

evidence.snippet: When cells were extracted with this strong denaturant, similar abundances of MT-CO2 were observed in proband and parental LCLs.
evidence.explanation: Urea extraction recovers MT-CO2, distinguishing solubility from total abundance.

steps/3.description: In p.Arg721Gly patient lymphoblastoid cells, MT-CO2 is poorly recovered with detergent but becomes recoverable with urea, supporting aggregation rather than simple loss of total protein. Lon knockdown in other cell lines increases MT-CO2 abundance. Impaired degradation or chaperone-mediated complex IV assembly are proposed explanations; direct cleavage of purified MT-CO2 was not measured.

evidence.snippet: R721G did not degrade the endogenous mitochondrial Lon substrate pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase isoform 4 (PDK4) effectively like WT hLon.
evidence.explanation: Purified human Lon was tested against recombinant murine PDK4; this is a biochemical assay, not an animal treatment.

evidence.snippet: Comparing the signal intensities of PDK4/GAPDH in cell lysates containing WT versus R721G hLon before the addition of CHX indicates that there is 2.2-fold more PDK4 in cells expressing R721G than WT hLon (Fig. 5A).
evidence.explanation: Steady-state protein abundance in the patient-derived line; this is not a measurement of PDK4 catalytic activity.

steps/4.description: Recombinant R721G Lon poorly degrades PDK4. In a patient-derived R721G lymphoblastoid line, PDK4 abundance is higher and its persistence after protein synthesis inhibition is greater than in a wild-type comparison line. PDH binding protects PDK4 from proteolysis in reconstituted assays. These experiments establish altered substrate handling, without demonstrating PDH inhibition or altered metabolic flux in CODAS tissues.

evidence.snippet: Transmission electron microscopy of proband LCLs revealed enlarged mitochondria with swollen intra- or intercristal compartments, uniform vesicular structures, and electron-dense intramitochondrial inclusions (Figures 6A and 6C), suggestive of abnormal inner-membrane topology.
evidence.explanation: Direct ultrastructural observation in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: Conversely, ultrastructural analysis of heterozygous enterocytes evidenced profound morphological alterations of mitochondria, which appeared increased in number, swollen and larger, with a lower complexity.
evidence.explanation: Reduced Lonp1 dosage in mice produces comparable mitochondrial swelling in vivo.

steps/5.description: EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid cells from p.Arg721Gly homozygotes contain enlarged mitochondria with swollen cristae, vesicular structures and electron-dense inclusions. Lonp1 heterozygous-null mouse enterocytes show partially similar changes; this does not establish the same pathology in every clinically affected CODAS tissue.

evidence.snippet: Normalized basal mitochondrial oxygen consumption and ATP-linked respiration were similar in proband and parental cells, but CODAS cells had significantly lower SRC when mitochondrial membrane potential was dissipated by the uncoupler FCCP (Figure 7C).
evidence.explanation: Specifies which respiratory measure changes in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: From the functional point of view, mitochondria from heterozygous MEF showed a lower oxygen consumption rate in basal conditions, either in the presence of glucose or galactose, and a reduced expression of mitochondrial complexes than wild type.
evidence.explanation: Reduced Lonp1 dosage lowers respiration in mouse cells.

steps/6.description: p.Arg721Gly patient lymphoblastoid cells have reduced spare respiratory capacity after FCCP uncoupling, while normalized basal oxygen consumption and ATP-linked respiration are similar to parental cells. Heterozygous-null mouse fibroblasts instead show reduced basal oxygen consumption, illustrating model-dependent effects.

steps/4.description: The core molecular lesion in RNF216-, OTUD4-, and STUB1/CHIP-related Gordon Holmes syndrome is disruption of the ubiquitin-proteasome system and protein quality control. RNF216 is an RBR/RING-class E3 ubiquitin ligase that attaches ubiquitin to substrates (including upstream activators of NF-kB signaling), marking them for proteasome-mediated degradation; OTUD4 is a partnering deubiquitinase. STUB1 encodes CHIP, a co-chaperone E3 ligase central to protein quality control. Biallelic loss-of-function (or loss of critical E3 activity) in these enzymes impairs ubiquitination and turnover of client proteins. The digenic RNF216/OTUD4 form reflects an epistatic interaction within a shared pathway.

steps/5.description: A genetically distinct arm of the ataxia-hypogonadism continuum is caused by biallelic PNPLA6 variants. PNPLA6 encodes neuropathy target esterase (NTE), an endoplasmic-reticulum-localized lysophospholipase regulating membrane phospholipid homeostasis. PNPLA6 disorders span Boucher-Neuhauser syndrome (ataxia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, chorioretinal dystrophy), Gordon Holmes syndrome, spastic paraplegia type 39, Oliver-McFarlane, and Laurence-Moon syndromes, with age-dependent, multisystem manifestations affecting cerebellum, retina, peripheral nerves, and endocrine axes.

steps/6.description: Progressive loss of Purkinje cells and cerebellar pathway neurons underlies the ataxia, while hippocampal and cortical neuronal loss contributes to cognitive decline and dementia. Cerebellar atrophy and subcortical cerebral white-matter hyperintensities are characteristic imaging correlates. In an Rnf216 knockout mouse model, age- and sex-dependent microglial alterations in hippocampus and cortex accompany learning impairments, suggesting microglial activation/neuroinflammation as a candidate intermediate.

steps/7.description: Central (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism arises from dysfunction at the hypothalamic GnRH-neuron and pituitary gonadotrope levels. The result is delayed/absent puberty, lack of secondary sexual characteristics, and low gonadotropins and sex steroids.

steps/1.description: Chronic inflammation of the biliary epithelium from conditions such as primary sclerosing cholangitis, hepatolithiasis, or liver fluke infection leads to repeated cycles of injury and repair. Persistent cholestasis and bile acid exposure cause oxidative stress and DNA damage in cholangiocytes, promoting malignant transformation. In Western countries about 50% of cases are diagnosed without any identifiable risk factor.

evidence.snippet: We identified 6 distinct fibroblast subsets, of which the majority were CD146-positive vascular cancer-associated fibroblasts (vCAFs), with highly expressed microvasculature signatures and high levels of interleukin (IL)-6.

steps/2.description: CCA is characterized by a prominent desmoplastic stroma comprising cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), extracellular matrix proteins, and inflammatory cells. Single-cell analysis identified six distinct fibroblast subsets, with vascular CAFs (vCAFs) dominant and expressing high levels of IL-6. Matricellular glycoproteins including periostin, osteopontin, and tenascin-C promote proliferation, invasion, EMT, and immune evasion. The dense stroma limits immune cell infiltration and drug delivery.

evidence.snippet: tumor-infiltrating CD4 regulatory T cells exhibited highly immunosuppressive characteristics

evidence.snippet: ICC displayed an inflamed immunophenotype with an enrichment of IFN-related pathways and high expression of LGALS1 in activated regulatory T cells
evidence.explanation: T cell landscape mapping showing LGALS1-expressing Tregs contribute to immunosuppression in iCCA.

steps/3.description: The CCA microenvironment is enriched with tumor-associated macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and regulatory T cells with highly immunosuppressive characteristics. PD-L1 expression is variable. The dense desmoplastic stroma acts as a physical barrier to T cell infiltration. Tumor-infiltrating B cells are scarce, immature, and immunosuppressive.

evidence.snippet: We provide a highly representative cartography of the genomic landscape of iCCA and outline the co-mutational spectra of seven therapeutically relevant oncogenic driver genes: IDH1/2, FGFR2, ERBB2, BRAF, MDM2, BRCA1/2, MET and KRASG12C.
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive genomic profiling of iCCA confirming the diverse mutational landscape with multiple actionable driver genes.

evidence.snippet: KRAS and PIK3CA mutations were more frequent in the large duct type, while IDH1/2 mutations and FGFR2 fusions were more common in the small duct type.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 10-16% of iCCA cases harbor FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, defining a distinct molecular subtype characterized by sensitivity to FGFR-targeted therapies.

steps/4.description: CCA harbors a diverse mutational landscape. Common alterations include IDH1/2 mutations (10-20% of iCCA), FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements (10-16% of iCCA), TP53 mutations, KRAS mutations, ARID1A mutations, BAP1 loss, and PBRM1 mutations. The mutational profile differs by anatomic and pathologic subtype, with IDH and FGFR alterations enriched in small duct iCCA and KRAS mutations more common in large duct and extrahepatic subtypes.

evidence.snippet: We observed a negative selection of RTK/RAS/ERK pathway co-alterations, and an enrichment of epigenetic modifiers such as ARID1A and BAP1 in patients with IDH1/2 and FGFR2 alterations.

evidence.explanation: Establishes both the age effect and the early onset during treatment.

evidence.snippet: Key consonants are heard at high frequencies (4 kHz through 8 kHz), and so their loss is debilitating, particularly in young children in whom speech has not yet developed
evidence.explanation: Source for the consonant point in this node's description, and for why a high-frequency loss matters more in a young child than its audiometric size suggests.

steps/11.description: Permanent high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. It is the toxicity with the worst long-term arithmetic, because it does not recover and because the frequencies lost first carry the consonants. In children under five the cumulative incidence reaches 75 percent at three years and it appears early in treatment.

evidence.snippet: Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent that induces peripheral neuropathy in 30% of patients.
evidence.explanation: Gives the proportion affected, stated as background in the cited paper.

evidence.snippet: Patients with cisplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy experience sensory loss, often accompanied by pain, starting in the distal extremities.
evidence.explanation: Gives the distribution and character of the deficit.

evidence.snippet: This phenomenon, commonly known as “coasting,” is observed exclusively in platinum-based chemotherapy and suggests that there is ongoing neuronal damage after discontinuing cisplatin.
evidence.explanation: Establishes coasting and its restriction to the platinum drugs, which is the feature this node is built around.

steps/12.description: Distal sensory loss, often painful, in about 30 percent of treated patients. Its distinguishing feature is coasting - the neuropathy keeps worsening for weeks to months after the drug is stopped, which is reported only for the platinum drugs.

evidence.snippet: One of the most common side effects of cisplatin is chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), affecting nearly 90% of patients who receive high-dose cisplatin without antiemetic treatment
evidence.explanation: Gives the proportion affected in the absence of prophylaxis, which is the claim in this node's description.

steps/13.description: Cisplatin is the archetypal highly emetogenic drug: without antiemetic prophylaxis it makes nearly nine in ten patients vomit. This arm is separated from the four injury arms because it is not a cytotoxic lesion - nothing dies - and because it is the toxicity that modern prophylaxis has most changed.

evidence.snippet: One of the most common side effects of cisplatin is chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), affecting nearly 90% of patients who receive high-dose cisplatin without antiemetic treatment
evidence.explanation: Establishes nausea as part of the near-universal untreated emetogenic response. No frequency band is asserted, because the figure quoted is the untreated rate and patients now receive prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: One of the most common side effects of cisplatin is chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV), affecting nearly 90% of patients who receive high-dose cisplatin without antiemetic treatment
evidence.explanation: Establishes vomiting as part of the same untreated response, with the same caveat about prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: Administration of cisplatin, a common chemotherapeutic drug, has an inevitable side effect of sensorineural hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the phenotype and its sensorineural character.

evidence.snippet: Three years after initiating therapy, the cumulative incidence of CIHL was highest in patients aged ≤5 years (75%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 66%-84%)
evidence.explanation: Gives a cumulative incidence in the highest-risk age group. No frequency band is asserted on this phenotype, because the incidence is strongly age-dependent - 75 percent under five against 48 percent over five in the same cohort - and a single band would misrepresent that.

steps/16.description: Permanent, bilateral, high-frequency first. The frequencies lost earliest are the ones carrying consonants, which is why even a mild loss matters in a child who has not finished learning to speak.

evidence.snippet: The main etiologies are stria vascularis injury, spiral ganglion degeneration, and hair cell death.
evidence.explanation: Supports the cochlear lesions underlying this symptom. The cited sentence names the cochlear pathology rather than tinnitus itself, and this entry does not claim a frequency for it.

evidence.snippet: The uptake of cisplatin in renal tubular cells is high, leading to cisplatin accumulation and tubular cell injury and death, culminating in acute renal failure.
evidence.explanation: States the renal endpoint. This is a mechanistic study in cells and mice, not a clinical incidence series.

evidence.snippet: Cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity (CIN) limits the use of this drug and affects up to 20% of patients.
evidence.explanation: Gives a clinical proportion affected. "Up to 20 percent" is an upper bound stated as background in a systematic review, so no frequency band is asserted from it.

steps/18.description: Falling filtration with tubular injury, typically several days after a dose, and usually reversible.

evidence.snippet: side effects in normal tissues and organs, notably nephrotoxicity in the kidneys, limit the use of cisplatin and related platinum-based therapeutics
evidence.explanation: Supports the renal toxicity this electrolyte disturbance belongs to. The cited sentence does not name magnesium wasting specifically, and the persistence claim in the description is not asserted by this source.

steps/19.description: Renal magnesium wasting, from injury to the tubular segments that reabsorb it. It often outlasts the fall in filtration and can persist long after treatment.

evidence.snippet: Patients with cisplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy experience sensory loss, often accompanied by pain, starting in the distal extremities.
evidence.explanation: Gives the distribution and character of the deficit.

evidence.snippet: This phenomenon, commonly known as “coasting,” is observed exclusively in platinum-based chemotherapy and suggests that there is ongoing neuronal damage after discontinuing cisplatin.
evidence.explanation: Supports the post-treatment worsening named in the description.

steps/20.description: Distal sensory loss, often painful, which can continue to worsen after the drug is stopped.

evidence.snippet: its clinical utility is hampered by its dose-limiting toxicities, including nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity, and myelosuppression
evidence.explanation: Supports the marrow toxicity this cytopenia belongs to. The cited sentence names myelosuppression, not the individual lineage.

evidence.snippet: its clinical utility is hampered by its dose-limiting toxicities, including nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity, and myelosuppression
evidence.explanation: Supports the marrow toxicity this cytopenia belongs to, at the level of myelosuppression rather than the individual lineage.

evidence.snippet: its clinical utility is hampered by its dose-limiting toxicities, including nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity, and myelosuppression
evidence.explanation: Supports the marrow toxicity this cytopenia belongs to, at the level of myelosuppression rather than the individual lineage.

evidence.snippet: The uptake of cisplatin in renal tubular cells is high, leading to cisplatin accumulation and tubular cell injury and death, culminating in acute renal failure.
evidence.explanation: States the uptake-to-accumulation-to-injury sequence this edge asserts, in the renal arm.

edges/0.description: Uptake delivers platinum to intracellular DNA. Everything downstream follows from the adducts; this edge is what makes uptake rate-limiting.

edges/1.description: Administration of cisplatin is also followed by severe emesis. The edge is recorded as indirect with unknown intermediates on purpose: unlike the four injury arms, this one is not established here as running through OCT2 or Ctr1 uptake into the affected tissue, and the sources cited in this entry do not supply the route.

edges/2.description: Adduct formation is accompanied by reactive oxygen species generation and mitochondrial damage, which is the arm that reaches post-mitotic cells.

edges/3.description: Unrepaired adducts activate the damage response and drive apoptosis.

edges/4.description: Oxidative and mitochondrial injury converge on the same apoptotic endpoint as the direct DNA damage arm.

edges/5.description: In dorsal root ganglion neurons the mitochondrial arm is not merely accompanying injury; platinum binds mitochondrial DNA directly.

edges/6.description: The renal arm. Tubular epithelium can regenerate, which is why this toxicity is often reversible where the cochlear one is not.

edges/7.description: The cochlear arm. Mammalian hair cells do not regenerate, so this cell death is the permanent one.

edges/8.description: The marrow arm. Progenitors are hit for the ordinary antiproliferative reason rather than for any transporter-specific one.

edges/9.description: The neural arm. Sensory neurons are post-mitotic and irreplaceable, so this arm shares the cochlear arm's arithmetic rather than the marrow's.

evidence.snippet: The uptake of cisplatin in renal tubular cells is high, leading to cisplatin accumulation and tubular cell injury and death, culminating in acute renal failure.
evidence.explanation: States tubular cell death culminating in acute renal failure, which is this edge.

edges/10.description: Loss of tubular epithelium produces the fall in filtration.

edges/11.description: The renal arm's clinical readout.

edges/12.description: Magnesium wasting from injury to the reabsorbing tubular segments, alongside the fall in filtration.

evidence.snippet: Cisplatin chemotherapy and surgery are effective treatments for children with standard-risk hepatoblastoma but may cause considerable and irreversible hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the irreversibility this edge asserts. The usual explanation - that mammalian cochlear hair cells are not regenerated - is not stated by the sources cited in this entry, so it is not asserted here.

edges/13.description: Hair cell loss gives permanent hearing loss, and the permanence is what separates this arm from the renal one, where the epithelium regenerates.

edges/14.description: The cochlear arm's clinical readout.

edges/15.description: Accompanies the hearing loss from the same cochlear injury.

evidence.snippet: CIPN is characterized by a substantial loss of primary afferent sensory axonal fibers leading to sensory disturbances in patients.
evidence.explanation: Names the fibre loss that stands between neuron injury and symptoms. The source covers chemotherapy-induced neuropathy across several drug classes, so this supports the shared endpoint rather than a cisplatin-specific route.

edges/16.description: Loss and dysfunction of sensory neurons produces the clinical neuropathy. The intermediate is loss of primary afferent sensory axonal fibres.

edges/17.description: Mitochondrial failure in sensory neurons contributes to the neuropathy on a slower clock than the nuclear-DNA route, and continues after dosing stops.

edges/19.description: Progenitor arrest and death reduce marrow output.

edges/23.description: The symptom that has responded least to modern prophylaxis.

edges/24.description: The symptom that prophylaxis controls best.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, an ACYP2 variant has been associated with ototoxicity in both children and adults, whereas TPMT variants are relevant in children.
evidence.explanation: Names ACYP2 as associated in both age groups, which is the claim curated here.

evidence.snippet: Considering GRADE criteria, genetic variants in 2 genes were strongly (ie, odds ratios ≥3) and consistently (ie, replication in ≥3 independent populations) predictive of cisplatin-induced ototoxicity.
evidence.explanation: Gives the evidence bar - odds ratio at least 3, replicated in at least three populations - that this gene clears and that most candidate loci do not.

genes/0.notes: One of only two genes reaching the strong-and-replicated tier in the Canadian Pharmacogenomics Network for Drug Safety systematic review, which graded 40 reports across 47 independent populations and 24 genes. The ACYP2 association holds in both children and adults.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, an ACYP2 variant has been associated with ototoxicity in both children and adults, whereas TPMT variants are relevant in children.
evidence.explanation: Names TPMT and restricts its relevance to children, which is the limit recorded in the notes.

evidence.snippet: Genetic variation in ACYP2 and TPMT may be helpful in predicting patients at the highest risk of developing cisplatin-induced ototoxicity.
evidence.explanation: The review's own conclusion, naming these two genes and no others as potentially clinically useful predictors.

genes/1.notes: The second gene reaching the strong-and-replicated tier. The association is reported as relevant in children; the review does not extend it to adults, and this entry does not either.

evidence.snippet: Encouraging evidence for associations involving several other genes also exists; however, further research is necessary to determine potential clinical relevance.
evidence.explanation: Supports the disputed grading. The sentence covers the non-top-tier genes as a class; it does not name COMT, and the placement of COMT in that class rather than the top tier follows from the same review naming only ACYP2 and TPMT as strong.

genes/2.notes: Curated deliberately as DISPUTED rather than SUSCEPTIBILITY. COMT is a frequently cited candidate ototoxicity locus and is easy to record as established. The systematic review that graded the field placed only ACYP2 and TPMT in the strong-and-replicated tier and assigned everything else to a further-research category. Recording COMT at the same strength as those two would misstate the evidence.

evidence.snippet: The identified data reconfirmed that no agents are recommended for the prevention of CIPN.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the surrounding negative: nothing prevents this neuropathy, so duloxetine's role is confined to treating pain once it exists. Carried on this treatment because it is what bounds the claim.

treatments/0.description: The only agent ASCO supports for established painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, and the guideline is careful to say the benefit is limited. It treats the pain, not the neuropathy - nothing regrows the sensory neurons - which is why it sits on the outcome node rather than upstream.

evidence.snippet: Duloxetine is the only agent that has appropriate evidence to support its use for patients with established painful CIPN.
evidence.explanation: The guideline's single positive recommendation for established CIPN.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Reduces painful symptoms of established neuropathy. Recorded as MODULATES because the guideline supports symptom benefit and does not claim reversal of the underlying nerve injury.

evidence.snippet: The use of acetyl-l-carnitine for the prevention of CIPN in patients with cancer should be discouraged.
evidence.explanation: An explicit negative recommendation, curated as REFUTE against the claim that this agent prevents the neuropathy.

treatments/1.description: Curated as a treatment that does not work. ASCO discourages its use for prevention of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. It is recorded here so the entry answers the question a clinician actually asks - not only what to give, but what to stop giving.

treatments/2.description: Where no drug prevents the neuropathy, the remaining lever is the cisplatin dose itself - delaying, reducing, substituting or stopping. This acts on the exposure rather than on any downstream injury, and it is what makes the neuropathy dose-limiting in practice.

evidence.snippet: clinicians should assess the appropriateness of dose delaying, dose reduction, substitutions, or stopping chemotherapy in patients who develop intolerable neuropathy and/or functional impairment
evidence.explanation: The guideline's recommendation for what to do when the neuropathy becomes intolerable, which is an intervention on exposure rather than on injury.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Reducing or stopping the drug reduces the platinum delivered to the transporter-expressing tissues at the head of every arm in this entry.

evidence.snippet: The addition of sodium thiosulfate, administered 6 hours after cisplatin chemotherapy, resulted in a lower incidence of cisplatin-induced hearing loss among children with standard-risk hepatoblastoma, without jeopardizing overall or event-free survival.
evidence.explanation: States the conclusion, including that tumour control was not compromised, which is the concern the delayed schedule exists to address.

evidence.snippet: Nonclinical studies and initial phase 1-2 trials indicated that sodium thiosulfate has a potential otoprotective effect, with maximum efficacy occurring when sodium thiosulfate is administered 4 to 8 hours after cisplatin
evidence.explanation: Gives the timing window this treatment's description is built on.

evidence.snippet: Sodium thiosulfate protects against cisplatin-induced hearing loss in children and is not associated with serious adverse events attributed to its use.
evidence.explanation: The second trial's own conclusion, including its safety finding. Both trials were in children; neither establishes the effect in adults.

treatments/3.description: A sulfur nucleophile that inactivates platinum, given six hours after the cisplatin infusion. The delay is the whole design: given at the same time it would protect the tumour too, and pharmacokinetic work put six hours as the interval that protects the ear without doing that. In a randomised phase 3 trial in children with standard-risk hepatoblastoma it cut hearing loss from 63 percent to 33 percent without reducing survival.

evidence.snippet: Hearing loss of grade 1 or higher occurred in 18 of 55 children (33%) in the cisplatin-sodium thiosulfate group, as compared with 29 of 46 (63%) in the cisplatin-alone group, indicating a 48% lower incidence of hearing loss in the cisplatin-sodium thiosulfate group (relative risk, 0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.33 to 0.81; P=0.002).
evidence.explanation: Randomised phase 3 result with effect size and confidence interval. This is the strongest treatment evidence in the entry.

evidence.snippet: Adjusted for stratification variables, the likelihood of hearing loss was significantly lower in the sodium thiosulfate group compared with the control group (odds ratio 0·31, 95% CI 0·13-0·73; p=0·0036).
evidence.explanation: A second, independent randomised phase 3 trial (ACCL0431, Children's Oncology Group) reaching the same conclusion in a mixed-tumour paediatric population. Two trials in different populations is materially stronger than one.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Reduces the incidence of hearing loss, which this entry places downstream of hair cell death. The trial measured hearing thresholds, not hair cell survival, so the effect is asserted on the clinical outcome and located at this node by inference.

evidence.snippet: Renoprotective approaches are being discovered, but the protective effects are mostly partial, suggesting the need for combinatorial strategies.
evidence.explanation: States that renoprotection is partial, which is the claim this treatment makes. The source speaks of renoprotective approaches in general; it does not name hydration, and this entry does not cite it as evidence for hydration specifically.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, it is unclear whether these approaches would limit the anticancer effects of cisplatin in tumors.
evidence.explanation: Records the open question that constrains every protective strategy here - the same concern the sodium thiosulfate schedule was designed around, left unresolved on the renal side.

evidence.snippet: There has been uncertainty regarding the best method to prevent CIN.
evidence.explanation: States that the optimal prevention protocol is unsettled, which is why this treatment is curated at the level of the magnesium arm rather than a named hydration regimen.

treatments/4.description: Measures aimed at the renal arm, of which intravenous saline hydration with magnesium replacement is the routine one. The honest summary of this area is that protection is partial: no single measure abolishes the nephrotoxicity, and the field is still combining them.

evidence.snippet: A meta-analysis of 11 retrospective studies that examined magnesium supplementation during hydration showed that this treatment provided significant protection against CIN (OR = 0.22, 95% CI = 0.14 to 0.35).
evidence.explanation: Gives the effect size and interval. The pooled studies are retrospective, which is a real limit on this estimate and is why the accompanying review still reports uncertainty about the best protocol.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Magnesium supplementation during hydration reduces cisplatin nephrotoxicity. The meta-analysis measured the clinical nephrotoxicity endpoint, not tubular cell death, so the effect is located at this node by inference.

evidence.snippet: TARS2 (MIM 612805) encodes a 718-amino acid mitochondrial threonyl tRNA-synthetase, which contains an N-terminal N1 domain (Leu20-Ser124), an N2 domain (for editing) (Pro125-Asp301), an aminoacylation domain (for amino acid activation and tRNA charging) (His302-Gly605), and an anticodon binding domain (for tRNA binding) (Lys606-Phe718)
evidence.explanation: Gives the domain architecture against which disease variants are located.

evidence.snippet: Some missense variants cluster, such as those in the TARS2-Rag GTPase binding region and in the editing and AB domains.
evidence.explanation: Records the three clusters into which the missense alleles fall.

evidence.snippet: one previously reported variant (c.470 C > G, p.Thr157Arg) recurred in six Chinese individuals with COXPD21 but was not present in populations of other races
evidence.explanation: Establishes a population-specific founder allele, which shifts the prior in Chinese patients.

steps/1.description:
TARS2 encodes a 718-residue mitochondrial threonyl-tRNA synthetase with four domains: an N1 domain, an editing domain that clears mischarged seryl-tRNA-Thr, an aminoacylation domain, and an anticodon-binding domain. Disease variants are predominantly missense and cluster in three places: the Rag GTPase-binding region between the editing and catalytic core domains, the editing domain, and the anticodon-binding domain. Recurrent alleles are common, including p.(Thr157Arg), which recurs in Chinese families and is absent from other populations, and p.(Pro155Leu), p.(Glu512Lys) and p.(Ser258Leu), each seen in more than one unrelated family.
Which domain an allele hits matters. Variants in the Rag-binding region behave differently from the rest, both in the laboratory and in the clinic, and are the basis of the second mechanistic hypothesis curated here.

evidence.snippet: TARS2, a mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (mt-aaRS), generates mitochondrial Thr-tRNAThr by catalyzing the binding of homologous tRNA to specific amino acids and clearing mischarged Ser-tRNAThr during mitochondrial translation, which safeguards normal and accurate mitochondrial protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: States both halves of the enzyme's function, charging and editing.

evidence.snippet: In vitro and in vivo analyses revealed that the mutation induces a decrease in Thr activation, aminoacylation, and proofreading activities and a change in the protein structure and/or stability, which might cause reduced catalytic efficiency.
evidence.explanation: Direct enzymological measurement for one disease allele, p.Pro282Leu, showing that a single variant reduces activation, aminoacylation and editing together rather than any one of them alone.

evidence.snippet: hmtThrRS misactivates non-cognate Ser and uses post-transfer editing to clear erroneously synthesized products.
evidence.explanation: Establishes why the editing function matters: the enzyme routinely mischarges serine and depends on proofreading to correct it.

steps/2.description: Charging mitochondrial tRNA-Thr with threonine is the enzyme's canonical job, and it has a second, quality-control half: clearing mischarged seryl-tRNA-Thr through the editing domain. Both matter, since disease alleles fall in the editing domain as well as the catalytic one. Measured threonyl-tRNA levels are reduced in patient samples in proportion to the genetic defect.

evidence.snippet: Translation of the 13 mtDNA-encoded, OXPHOS-related proteins takes place within the mitochondrial matrix. This complex process requires ribosomal and transfer RNAs (rRNAs and tRNAs), encoded by mtDNA, and more than 100 proteins, encoded by nuclear genes, translated by cytosolic ribosomes and imported into mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: Describes the apparatus and why a nuclear-encoded component sits inside it.

steps/3.description: Mitochondria translate only thirteen proteins, all of them subunits of the respiratory chain, but they need a full translation apparatus to do it: two ribosomal RNAs and twenty-two transfer RNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA, plus more than a hundred nuclear-encoded proteins imported from the cytosol. The aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are among those imported proteins, which is why a nuclear gene defect produces what looks like a mitochondrial DNA disease.

evidence.snippet: compound heterozygous mutations in TARS2 in two siblings presenting with axial hypotonia and severe psychomotor delay associated with multiple MRC defects
evidence.explanation: Records the combined respiratory chain defect in the two patients in whom the gene was first implicated.

evidence.snippet: One of the 2 patients who underwent muscle biopsy showed features of complex I deficiency similar to 4 previously reported patients who had multiple complex deficiency9,11
evidence.explanation: Shows the enzymatic defect is neither universal nor uniformly combined when it is looked for, which is why this evidence is PARTIAL.

evidence.snippet: Expression of the corresponding wild-type transcripts in immortalized mutant fibroblasts rescued the biochemical impairment of mitochondrial respiration
evidence.explanation: A rescue experiment, which is what establishes the causal direction from the gene defect to the respiratory impairment rather than merely their co-occurrence.

steps/4.description: The defining biochemical lesion, and the one the disease is named for. Complexes I, III, IV and V are deficient together because each contains mitochondrially encoded subunits; complex II is normal because it does not. Two practical qualifications attach to it. The defect is tissue-restricted and is found in muscle rather than reliably in fibroblasts or liver, so a normal fibroblast enzymology does not exclude the diagnosis. And it is inconsistently found even when looked for: of two patients biopsied in the largest cohort, one showed complex I deficiency and the other did not, so modern diagnosis rests on sequencing rather than on enzymology.

evidence.snippet: Upon threonine supplementation, TARS2 preferentially binds RagCGTP and promotes the conversion of inactive Rag GTPases (RagAGDP/RagCGTP) into the active form (RagAGTP/RagCGDP). This is sufficient to recruit mTORC1 to lysosomes.
evidence.explanation: Describes the normal non-translational function whose loss this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Despite being cloned from the same wild-type (WT) backbone, the TARS2 variants had reduced basal expression levels
evidence.explanation: The confound that keeps this node PROVISIONAL: the constructs expressed less protein, between 39 and 66 percent of wild type, as well as binding less well, so the two effects are not cleanly separated. The reporting authors attribute the lower expression to intrinsic instability of the variant proteins.

evidence.snippet: As expected, we found that PGC1α and PPARα were downregulated and upregulated, respectively, in tars2 knock-down animals, likely leading to dysregulation of mTORC1 signaling.
evidence.explanation: The in vivo readout of the pathway, in a zebrafish knockdown rather than in patient cells.

steps/5.description:
The non-translational arm. mTORC1 is recruited to and activated at the lysosomal surface by Rag GTPases in response to amino acid availability, and TARS2 is part of how threonine availability is read: on threonine supplementation it binds RagC preferentially and drives the conversion of the Rag heterodimer to its active form. The region responsible, residues 301 to 381, sits between the editing and catalytic core domains, and four disease variants fall inside it. All four bound RagA and RagC significantly less than wild type.
The confidence is PROVISIONAL and the limitations are specific. The transfected variant constructs also had reduced basal expression, between 39 and 66 percent of wild type, which the authors attribute to intrinsic instability, so reduced binding cannot be entirely separated from reduced protein. mTORC1 activity itself was not measured in patient cells. What is measured downstream comes from the zebrafish knockdown, where two mTORC1 targets move in opposite directions as expected.

evidence.snippet: Notably, increased blood lactate is a consistent finding in all affected individuals for whom it was checked (17/20 85%)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the biochemical readout of impaired oxidative phosphorylation across the pooled cohort.

evidence.snippet: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy from 2 individuals showed lactate peak at the level of the basal ganglia in 1 of them.
evidence.explanation: Places the lactate accumulation in the brain tissue where the imaging lesions occur, rather than only in blood.

steps/6.description: Falling ATP output from oxidative phosphorylation forces reliance on glycolysis, and the resulting raised blood lactate is the most consistent laboratory abnormality in the disorder, present in 85 percent of those tested. Lactate can also be seen directly in the brain: magnetic resonance spectroscopy has shown a lactate peak at the basal ganglia in a patient whose imaging lesions were progressing there.

evidence.snippet: Three individuals, all diagnosed with diabetes in the first week of life, shared a rare homozygous missense variant, p.(Arg327Gln), in TARS2. Replication studies identified the same homozygous variant in a fourth individual diagnosed with diabetes at 1 year.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the genotype-restricted association, in a discovery cohort plus a replication cohort.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic TARS2 variants cause a mitochondrial encephalopathy (COXPD-21) characterised by severe hypotonia, epilepsy and developmental delay. Diabetes is not a known feature of COXPD-21.
evidence.explanation: States explicitly that diabetes falls outside the recognised phenotype, which is why it is curated here as an allele-specific branch rather than as a general feature.

steps/7.description: A phenotype outside the classical description of the disorder, and one that is genotype-restricted rather than general. Four individuals homozygous for p.(Arg327Gln) presented with diabetes, three of them in the first week of life, alongside epilepsy and developmental delay. Diabetes is not a recognised feature of COXPD21 and none of the larger cohorts report it, which is what makes the association with a specific Rag-binding-region allele informative rather than incidental.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI was abnormal in all individuals for whom it was available (Figure 2), revealing mild to severe cerebellar atrophy with prevalent vermian involvement in 12 of 16 (75%) cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the dominant structural finding and its cerebellar predominance.

evidence.snippet: Notably, the cerebellum was initially normal in 1 infant who underwent brain MRI in the first months of life. Therefore, we hypothesize that cerebellar atrophy might develop later in TARS2-related disorders and be missed without follow-up MRI studies
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the atrophy is acquired and progressive rather than congenital, with the diagnostic consequence the authors draw.

evidence.snippet: thus suggesting that TARS2 variants might also be associated with a Leigh-like neuroimaging pattern, in keeping with the phenotypic heterogeneity of ARS2-related disorders.
evidence.explanation: Records the Leigh-like imaging pattern seen on follow-up in two patients.

steps/8.description:
The structural consequence, and the point at which the two mechanistic arms converge on tissue. Imaging shows cerebellar atrophy with a vermian predominance in three quarters of patients, basal ganglia signal change in about two thirds, and progressive loss of periventricular white matter with callosal thinning in over 40 percent.
Two temporal points matter for diagnosis. The cerebellum was normal in one infant imaged in the first months of life, so a normal early MRI does not exclude the disorder and follow-up imaging is needed. And in at least two patients the basal ganglia lesions progressed with lactate peaks and new dentate signal change, producing a Leigh-like pattern.

evidence.snippet: All but 1 individual had moderate (n = 7) or severe (n = 10) developmental delay/intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the developmental impairment across the largest cohort.

evidence.snippet: The regression of developmental milestones occurred within the first year of life for 3 individuals, typically triggered by intercurrent illnesses.
evidence.explanation: Records the regression and its catabolic-stress trigger.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, these patients display hypotonia, cerebellar signs, varying degrees of spasticity, dystonia, seizures, and secondary microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the clinical deficits that constitute this endpoint.

steps/9.description: The clinical endpoint. Almost all patients have moderate or severe developmental delay or intellectual disability, and about a third lose acquired milestones, typically triggered by an intercurrent illness and often within the first year of life. That regression pattern is what marks the disorder as metabolic rather than statically developmental, and it is curated as its own node rather than folded into the structural one because the two are measured differently and can diverge: a child can regress after an illness without a new imaging finding.

evidence.snippet: All four probands were born to unaffected parents, had low birthweight (Z-score range - 4.72 to -1.90) and were diagnosed with insulin-treated diabetes at a median age of 1 week (range: 1 day-52 weeks).
evidence.explanation: Documents the phenotype, its age at diagnosis and the accompanying low birthweight in all four reported individuals.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic TARS2 variants cause a mitochondrial encephalopathy (COXPD-21) characterised by severe hypotonia, epilepsy and developmental delay. Diabetes is not a known feature of COXPD-21.
evidence.explanation: States that diabetes falls outside the recognised phenotype, which is why no frequency is given.

steps/10.description: Genotype-restricted rather than general. Four individuals homozygous for p.(Arg327Gln), one of the Rag GTPase-binding-region variants, presented with insulin-treated diabetes, three of them within the first week of life and the fourth at one year. All four had low birthweight. Diabetes is not a recognised feature of this disorder and no cohort reports it, which is what makes its association with one specific allele informative rather than incidental.

evidence.snippet: The amount of VARS2 and TARS2 proteins and valyl-tRNA and threonyl-tRNA levels were decreased in samples of afflicted patients according to the genetic defect.
evidence.explanation: Measures both the reduced synthetase and the reduced charged tRNA in patient samples.

edges/1.description: Reduced amount and function of the synthetase lowers the supply of charged mitochondrial threonyl-tRNA.

evidence.snippet: Given that 4 TARS2 variants, namely, F323C, R327Q, E342D, and R346C, occur within this region, we tested whether these amino acid changes interfere with the interaction between TARS2 and Rag GTPases.
evidence.explanation: Names the four disease variants that fall in the Rag-binding region and were tested for that interaction.

edges/2.description: Variants in the residue 301 to 381 region reduce binding to Rag GTPases, which is a separate consequence from any effect on aminoacylation.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in mt-aaRS genes lead to a reduction in charged tRNA, which impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and decreases the amount of mtDNA-encoded subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation system (OXPHOS)
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from reduced charged tRNA to impaired mitochondrial protein synthesis.

edges/3.description: Mitochondrial translation cannot proceed without an adequate supply of the charged tRNA for every amino acid.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in any component of the mitochondrial translation machinery can in principle cause inherited mitochondrial disorders affecting the MRC complexes containing mtDNA-encoded subunits (cI, cIII, cIV, cV), with the preservation of complex II, the only complex which has no mtDNA-encoded proteins.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step and, critically, why complex II is spared, which is the biochemical signature of the disease family.

edges/4.description: Insufficient synthesis of the mitochondrially encoded subunits leaves the complexes that contain them unable to assemble and remain stable.

evidence.snippet: Their biochemical signature is the presence of defective activity in the mitochondrial respiratory chain (MRC) complexes, resulting in faulty oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which can impair ATP production.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from complex deficiency to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production.

edges/5.description: Deficient respiratory complexes cannot sustain electron transport and proton pumping, so ATP output falls and pyruvate is diverted to lactate.

evidence.snippet: Symptoms include developmental delay, intellectual disability, regression, and brain atrophy, along with changes in basal ganglia signals and mitochondrial characteristics, such as lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy, and distal renal tubulopathy.
evidence.explanation: Links the mitochondrial biochemical picture to the neurological and systemic phenotype in the same sentence.

edges/6.description: Energy failure in the developing brain, and particularly in the cerebellum and basal ganglia, produces the developmental, cerebellar and extrapyramidal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, our results suggest that TARS2 plays an essential role in early CNS development, possibly affecting neuronal proliferation and apoptosis through aberrant mTORC1 signaling.
evidence.explanation: The authors' proposal, stated with their own hedges, that the mTORC1 arm reaches the brain phenotype through proliferation and apoptosis.

edges/7.description: Proposed as a route to the neurodevelopmental phenotype independent of the respiratory chain defect, acting through neuronal proliferation and apoptosis. The intermediates between mTORC1 dysregulation and the human brain phenotype are not established, hence the indirect link type.

evidence.snippet: Current evidence suggests that the p.(Arg327Gln) variant disrupts TARS2's regulation of the mTORC1 pathway which is essential for β-cells.
evidence.explanation: Attributes a beta cell phenotype to the mTORC1 arm specifically, in patients carrying one of the four Rag-binding-region variants.

edges/8.description: The most striking prediction of this arm, because it explains a phenotype the translational model does not. One Rag-binding-region variant, p.(Arg327Gln), was found homozygously in four individuals with neonatal diabetes, and mTORC1 is essential to beta cells.

evidence.snippet: All four probands were born to unaffected parents, had low birthweight (Z-score range - 4.72 to -1.90) and were diagnosed with insulin-treated diabetes at a median age of 1 week (range: 1 day-52 weeks).
evidence.explanation: Documents the clinical presentation of the beta cell defect, including age at diagnosis.

edges/9.description: Beta cell failure presents clinically as insulin-treated diabetes, diagnosed within the first week of life in three of the four reported individuals.

evidence.snippet: Symptoms include developmental delay, intellectual disability, regression, and brain atrophy, along with changes in basal ganglia signals and mitochondrial characteristics, such as lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy, and distal renal tubulopathy.
evidence.explanation: Reports the structural and functional findings together as one clinical picture.

edges/10.description: Progressive loss of cerebellar, basal ganglia and white matter tissue produces the developmental, cerebellar and extrapyramidal deficits.

evidence.snippet: It is noteworthy that 17 of the 24 families reported to date harbor recurrent TARS2 variants
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how far the mutational spectrum is dominated by recurrent alleles.

evidence.snippet: Although we did not recognize a specific genotype-phenotype correlation, some interesting findings emerged.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own assessment that no general correlation was established, which bounds the allele-specific observations that follow it.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, all but 1 individual harboring compound heterozygous variants in the TARS2-Rag GTPase binding region showed basal ganglia and cerebellar signal alterations without cerebellar atrophy.
evidence.explanation: The clearest genotype-phenotype signal in the disorder, and the one that groups the Rag-binding-region alleles together clinically as well as biochemically.

genes/0.notes:
TARS2 encodes the mitochondrial threonyl-tRNA synthetase. The mutational spectrum is dominated by missense variants and by recurrence: of the twenty-four families reported by 2023, seventeen carried a recurrent variant. Recurrent alleles include p.(Thr157Arg), which is a Chinese-specific founder variant recurring in six Chinese individuals and absent from other populations, plus p.(Pro155Leu), p.(Glu512Lys), p.(Ser258Leu), p.(Phe323Cys) and p.(Arg346Cys). Two splice variants also recur, c.387+6T>C and c.695+3A>G.
Genotype-phenotype correlation is weak but not absent. p.(Pro155Leu) was associated with a severe phenotype in two unrelated individuals, while p.(Glu512Lys) and p.(Ser258Leu) were associated with moderate intellectual disability and milder motor and cerebellar dysfunction. Variants in the Rag-binding region behave as a group: all but one individual carrying them in compound heterozygosity showed basal ganglia and cerebellar signal change without cerebellar atrophy, and one of them, p.(Arg327Gln), is the allele associated with neonatal diabetes.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy, including tonic-clonic seizures, myoclonic seizures, and infantile spasms, occurred in 8 individuals and was successfully controlled with anti-seizure medications in half of them.
evidence.explanation: Supports antiseizure medication while quantifying the partial response, which is why the support is PARTIAL.

treatments/0.description: Symptomatic, and the only pharmacological intervention with reported outcomes in this disorder. Seizures occurred in eight individuals in the largest cohort and were successfully controlled in half of them, so the response is real but partial. No agent is established as preferable, and no disease-modifying therapy exists.

evidence.snippet: We referred the patient to paediatric centre that provides renal replacement therapy.
evidence.explanation: The only organ-directed intervention reported by name in this disorder, in the single patient who progressed to end-stage kidney disease.

evidence.snippet: A cardiological evaluation, urine analysis for tubulopathy and hearing screening is warranted in patients with biallelic TARS2 variants.
evidence.explanation: The surveillance recommendation from which the content of supportive care follows: what is looked for is what gets treated.

treatments/1.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy, so management is supportive and its content follows from the surveillance recommendations: alkali and electrolyte replacement for renal tubular acidosis, and renal replacement therapy in the one patient who reached end-stage kidney disease; cardiac management where hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is found; and the usual developmental therapies and nutritional support. Nothing in this list is specific to TARS2, and none of it has been evaluated in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: The amount of VARS2 and TARS2 proteins and valyl-tRNA and threonyl-tRNA levels were decreased in samples of afflicted patients according to the genetic defect.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of the two steps this model asserts, reduced synthetase and reduced charged tRNA, in patient material.

hypotheses/0.description: The mechanism shared by the whole family of mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase disorders. Reduced TARS2 protein lowers the supply of charged mitochondrial threonyl-tRNA, mitochondrial translation of the thirteen mitochondrially encoded respiratory chain subunits falls, and the four complexes that contain those subunits are deficient together while complex II is spared. This is the model the disease was named for, and it is supported by direct measurement in patient material and by rescue of the respiratory defect on re-expression of wild-type TARS2.

evidence.snippet: In vitro studies showed that variants within the TARS2301-381 region had decreased binding to Rag GTPases, likely impairing mTORC1 activity.
evidence.explanation: States the mechanism and, in the word "likely", the authors' own hedge about mTORC1 activity not having been measured directly.

evidence.snippet: We define the clinico-radiological spectrum of TARS2-related mitochondrial disease, unveil the likely involvement of the mTORC1 signaling pathway as a distinct molecular mechanism
evidence.explanation: The authors present the mTORC1 arm as a distinct mechanism, not as a restatement of the translational one.

hypotheses/1.description:
A mechanism that does not involve translation at all. TARS2 senses threonine and binds Rag GTPases at the lysosome, which recruits and activates mTORC1. A cluster of disease variants falls in the residue 301 to 381 region that mediates that binding and reduces it, downstream mTORC1 targets are dysregulated in a zebrafish knockdown, and one Rag-binding-region variant is associated with neonatal diabetes, a beta cell phenotype where mTORC1 is essential and which the translation model does not predict.
It is EMERGING rather than CANONICAL for three reasons. The binding reduction was measured by co-immunoprecipitation of transfected constructs, and those constructs also had reduced basal expression, so reduced binding and reduced protein cannot be fully separated. mTORC1 activity itself was not measured in patient cells, only inferred. And the in vivo evidence is a morpholino knockdown in zebrafish rather than a model of the human alleles.

evidence.snippet: Besides impaired aminoacylation, other factors have been reported to explain the variety of phenotypes present in ARS2-related disorders. These factors include non-canonical functions, tissue-specific developmental differences in energy requirements, and downstream effects of mitochondrial dysfunction on other intracellular organelles.
evidence.explanation: Frames the question: aminoacylation alone is not thought to account for the phenotypic range in this disease family.

evidence.snippet: Consequently, these observations raise the question whether mTORC1 drug modulators could be therapeutic for individuals with TARS2-related disorder in the future.
evidence.explanation: States the therapeutic stake that makes resolving the relative contribution worth doing.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Two mechanisms are curated here as separate hypothesis groups, and the honest position is that their relative contribution is unknown. The translational one is established: reduced synthetase, reduced charged tRNA, combined respiratory chain deficiency, rescued by wild-type TARS2. The mTORC1 one is supported but not established, and the evidence for it is indirect at every step.
There are three concrete reasons to think it is not merely a laboratory artefact. Four disease variants cluster in the residue 301 to 381 Rag-binding region, which is not where you would put variants if aminoacylation were the only thing that mattered. Those variants group clinically as well as biochemically, showing basal ganglia and cerebellar signal change without cerebellar atrophy. And one of them, p.(Arg327Gln), is associated with neonatal diabetes, a beta cell phenotype that the translational model does not predict and that no other TARS2 allele produces.
Against that, the binding experiments used transfected constructs whose basal expression was itself reduced to between 39 and 66 percent of wild type, so less binding and less protein are confounded. mTORC1 activity was never measured in patient cells. And the in vivo evidence is a morpholino knockdown, which removes the protein altogether and therefore cannot separate a specific Rag-binding defect from general loss of the synthetase.
The question is not academic. The cohort authors end by asking whether mTORC1 drug modulators could be therapeutic here, and that question cannot be answered without knowing whether mTORC1 dysregulation drives the phenotype or accompanies it.

evidence.snippet: It is caused by variants in any one of seven genes, all of which have a structural or regulatory function in the cohesin complex.
evidence.explanation: The consensus statement's framing of CdLS as a cohesin-complex disorder, which is the class this node's lesion sits in.

evidence.snippet: in both man and mouse, Nipbl heterozygotes show only a ,30% reduction in Nipbl mRNA and protein
