evidence.explanation: The quantitative basis for calling this a dosage disorder: a transcript and protein deficit of under about 30%, in humans as well as mice, is enough to produce the syndrome. Graded OTHER because this is the paper's background summary of the three studies it cites rather than a result of its own zebrafish work. The comma is a PDF-extraction artifact for the less-than sign.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous loss-of-function variant halves functional NIPBL, the cohesin loading factor. In humans and in the mouse models alike the transcript and protein deficit is modest, under about 30% below normal, so the disorder is a dosage disorder rather than a null-allele one: there is no second hit and no threshold below which the phenotype appears.

evidence.snippet: The results suggest that gene activation is the primary cohesin function sensitive to Nipbl reduction.
evidence.explanation: The paper's own conclusion that the sensitive cohesin function is transcriptional, which is the claim this whole chain rests on.

steps/2.description: Less loader means less chromatin-bound cohesin, at CTCF boundary sites and at repeats. Cohesin-bound genes are enriched for H3K4me3 at their promoters and are disproportionately downregulated, which points at gene activation rather than cohesion as the sensitive function.

evidence.snippet: NIPBL specifically regulates cell identity genes by supporting a unique local genome conformation defined by greater spatial proximity to nearby super-enhancers and weaker transcription start site insulation of genomic contacts
evidence.explanation: Explains why loss of a general chromatin factor produces a developmental rather than a global phenotype.

steps/3.description: Reduced chromatin-bound cohesin weakens enhancer-promoter contacts and CTCF insulation. Acute NIPBL depletion in vivo diminishes chromatin loops rapidly, and the genes that depend most on NIPBL-supported conformation are cell-identity and developmental genes sitting near super-enhancers. That selectivity is what turns a globally acting chromatin factor into a developmental disorder.

evidence.snippet: mutant cohesin impairs both RNA polymerase II (Pol II) transcription initiation at promoters and elongation in the gene body
evidence.explanation: Locates the transcriptional lesion at two specific steps rather than asserting a general dysregulation.

steps/4.description: Transcription itself is impaired at both ends: initiation at promoters and elongation through gene bodies. This is measured in CdLS patient cells, not only in models.

evidence.snippet: Nearly all such changes are modest, however--usually less than 1.5-fold--raising the intriguing possibility that, in CdLS, severe developmental defects result from the collective action of many otherwise innocuous perturbations.
evidence.explanation: States the collective-perturbation hypothesis in the terms this node curates it in, including that it remains a hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: identified hundreds of mRNAs, pseudogenes, and non-coding RNAs with altered expression
evidence.explanation: Reproduces the many-small-changes signature in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, which is disease-relevant tissue rather than a fibroblast proxy.

steps/5.description: The distinctive feature of this disease's mechanism, and the reason it resists the usual one-pathway account. Hundreds to thousands of genes change expression and nearly all the changes are modest, usually under 1.5-fold. No single perturbation is individually pathogenic; the phenotype is the sum. This is also why there is no obvious therapeutic target: there is no dominant node to correct.

evidence.snippet: Studies of these vertebrate animal models have yielded novel insights into the developmental etiology and genes/gene pathways that contribute to CdLS-associated birth defects, particularly defects of the gut, heart, craniofacial structures, nervous system, and limbs.
evidence.explanation: Names the specific organ systems whose developmental programmes fail, which is what this node asserts.

steps/6.description: Developmental programmes fail across limb bud, cardiac and left-right patterning, foregut and diaphragm, craniofacial structures and the central nervous system. In the zebrafish model the deregulation is detectable from gastrulation onwards in endodermal differentiation and left-right patterning genes, which places the lesion early enough to explain heart and gut defects.

evidence.snippet: Severe (classic) CdLS is characterized by distinctive facial features, growth failure (often prenatal onset; height and weight <5th centile throughout life), hypertrichosis, and limb abnormalities
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists hypertrichosis among the features that characterise severe classic CdLS, alongside the facial gestalt, growth failure and limb defects this entry already curates.

steps/7.description: Generalised hypertrichosis is one of the cardinal features of the classic phenotype, listed alongside the facial gestalt, growth failure and limb defects.

evidence.snippet: Aggressive management of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names GERD as requiring aggressive management, which presupposes it as a feature of the disease.

steps/8.description: Reflux is the manifestation the first-line management measure exists for, and GeneReviews puts its aggressive control at the head of the management list.

evidence.snippet: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is an archetypical genetic syndrome that is characterized by intellectual disability, well-defined facial features, upper limb anomalies and atypical growth, among numerous other signs and symptoms.
evidence.explanation: The consensus statement names well-defined facial features as one of the four cardinal characteristics, which is what makes the gestalt diagnostic rather than merely associated.

evidence.snippet: All of them presented the characteristic (classic) CdLS craniofacial features such as synophrys, thick arched eyebrows, thin upper lip vermilion and downturned corners of mouth (11/11).
evidence.explanation: The only counted figure bearing on synophrys in any cited source: eleven of eleven. Two limits on what it counts. The eleven of eleven attaches to the composite craniofacial gestalt that synophrys is named within, not to synophrys measured on its own, so it is a ceiling for this phenotype rather than a measurement of it. And the cohort is individuals with postzygotic mosaic NIPBL variants, ten of the eleven scoring as classic CdLS, so it is a selected series rather than an unselected prevalence. It is quoted because it is a count, where the consensus statement above states a cardinal feature without one.

steps/9.description: Part of the craniofacial gestalt that makes the syndrome clinically recognizable, together with arched eyebrows, long philtrum and thin down-turned lips.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent associated congenital malformations were limb defects (73.1%), congenital heart defects (45.6%), central nervous system malformations (40.2%), and cleft palate (21.7%).
evidence.explanation: Registry frequencies for the four commonest malformations, used as the source for this and three other phenotype bands in this entry.

steps/10.description: Limb defects are the commonest associated malformation in registry data, at 73.1%, and were present in every case in one national series. Involvement is predominantly upper-limb and often asymmetric.

evidence.snippet: A cardiac anomaly was identified in 29/87 (33.3%) including 28 (32.2%) patients with a structural CHD, and an additional patient (1.2%) with isolated non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).
evidence.explanation: The prospective echocardiographic frequency, from consecutive patients.

steps/11.description: Reported in 33.3% of an echocardiographic cohort and 45.6% in registry data. The discrepancy is real and probably reflects ascertainment: registries capture more severely malformed cases. Pulmonary stenosis is the single commonest lesion, and late mitral and tricuspid valve dysplasia appearing after age ten is the reason surveillance rather than a single neonatal echocardiogram is recommended.

evidence.snippet: Overall incidence of pulmonary stenosis was 39% (11/28).
evidence.explanation: Gives the lesion distribution within the cardiac subgroup.

steps/12.description: The commonest single structural lesion within the cardiac subgroup, in 39% of those with a congenital heart defect. That is 11 of the 28 patients with a structural defect, in a cohort of 87, so roughly 13% of patients overall, which is the figure the frequency band carries.

evidence.snippet: Mortality was 76% for CdLS patients compared with 29% for non-CdLS patients
evidence.explanation: The mortality comparison that makes CDH the principal prognostic lesion.

steps/13.description: Uncommon but the dominant driver of mortality. Infants with both CdLS and CDH fare markedly worse than infants with CDH alone: 76% mortality against 29%, with only a third undergoing repair. Of the seven who were repaired, five survived to discharge, which suggests surgical candidacy rather than the syndrome itself is the discriminator.

evidence.snippet: similarly delayed across motor and language milestones with about 70% not using phrase speech and 30-50% not walking by 5 years of age
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the developmental delay through milestone attainment rather than through an IQ band.

evidence.snippet: Patients reported here had consistent global developmental delay and intellectual disability (10/11).
evidence.explanation: Ten of eleven, which is the counted figure the band rests on. The same selected mosaic cohort as the synophrys count, so it supports the band without being an unselected prevalence.

evidence.snippet: All children had ≥ 1 type of RB; 44% had some form of SIB.
evidence.explanation: Gives both the self-injury frequency and the universality of repetitive behaviour in the same measured cohort.

steps/15.description: Present in 44% of a cohort of 50 children. Lower adaptive functioning correlates with higher stereotypy and self-injury scores.

evidence.snippet: All children had ≥ 1 type of RB; 44% had some form of SIB.
evidence.explanation: The repetitive-behaviour half of the same sentence. HPO has no general repetitive-behaviour term at this level, so the binding is to Motor stereotypy and preferred_term carries the broader concept the cohort measured.

steps/16.description: Every child in the cohort had at least one type of repetitive behaviour, and 64% spent more than an hour a day displaying them.

evidence.snippet: about 70% not using phrase speech and 30-50% not walking by 5 years of age
evidence.explanation: Milestone attainment for language.

steps/17.description: About 70% are not using phrase speech by five years of age.

evidence.snippet: about 70% not using phrase speech and 30-50% not walking by 5 years of age
evidence.explanation: Milestone attainment for gross motor function.

steps/18.description: Between 30% and 50% are not walking by five years of age.

evidence.snippet: Around one in four children with Cornelia de Lange syndrome and Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome had a gastrostomy
evidence.explanation: A population-based measure of feeding failure severity, expressed as an intervention rate rather than a symptom report.

steps/19.description: Severe and a defining part of the morbidity. Roughly one in four children with CdLS has a gastrostomy before age five, against 0.016% of reference children in the same data-linkage study.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent associated congenital malformations were limb defects (73.1%), congenital heart defects (45.6%), central nervous system malformations (40.2%), and cleft palate (21.7%).
evidence.explanation: Registry frequency for central nervous system malformation.

steps/20.description: Central nervous system malformations in 40.2% of registry cases.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent associated congenital malformations were limb defects (73.1%), congenital heart defects (45.6%), central nervous system malformations (40.2%), and cleft palate (21.7%).
evidence.explanation: Registry frequency for cleft palate.

evidence.snippet: growth failure (often prenatal onset; height and weight <5th centile throughout life)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states both the prenatal onset and that the deficit persists lifelong, which is why this is curated as intrauterine growth retardation rather than as short stature alone.

evidence.snippet: Almost 70% of patients, born after the 37th week of gestation, weighed <or=2,500 g.
evidence.explanation: The registry's counted figure for growth restriction at birth. It is low birth weight rather than antenatally diagnosed growth restriction, and it counts only term births, so it is a floor for this phenotype rather than a measurement of it.

steps/22.description: Growth restriction begins prenatally and continues postnatally, and is one of the features detectable on antenatal ultrasound.

evidence.snippet: We found a global decrease in cohesin binding, including at CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) binding sites and repeat regions.
evidence.explanation: A ChIP-seq measurement in Nipbl+/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts, which is what makes this an edge rather than two separately supported nodes.

edges/5.description: The step from a distributed expression signature to specific organ malformations is asserted by the sources as an integration of demonstrated components rather than demonstrated end to end, so the edge is typed indirect.

edges/8.description: Curated as its own edge rather than as a consequence of the congenital heart defect above, because it is a specific lesion within that category rather than something the category causes.

edges/12.description: The craniofacial programme this node names. Synophrys is the recognition sign of the syndrome and belongs to the same developmental failure as the cleft palate.

edges/13.description: The central nervous system programme this node names, in its structural form.

edges/14.description: The node names foregut development among the failing programmes, but no cited source traces a route from that to the feeding difficulty, which in practice is a mix of structural, oromotor and reflux contributions. Typed indirect for that reason.

edges/15.description: Attached to the developmental node rather than to the intellectual disability, because the two are parallel manifestations of the same programme failure rather than one causing the other. The specific route is not established.

edges/16.description: Same reasoning as the speech delay above.

edges/17.description: No cited source traces a route from the transcriptional lesion to this behavioural phenotype. The edge records that it belongs to the disease's central nervous system involvement, and its type records that the intermediates are unknown.

edges/18.description: Same reasoning as the self-injurious behaviour above.

edges/19.description: The integument is not among the programmes this node's evidence names, and no cited source traces a route from the transcriptional lesion to the hair phenotype. The edge records membership of the developmental syndrome; the type records that the mechanism is unknown.

edges/20.description: The node names foregut development, but reflux is a functional outcome and no cited source connects the two, so the intermediates are unknown.

edges/22.description: Reflux is one contributor to the feeding failure, which is why its aggressive control and the gastrostomy sit together in the management list. It is not the only contributor, so the feeding node keeps its own incoming edge from the developmental programme.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in NIPBL, which encodes a protein related to the cohesin complex, have been identified in more than 60% of patients, and pathogenic variants in other genes related to this complex in another 15%: SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, and HDAC8.
evidence.explanation: Establishes NIPBL as the major causal gene and gives the share of cases that defines type 1.

evidence.snippet: Truncating mutations were generally found to cause a more severe phenotype but this correlation was not absolute.
evidence.explanation: States the genotype-phenotype trend together with the caveat that limits its predictive use. Both halves of the sentence matter here.

evidence.snippet: unusual high prevalence of mosaicism in CdLS, occurring in 13.1% of patients with a positive molecular diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies postzygotic mosaicism among molecularly diagnosed patients.

genes/0.notes: Truncating variants are generally more severe than missense, but the correlation is explicitly not absolute and should not be used to predict an individual's course. Postzygotic mosaicism is common and is under negative selection in blood, so a phenotypically classical patient with negative blood testing needs buccal or fibroblast sequencing before NIPBL is excluded.

evidence.snippet: Here, we outline a series of recommendations that document the consensus of a group of international experts on clinical diagnostic criteria, both for classic CdLS and non-classic CdLS phenotypes, molecular investigations, long-term management and care planning.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that management is delivered as expert-consensus long-term care planning rather than as a disease-modifying therapy.

evidence.snippet: Aggressive management of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews puts reflux control first among the management measures, which is what the entry's prose asserts.

evidence.snippet: Physical, occupational, and speech therapy to optimize psychomotor development and communication skills.
evidence.explanation: The therapy triad the entry's description names, stated by GeneReviews.

evidence.snippet: Standard treatment for epilepsy, limb defects, gastrointestinal malformations, ocular issues, hearing loss, cleft palate, dental anomalies, cryptorchidism/hypospadias, bicornuate uterus, vesicoureteral reflux, cardiac defects, immunodeficiency, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
evidence.explanation: Source for the cardiac-defect and cleft-palate arms of this entry: GeneReviews directs standard rather than CdLS-specific treatment at both.

evidence.snippet: behavioral assessment for anxiety, attention deficits, and aggressive or self-injurious behaviors
evidence.explanation: Source for the behavioural arm: self-injury is managed through recurring assessment rather than a one-time intervention.

treatments/0.description: No curative or disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is symptomatic: reflux control and gastrostomy for feeding failure, cardiac repair and ongoing echocardiographic surveillance, diaphragmatic hernia repair where the infant is a candidate, and speech, occupational and physical therapy alongside behavioural management of self-injury.

evidence.snippet: Around one in four children with Cornelia de Lange syndrome and Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome had a gastrostomy
evidence.explanation: Establishes gastrostomy as a routine rather than exceptional intervention in this population.

treatments/1.description: Enteral access for feeding failure, required by roughly a quarter of children before age five.

open_questions/0.rationale: The observation is solid: hundreds of genes change and nearly all the changes are under 1.5-fold. The inference that severe developmental defects result from their collective action is stated by its own authors as an intriguing possibility raised by the data, and no experiment has since shown that summing subthreshold perturbations produces the phenotype. The alternative that has not been excluded is that a small number of the changes are the pathogenic ones and the rest are downstream noise. This matters therapeutically: under the collective model there is nothing to target, and under the alternative there is.

open_questions/1.rationale: Both numbers are curated here rather than one being chosen, because the difference is informative. Registries ascertain through malformation and so over-represent severely affected cases; the echocardiographic cohort was consecutive and so should be closer to the true rate among diagnosed patients, but is smaller and single-centre. Neither is stratified by gene, so the NIPBL-specific cardiac frequency, which is what this entry would want, is unpublished. A curator reading either figure alone would be over-reading it.

evidence.snippet: The combustion of synthetic plastics in structural fires releases hydrogen cyanide gas, making it the most common source of inhalation exposure.
evidence.explanation: Supports fire smoke as the dominant inhalational exposure route.

evidence.snippet: Residential fires may cause cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Establishes residential fires as a genuine cause of cyanide poisoning, measured at the scene before treatment.

evidence.snippet: Cyanide forms as a  result of incomplete combustion of materials containing nitrogen (plastics, vinyl, acrylics, nylon, neoprene, rubber, insulation).
evidence.explanation: Names the nitrogen-containing building materials whose incomplete combustion generates the hydrogen cyanide in fire smoke.

evidence.snippet: Cyanide poisoning is infrequent in fire fatalities, and when present it is associated with significant carboxyhemoglobinemia.
evidence.explanation: A forensic series that argues against fire smoke being a frequent cause of clinically decisive cyanide poisoning, and against cyanide acting independently of carbon monoxide. Recorded here because the weight of this exposure route is genuinely contested.

evidence.snippet: Industrial intoxications occur due to extensive use of cyanide compounds as reaction products.
evidence.explanation: Supports industrial cyanide use as an exposure category.

evidence.snippet: The patient was found to be unconscious in a metal chrome plating shop for undetermined duration of time near another unconscious male (Case #2).
evidence.explanation: Documents a real two-casualty occupational exposure in a metal plating shop.

evidence.snippet: Other sources include workplace exposure, prolonged administration of sodium nitroprusside, insecticides, metalworking, bitter almonds, and the seeds of some fruits such as apricots.
evidence.explanation: Independently names workplace exposure and metalworking among the recognised cyanide exposure sources.

evidence.snippet: On detailed questioning of the parents, the use of CAM including intravenous and oral "vitamin B 17" (amygdalin) and oral apricot kernel was reported.
evidence.explanation: Documents amygdalin and apricot kernel as the exposure source in a severe paediatric poisoning.

evidence.snippet: Serum cyanide level was markedly elevated.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the cyanogenic-glycoside exposure produced a measurable systemic cyanide burden.

evidence.snippet: Other sources include workplace exposure, prolonged administration of sodium nitroprusside, insecticides, metalworking, bitter almonds, and the seeds of some fruits such as apricots.
evidence.explanation: Independently names bitter almonds and apricot seeds among the recognised cyanide exposure sources.

evidence.snippet: High-dose or prolonged therapy with nitroprusside in patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction increases the risk for nitroprusside-induced cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Supports nitroprusside infusion as an iatrogenic cyanide exposure and names its risk modifiers.

evidence.snippet: Other sources include workplace exposure, prolonged administration of sodium nitroprusside, insecticides, metalworking, bitter almonds, and the seeds of some fruits such as apricots.
evidence.explanation: Independently names prolonged sodium nitroprusside administration among the recognised cyanide exposure sources.

evidence.snippet: Dermal absorption and injection are rare but possible sources of cyanide exposure.
evidence.explanation: Supports the breadth of absorption routes feeding this node, including the uncommon ones.

steps/4.description: Cyanide reaches the systemic circulation by inhalation of hydrogen cyanide gas, gastric absorption of ingested cyanide salts, enzymatic hydrolysis of ingested cyanogenic glycosides, dermal absorption, or metabolic release from infused nitroprusside. Inhaled hydrogen cyanide acts fastest because it crosses the alveolar membrane directly.

evidence.snippet: Acute cyanide toxicity is attributed to inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase (CcOX), the oxygen-reducing component of mitochondrial electron transport
evidence.explanation: Identifies Complex IV as the molecular target responsible for acute cyanide toxicity.

evidence.snippet: It is concluded that the rapid, potent action of cyanide is due in part to mitochondrial generation of NO, which enhances inhibition of CcOX.
evidence.explanation: Supports nitric-oxide potentiation as a contributor to the speed of Complex IV inhibition.

evidence.snippet: When cyanide enters the body via inhalation, it blocks the cells from utilizing oxygen by binding to the cytochrome oxidase in the mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: Supports the histotoxic character of the lesion - oxygen is present but cannot be used.

steps/5.description: Cyanide binds with high affinity to the ferric heme a3 centre of cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), the oxygen-reducing terminus of the electron transport chain, and reversibly arrests the transfer of electrons to molecular oxygen. Nitric oxide modulates this in a dose-dependent and two-directional way: constitutive, low-level mitochondrial NO potentiates the inhibition, which is part of why onset is so fast, while high exogenous NO attenuates it - which is why the same molecule appears here as an aggravating factor and under Sodium Nitrite as the antidotal one.

evidence.snippet: Rhodanese or thiosulfate sulfurtransferase (TST) is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme that plays roles in cyanide detoxification, the formation of iron-sulfur proteins and the modification of sulfur-containing enzymes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TST as the mitochondrial enzyme that carries out cyanide detoxification.

evidence.snippet: This reaction offers a rational behind the use of thiosulfate as antidote for cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Connects the endogenous sulfurtransferase reaction to the pharmacologic use of thiosulfate. Quoted verbatim including the source's own wording; a snippet never corrects the text it quotes.

steps/6.description: Mitochondrial rhodanese (thiosulfate sulfurtransferase, TST) transfers sulfur from thiosulfate to cyanide, yielding thiocyanate that is excreted renally. 3-mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase provides a complementary cytosolic route. The pathway is limited by sulfur-donor supply and is overwhelmed at high cyanide loads, which is exactly why supplying exogenous thiosulfate is an antidote rather than merely a supplement.

evidence.snippet: For example, in addition to binding to and poisoning hemoglobin, cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, thus blocking electron transport in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and disrupting oxidative phosphorylation
evidence.explanation: Supports disruption of oxidative phosphorylation as the immediate consequence of Complex IV inhibition.

steps/7.description: With Complex IV blocked, the mitochondrial proton-motive force collapses and oxidative phosphorylation ceases, depleting cellular ATP within minutes despite adequate arterial oxygen content and delivery.

evidence.snippet: Using Spearman's test, there was a significant correlation between plasma lactate and blood cyanide concentrations
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the link between the cyanide burden and the lactate produced by this node.

evidence.snippet: Elevated plasma lactate, associated with cardiovascular collapse, should suggest cyanide intoxication.
evidence.explanation: Supports lactic acidosis as the characteristic metabolic signature of this node.

steps/8.description: Anaerobic glycolysis becomes the only remaining ATP source and is grossly insufficient, generating pyruvate that is converted to lactate. The systemic consequence - a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis whose magnitude tracks the cyanide burden closely enough to serve as a surrogate assay - is modelled as the downstream Lactic acidosis and Elevated serum anion gap phenotypes rather than bundled into this cellular node.

evidence.snippet: In severe cases, poisoning can result in coma, convulsions, circulatory failure, and death.
evidence.explanation: Supports circulatory failure as an outcome of severe poisoning.

evidence.snippet: Emergency medical services arrived and found the patient in asystole and started advanced cardiac life support protocol.
evidence.explanation: Documents asystolic cardiac arrest as the terminal cardiovascular event in an occupational cyanide exposure.

steps/9.description: Cardiomyocyte ATP failure produces progressive myocardial depression. This node is the cellular lesion in the heart; its organism-level consequence is modelled separately as Cardiovascular Collapse.

evidence.snippet: Particularly harmful to neurons is the malfunction of glutamate transport and sodium/potassium ion exchangers, contributing to excitotoxicity due to excessive extracellular glutamate
evidence.explanation: Supports failure of glutamate transport and ion exchange as the immediate neuronal consequence of energy failure. Quoted from a rodent and iPSC study whose introduction is summarising the mechanism, hence OTHER.

steps/10.description: Neuronal ATP failure disables the sodium/potassium exchangers that maintain membrane potential and the transporters that clear synaptic glutamate. The clinical expression is immediate and graded, from headache and vertigo through confusion to seizures and coma.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated in response to cyanide poisoning initiate lipid peroxidation that is toxic to neurons
evidence.explanation: Supports the oxidative-stress arm that amplifies excitotoxic neuronal injury. This paper reports rodent and iPSC-neuron work; the quoted sentence is its introduction summarising the mechanism, hence OTHER.

steps/11.description: Extracellular glutamate over-activates NMDA receptors, admitting calcium and driving neuronal death, amplified by reactive oxygen species and lipid peroxidation. Sustained injury in the most metabolically demanding grey matter progresses to frank necrosis.

evidence.snippet: The toxicity of cyanide causes damage, primarily to the basal ganglia, and those changes were visible as altered signal intensity on the first MR images.
evidence.explanation: Supports basal ganglia as the primary site of structural cyanide injury.

evidence.snippet: Extensive areas of hemorrhagic necrosis were seen 6 weeks later.
evidence.explanation: Supports the necrotic, haemorrhagic character of the lesion and its evolution over weeks.

evidence.snippet: CT scan and MRI showed lesions in the basal ganglia, cerebellum and cerebral cortex consistent with reported pathological findings.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the basal ganglia as the lesion site and records the wider cerebellar and cortical involvement noted in the node description.

steps/12.description: The globus pallidus and putamen sustain bilateral, often haemorrhagic necrosis, visible as altered signal on MRI within weeks. The lesion is not confined there: the sensorimotor cortex can show pseudolaminar necrosis for the same reason - high oxygen dependency - and imaging series also report cerebellar and cortical involvement. The node is named for the basal ganglia because that is the consistent and clinically decisive site, and it is the substrate of the delayed dystonic-parkinsonian syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Before antidotal treatment, plasma lactate concentration correlated positively with anion gap and inversely with systolic blood pressure, spontaneous respiratory rate, and arterial pH.
evidence.explanation: Ties progressive circulatory failure, measured as falling systolic blood pressure, to the severity of the underlying poisoning.

steps/13.description: An early catecholamine-driven hypertensive phase gives way to hypotension, bradyarrhythmia and atrioventricular block, and in severe poisoning to ventricular dysrhythmia and asystole.

evidence.snippet: Signs of cyanide poisoning include headache, vertigo, agitation, confusion, coma, convulsions and death.
evidence.explanation: Lists coma among the clinical signs of cyanide poisoning.

steps/14.description: Depressed consciousness progressing to unresponsiveness is the dominant presenting feature of significant acute poisoning.

evidence.snippet: In severe cases, poisoning can result in coma, convulsions, circulatory failure, and death.
evidence.explanation: Names convulsions among the severe manifestations.

steps/15.description: Generalized convulsions accompanying severe cerebral energy failure.

evidence.snippet: Cyanide poisoning can be the cause of severe encephalopathy in children receiving CAM treatment with substances containing cyanogenic glycosides.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports encephalopathy as a manifestation of cyanide poisoning.

steps/16.description: Diffuse cerebral dysfunction, ranging from agitation and confusion to profound obtundation. The cited evidence establishes it for cyanogenic-glycoside poisoning specifically; the coma and confusion phenotypes carry the corresponding evidence for the other exposure routes.

evidence.snippet: Signs of cyanide poisoning include headache, vertigo, agitation, confusion, coma, convulsions and death.
evidence.explanation: Lists headache among the clinical signs.

steps/17.description: An early, non-specific symptom of lower-level exposure.

evidence.snippet: Signs of cyanide poisoning include headache, vertigo, agitation, confusion, coma, convulsions and death.
evidence.explanation: Lists vertigo among the clinical signs.

steps/18.description: Dizziness and vertigo among the earliest neurological symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Signs of cyanide poisoning include headache, vertigo, agitation, confusion, coma, convulsions and death.
evidence.explanation: Lists confusion among the clinical signs.

steps/19.description: Altered mentation preceding loss of consciousness.

evidence.snippet: Progressive Parkinsonism, dystonia and apraxia of eye opening were seen after cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Primary human report of progressive parkinsonism following cyanide poisoning.

evidence.snippet: Typically, these patients begin to manifest symptoms and signs after a few weeks or months, with progressive rigidity accompanied by flexed upper limbs and extended lower limbs.
evidence.explanation: Describes the delayed rigid-parkinsonian presentation. Graded OTHER: this is a rodent and iPSC-neuron study, and the sentence is its introduction summarising the human case-report literature it cites, not its own data.

steps/20.description: Delayed-onset parkinsonism with progressive rigidity, appearing weeks to months after apparent recovery from severe acute poisoning.

evidence.snippet: A few days after an apparently full recovery he developed a severe dystonia syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Primary human report of delayed dystonia after potassium cyanide ingestion.

evidence.snippet: He had a positive response to an apomorphine test and showed improvement with levodopa treatment.
evidence.explanation: Documents dopaminergic responsiveness of the delayed dystonia, consistent with a striatal rather than a cortical lesion.

evidence.snippet: In fact, in over a dozen human suicide cases of cyanide intoxication, a delayed neurological syndrome has been documented that includes dystonia and parkinsonian signs and symptoms, even in patients who had initially appeared to have had a full recovery after the exposure
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the delayed syndrome is a recurring finding across more than a dozen reports, not a single case. Graded OTHER: the citing paper reports rodent and iPSC-neuron work and is summarising others' cases here.

steps/21.description: Dystonic posturing accompanying the delayed extrapyramidal syndrome in survivors of severe poisoning.

evidence.snippet: Before antidotal treatment, plasma lactate concentration correlated positively with anion gap and inversely with systolic blood pressure, spontaneous respiratory rate, and arterial pH.
evidence.explanation: Links falling systolic blood pressure to increasing poisoning severity as measured by lactate.

evidence.snippet: Following return to spontaneous circulation, the patient was hypotensive requiring dopamine and norepinephrine.
evidence.explanation: Documents vasopressor-dependent hypotension in an occupational cyanide poisoning.

steps/22.description: Hypotension follows the early hypertensive phase and marks decompensating myocardial energy failure.

evidence.snippet: Ventricular bigeminy was observed immediately after ICU admission; therefore, intravenous lidocaine (10 mg) was administered, after which the ECG reverted to sinus rhythm.
evidence.explanation: Documents ventricular bigeminy during the intensive-care course of acute cyanide poisoning.

steps/23.description: Ventricular ectopy and dysrhythmia accompany myocardial energy failure and may appear or persist after antidotal therapy has begun.

evidence.snippet: Emergency medical services arrived and found the patient in asystole and started advanced cardiac life support protocol.
evidence.explanation: Documents asystolic cardiac arrest following occupational cyanide exposure.

steps/24.description: Asystolic or dysrhythmic arrest is the terminal event in severe untreated poisoning and carries a poor prognosis even with prompt antidote.

evidence.snippet: This process prevents aerobic metabolism, which results in diffuse clinical symptoms such as dizziness, headache, weakness, and tachypnea, with progression to seizures, paralysis, and coma
evidence.explanation: Lists tachypnea among the early manifestations.

steps/25.description: Hyperventilation and tachypnea appear early as a respiratory response to metabolic acidosis, before respiratory depression supervenes.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, clinicians should suspect cyanide poisoning in cases of unexplained hyperlactatemia, particularly in patients with symptoms such as respiratory failure, abnormal pulse rate, and even coma.
evidence.explanation: Names respiratory failure among the presenting features that should prompt suspicion of cyanide poisoning alongside unexplained hyperlactatemia.

steps/26.description: Failure of ventilation from depression of the brainstem respiratory centres, the terminal end of the respiratory course. Distinct from the early tachypnea, which is respiratory compensation for the metabolic acidosis and appears at the opposite end of the same course.

evidence.snippet: The immediate and serial measurement of plasma lactate concentrations is useful in assessing the severity of cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Supports serial lactate as the severity measure for this laboratory phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Laboratory findings revealed severe lactic acidosis (pH 7.07) with a high lactate level (19.0 mmol/L) and hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Documents the magnitude of lactic acidosis in a severe poisoning.

steps/27.description: High-anion-gap lactic acidosis is close to universal in significant poisoning and is the practical diagnostic and monitoring surrogate for a blood cyanide assay that is rarely available in time.

evidence.snippet: Laboratory tests showed the following: sodium 145 mEq/L, potassium 5.4 mEq/L, chloride 107 mEq/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 8 mg/dL, creatinine 1.91 mg/dL, and anion gap 32.6.
evidence.explanation: Documents a markedly elevated anion gap in a fatal cyanide exposure.

steps/28.description: The lactic acidosis of cyanide poisoning presents as a wide-anion-gap metabolic acidosis on the basic metabolic panel.

evidence.snippet: Once ingested, cyanide compounds are rapidly absorbed in the stomach as hydrogen cyanide and exert toxicity through cyanide ions.
evidence.explanation: Supports the step from absorption to delivery of free cyanide ion to its cellular target.

edges/0.description: Absorbed cyanide ion distributes rapidly into cells and mitochondria, where it reaches its principal molecular target.

evidence.snippet: Rhodanese or thiosulfate sulfurtransferase (TST) is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme that plays roles in cyanide detoxification, the formation of iron-sulfur proteins and the modification of sulfur-containing enzymes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that circulating cyanide is routed into the mitochondrial sulfurtransferase pathway, which is the step this edge represents.

edges/1.description: The same absorbed cyanide load is the substrate for the endogenous sulfurtransferase clearance pathway, which runs in parallel with toxicity.

evidence.snippet: These ions bind to cellular cytochrome oxidase and interfere with aerobic metabolism, which generates intracellular adenosine triphosphate.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from Complex IV binding to failure of aerobic ATP generation.

edges/2.description: Blocking the terminal electron acceptor step collapses the respiratory chain and with it mitochondrial ATP synthesis.

evidence.snippet: As intracellular adenosine triphosphate depletes, anaerobic metabolism accelerates, leading to increased lactic acid production and venous blood oxygen saturation.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from ATP depletion to lactate accumulation, and notes the accompanying rise in venous oxygen saturation.

edges/3.description: ATP depletion forces compensatory anaerobic glycolysis, whose lactate output accumulates far faster than it can be cleared.

evidence.snippet: Given the high oxygen demand of the brain and heart, early symptoms primarily affect the central nervous and cardiovascular systems.
evidence.explanation: Supports selective early failure of the heart on the basis of its oxidative demand.

edges/4.description: The myocardium is among the tissues whose contractile function fails first when oxidative ATP supply is cut off.

evidence.snippet: Given the high oxygen demand of the brain and heart, early symptoms primarily affect the central nervous and cardiovascular systems.
evidence.explanation: Supports selective early failure of the brain on the basis of its oxidative demand.

edges/5.description: Neurons, with little energy reserve and high oxidative demand, lose ion-gradient maintenance as soon as ATP falls.

edges/8.description: Respiratory compensation for the metabolic acidosis, which is why tachypnea appears before any respiratory depression.

edges/9.description: Loss of contractile ATP supply across the myocardium is what converts a cellular energy deficit into failure of the circulation as a whole.

edges/13.description: Failure of glutamate clearance is the step that converts a reversible energy deficit into structural neuronal injury.

edges/20.description: Depression of the brainstem respiratory centres, which are as oxidative-metabolism-dependent as the rest of the CNS. This is the opposite end of the respiratory course from the early tachypnea driven by metabolic acidosis, and is a late and terminal event.

edges/21.description: Sustained excitotoxic injury in the most metabolically demanding grey-matter regions progresses to frank tissue necrosis.

evidence.snippet: Ingestion and inhalation of toxic salts and gases are the most common sources of toxicity, respectively, though ingestion of plants, medications, and cyanogenic chemicals are alternative routes of exposure.
evidence.explanation: Supports inhalation of hydrogen cyanide gas as a principal route by which the systemic burden is established.

edges/24.description: Hydrogen cyanide in fire smoke crosses the alveolar membrane directly, establishing the systemic cyanide burden within seconds of inhalation.

evidence.snippet: Cyanide salts, eg, potassium cyanide, are the most common type of cyanide ingestant, though exposure to cyanogenic glycosides in plants like cassava root can be fatal as well.
evidence.explanation: Supports cyanide salts as the principal ingested form feeding the systemic burden.

edges/25.description: Workplace cyanide salts and the hydrogen cyanide they liberate on acidification are absorbed by inhalation, ingestion, or through skin, establishing the systemic cyanide burden.

evidence.snippet: Cyanide salts, eg, potassium cyanide, are the most common type of cyanide ingestant, though exposure to cyanogenic glycosides in plants like cassava root can be fatal as well.
evidence.explanation: Supports ingested cyanogenic glycosides as a route to a fatal systemic cyanide burden.

edges/26.description: Ingested cyanogenic glycosides are hydrolysed by plant or gut-microbial beta-glucosidases to release hydrogen cyanide into the gut lumen, from which it is absorbed.

evidence.snippet: High-dose or prolonged therapy with nitroprusside in patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction increases the risk for nitroprusside-induced cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity, respectively.
evidence.explanation: States that nitroprusside therapy itself generates a cyanide burden, which is the step this edge represents.

edges/27.description: Cyanide liberated from the nitroprusside molecule enters the circulation directly, bypassing any absorptive barrier.

evidence.snippet: The P(285)A variant appears to encode a protein with a 50% decrease of in vitro intrinsic clearance compared to the wild-type enzyme.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates a functional TST coding variant with halved intrinsic clearance.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, the six polymorphisms located upstream the ATG initiation codon are responsible for a significant decrease (ranging from 40% to 73%) in promoter activity of a reporter gene compared to the corresponding wild-type sequence.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates regulatory TST variants that reduce expression of the detoxifying enzyme.

genes/0.notes: TST encodes rhodanese (thiosulfate sulfurtransferase), the mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies cyanide to thiocyanate. Functional promoter and coding polymorphisms reduce enzyme expression and intrinsic clearance, so TST genotype is a plausible determinant of individual cyanide susceptibility. These are population-frequency modifier alleles, not Mendelian pathogenic variants, and they have not been validated as clinical risk predictors in poisoned cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Hydroxocobalamin is an attractive antidote due to its rapid cyanide binding and its lack of serious side-effects, even in the absence of cyanide intoxication.
evidence.explanation: Supports hydroxocobalamin as the preferred antidote on binding speed and safety grounds.

evidence.snippet: That 71% of patients survived after treatment with hydroxocobalamin suggests that hydroxocobalamin as first-line antidotal therapy is effective and safe in acute cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Provides the clinical survival data behind first-line use in severe poisoning.

evidence.snippet: In light of the uncertain benefits and potential risks associated with hydroxocobalamin use for cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation injury, its administration should be approached with caution.
evidence.explanation: A 2025 systematic review contradicting the benefit of empiric hydroxocobalamin in the specific case of smoke inhalation, where cyanide toxicity is suspected rather than confirmed.

treatments/0.description: First-line antidote for confirmed cyanide poisoning. The cobalt(III) centre binds cyanide in a 1:1 ratio to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in urine. It does not impair oxygen-carrying capacity, which is the basis for giving it empirically to a fire victim whose carboxyhaemoglobin status is unknown - unlike the nitrites, which would compound the hypoxia. That empiric indication is where the evidence is weakest: a 2025 systematic review of 1238 patients found no mortality benefit in smoke inhalation and signals for acute kidney injury and methaemoglobinaemia. Chromaturia and pink skin discoloration are the usual adverse effects in confirmed poisoning.

evidence.snippet: Hydroxocobalamin has been shown to significantly reduce RBC and plasma cyanide concentrations in animals and surgical patients without producing clinically important adverse effects or toxic metabolites.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that hydroxocobalamin lowers the circulating cyanide burden this node represents.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Hydroxocobalamin sequesters free circulating cyanide as cyanocobalamin, removing it from the pool available to reach mitochondria.

evidence.snippet: Sodium thiosulphate acts more slowly than other antidotes and is indicated in subacute cyanogen poisoning and as an adjunct to acute cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Supports the adjunctive positioning of thiosulfate and its slower onset.

evidence.snippet: After administering sodium thiosulfate, rapid improvement in his medical condition with complete recovery without need for further intensive care treatment was seen.
evidence.explanation: Documents clinical recovery after thiosulfate in cyanogenic-glycoside poisoning.

treatments/1.description: Sulfur donor that accelerates the endogenous rhodanese reaction converting cyanide to renally excreted thiocyanate. Slower in onset than hydroxocobalamin, so it is used as an adjunct rather than sole therapy in fulminant poisoning, but it is safe to combine with hydroxocobalamin.

evidence.snippet: This reaction offers a rational behind the use of thiosulfate as antidote for cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: States that the rhodanese reaction is the rationale for thiosulfate therapy, quoted verbatim from the source.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Exogenous thiosulfate relieves the sulfur-donor limitation on the rhodanese reaction, raising the rate at which cyanide is converted to thiocyanate.

evidence.snippet: Antidotes include oxygen, hydroxocobalamin, di-cobalt EDTA and methaemoglobin-inducers.
evidence.explanation: Places methaemoglobin inducers such as sodium nitrite within the accepted antidote set.

treatments/2.description: Methaemoglobin-forming antidote used when hydroxocobalamin is unavailable. Oxidising haemoglobin iron creates methaemoglobin, which binds cyanide in preference to cytochrome c oxidase. Because the induced methaemoglobinaemia itself reduces oxygen-carrying capacity, it is a poor first choice in a fire victim who may already be carboxyhaemoglobinaemic.

evidence.snippet: Also, the antidotal action of sodium nitrite is partly explained by generation of high mitochondrial levels of NO, which antagonizes the CcOX inhibition.
evidence.explanation: Supports sodium nitrite acting on the Complex IV inhibition node itself, not only as a peripheral cyanide sink.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Nitrite therapy draws cyanide away from Complex IV, both by providing a methaemoglobin sink and, per in vitro work, by generating mitochondrial nitric oxide at levels high enough to antagonise the inhibition. Note this is the high-NO arm of a dose-dependent effect whose low-NO arm potentiates the inhibition instead; see the Cytochrome c Oxidase Inhibition node.

evidence.snippet: He was intubated with rocuronium and fentanyl and administered 0.25 mL of amyl nitrite inhalation every 5 minutes.
evidence.explanation: Documents inhalational amyl nitrite given as initial antidote before hydroxocobalamin.

evidence.snippet: However, as amyl nitrite and sodium nitrite induce methemoglobin, care must be taken to avoid excessive methemoglobin levels when administering these agents.
evidence.explanation: States the methaemoglobinaemia ceiling that limits both nitrite antidotes.

treatments/3.description: Inhalational methaemoglobin-forming antidote, used as a bridge while intravenous access and definitive antidote are being arranged. Same mechanism as sodium nitrite and the same caution: the induced methaemoglobinaemia itself costs oxygen-carrying capacity, so cumulative methaemoglobin has to be watched, and it is a poor choice for a fire victim who may already be carboxyhaemoglobinaemic.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Induced methaemoglobin competes with cytochrome c oxidase for cyanide, drawing it off the mitochondrial target.

evidence.snippet: Dicobalt edetate and hydroxocobalamin are widely used to treat hydrogen cyanide poisoning.
evidence.explanation: Establishes dicobalt edetate as an established antidote in clinical use.

evidence.snippet: Dicobalt edetate is associated with hypertension, tachycardia, and retrosternal pain
evidence.explanation: Gives the adverse-effect profile that explains why hydroxocobalamin is preferred where both are available. Quoted up to the source's inline citation marker, which the snippet matcher strips.

evidence.snippet: Antidotes include oxygen, hydroxocobalamin, di-cobalt EDTA and methaemoglobin-inducers.
evidence.explanation: Places dicobalt edetate within the accepted antidote set.

treatments/4.description: Direct cyanide chelator, the licensed UK antidote and used in some other countries, largely displaced by hydroxocobalamin in North America. It has a narrower therapeutic index - hypertension, tachycardia and retrosternal pain are recognised adverse effects - and a porcine model found licensed doses of both it and hydroxocobalamin ineffective at less than twice the estimated lethal dose.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Chelates circulating cyanide directly, removing it from the pool available to reach mitochondria.

evidence.snippet: Immediate treatment includes 100% oxygen, assisted ventilation, decontamination, correction of acidosis and blood pressure support.
evidence.explanation: Supports 100% oxygen as part of immediate management.

evidence.snippet: Oxygen therapy was initially initiated at 100% concentration and gradually reduced following improvement in lactate levels.
evidence.explanation: Documents 100% oxygen in practice, titrated against the lactate response.

treatments/5.description: 100% oxygen is given despite the lesion being one of utilization rather than delivery; raising the oxygen tension appears to help overcome the reversible Complex IV inhibition by mass action and treats any co-existing carbon monoxide poisoning or hypoxaemia.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: High-concentration oxygen is standard immediate care and is presumed to act by mass action against the reversible Complex IV inhibition. This edge is deliberately left uncited: the clinical recommendation is well sourced (see the treatment-level evidence), but no cited source here states the mass-action mechanism, so the link is recorded as MODULATES rather than asserted as competitive inhibition.

evidence.snippet: In survivors of fire, detoxification of cyanide can occur without specific antidotes with the use of aggressive supportive care.
evidence.explanation: States that cyanide detoxification can occur under supportive care alone in fire survivors. The source (1994) goes further than current practice, concluding that specific assay and treatment are rarely necessary in fire victims; the quote is recorded for what it says, not as an endorsement of withholding antidote.

treatments/6.description: Airway control and mechanical ventilation, vasopressor and fluid support for haemodynamic instability, benzodiazepines for seizures, and correction of acidosis. Extracorporeal support has been used in refractory cardiogenic shock.

evidence.snippet: Immediate treatment includes 100% oxygen, assisted ventilation, decontamination, correction of acidosis and blood pressure support.
evidence.explanation: Supports blood-pressure support and assisted ventilation as management of the cardiovascular failure node.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Vasopressors and ventilatory support maintain perfusion and oxygenation while antidotal therapy and endogenous detoxification remove cyanide.

evidence.snippet: Well-designed randomized controlled trials are urgently needed to establish optimal treatment strategies for this patient population.
evidence.explanation: States the gap directly, as the systematic review's own conclusion.

evidence.snippet: Two studies reported mortality rates, which were found to be similar between the hydroxocobalamin and supportive treatment groups.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the absent mortality benefit that makes this a live question.

evidence.snippet: Although a small sample, patients who received prehospital hydroxocobalamin had improved survival.
evidence.explanation: Cuts the other way from the systematic review, which is why the question is open rather than settled. Its own authors flag the sample size; the survey arm reports only 38 percent of responding US EMS agencies carrying any cyanide antidote, so practice is not converging either.

open_questions/0.rationale: Hydroxocobalamin is first-line for confirmed cyanide poisoning, and its safety profile is what justifies giving it empirically at a fire scene where no cyanide assay is available. But the evidence for that empiric use is thin: a 2025 systematic review of six studies and 1238 patients found similar mortality between hydroxocobalamin and supportive treatment, with signals for acute kidney injury and methaemoglobinaemia, and could not pool the data. The same uncertainty runs the other way in the exposure literature, where a forensic series argues cyanide is an infrequent independent contributor to fire deaths. Resolving it needs a randomised trial that has never been done.

evidence.snippet: This work constitutes the first report of the existence of a functional genetic polymorphism affecting TST activity and should be of great help to investigate certain disorders for which impairment of CN(-) or H(2)S detoxification have been suggested to be involved.
evidence.explanation: The source frames its own result as a tool for future investigation of cyanide-detoxification disorders, which is precisely the study that has not been done.

open_questions/1.rationale: The enzymology is settled: functional TST promoter and coding variants cut expression by 40-73% and intrinsic clearance by half. What is missing is any demonstration that carriers of these alleles are actually more susceptible. The variants were characterised in fifty French individuals with no exposure outcome attached, and no poisoned or occupationally exposed cohort has been genotyped. Until one is, the pathway from genotype to clinical risk is an inference from in vitro clearance, not an observation.

evidence.snippet: Through trio exome sequencing we identified de novo mutations in SLC12A2 in six children with neurodevelopmental disorders. All had developmental delay or intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: Landmark study identifying de novo SLC12A2 mutations as causal in neurodevelopmental disorders.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the SLC12A2 gene, which encodes the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter-1 (NKCC1), are linked to various conditions such as neurodevelopmental deficits, deafness, and fluid secretion in different epithelia.
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive review establishing SLC12A2 as a haploinsufficient human disease gene.

steps/1.description: Delpire-McNeill syndrome is caused by de novo heterozygous mutations in the SLC12A2 gene, which encodes the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter 1 (NKCC1). NKCC1 is a widely expressed electroneutral cation-chloride cotransporter that mediates coupled transport of sodium, potassium, and chloride ions across cell membranes. Loss-of-function mutations disrupt intracellular chloride homeostasis, affecting neuronal development, auditory function, and multiple organ systems. All tested variants reduce cotransporter function in Xenopus laevis oocytes.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of SLC12A2 expression in foetal brain at 16-18 weeks post-conception revealed high expression in radial glial cells, compatible with a role in neurogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that SLC12A2 is highly expressed in radial glial cells during critical neurogenic period.

evidence.snippet: Gene co-expression analysis in cells robustly expressing SLC12A2 at 16-18 weeks post-conception identified a transcriptomic programme associated with active neurogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Shows SLC12A2-expressing cells have a transcriptomic program reflecting active neurogenesis.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to control neurons, little or no net current was observed at the resting membrane potential in homozygote NKCC1 mutant DRG neurons. E(GABA) was significantly more negative, demonstrating the absence of Cl(-) accumulation in these cells.
evidence.explanation: NKCC1 knockout mice show loss of chloride accumulation and absence of GABA-mediated depolarization.

steps/2.description: NKCC1 plays a critical role in establishing intracellular chloride concentration in developing neurons. In radial glial cells during fetal corticogenesis (16-18 weeks post-conception), NKCC1 maintains elevated intracellular chloride, making GABA depolarizing and excitatory, which supports neuronal migration, differentiation, and synaptogenesis. Mutations disrupting NKCC1 function prematurely shift the developmental GABA excitatory-inhibitory switch, impairing neural progenitor expansion and cortical development.

evidence.snippet: We show here that lte mutations correspond to lesions in nkcc1.
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish model demonstrates NKCC1 is required for regulation of endolymph volume.

evidence.snippet: In the inner ear, K+ transport is required for the mechano-transduction of auditory stimuli. SLC12A2 functions as a dimer and has several isoforms; only one isoform contains exon 21, and this isoform is almost exclusively expressed in the inner ear/cochlea.
evidence.explanation: Confirms cochlear-specific expression of NKCC1 exon 21 isoform essential for endolymph homeostasis.

steps/3.description: NKCC1 is essential for endolymph production in the inner ear. It is expressed in the strial marginal cells of the cochlea and vestibular dark cells, where it drives potassium and chloride transport into the endolymph. Loss of NKCC1 function leads to reduced endolymph volume, decreased endocochlear potential, hair cell degeneration, and bilateral sensorineural deafness with vestibular areflexia.

evidence.snippet: This study describes a 13-yr-old girl with orthostatic intolerance, respiratory weakness, multiple endocrine abnormalities, pancreatic insufficiency, and multiorgan failure involving the gut and bladder.
evidence.explanation: First human case demonstrating multisystem secretory dysfunction from heterozygous SLC12A2 truncation.

evidence.snippet: Herein we describe a child admitted to the NIH Undiagnosed Diseases Program with global developmental delay, sensorineural hearing loss, gastrointestinal abnormalities, and absent salivation.
evidence.explanation: Kilquist syndrome case showing severe secretory epithelial dysfunction from homozygous SLC12A2 deletion.

steps/4.description: NKCC1 is expressed on basolateral membranes of secretory epithelia including salivary glands, pancreas, trachea, intestine, and sweat glands, where it supports transepithelial fluid secretion. Severe NKCC1 deficiency causes absent or reduced salivation, tear production, and sweat production, as well as respiratory complications from dry mucosa and mucus plugging.

evidence.snippet: All had developmental delay or intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: All six children with de novo SLC12A2 mutations had developmental delay.

steps/5.description: Delayed attainment of developmental milestones is a hallmark feature, with all identified patients showing motor and cognitive delays from infancy.

evidence.snippet: All had developmental delay or intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: Intellectual disability across the spectrum was documented in the McNeill cohort.

steps/6.description: Mild to moderate intellectual disability is present in most affected individuals, with some cases showing severe impairment.

evidence.snippet: All had developmental delay or intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: Speech and language delay is part of the global developmental delay phenotype described in SLC12A2 patients.

steps/7.description: Speech and language development is significantly delayed or absent.

evidence.snippet: hypotonia with delayed or absent walking
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists hypotonia with delayed or absent walking among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

steps/8.description: Reduced muscle tone is commonly observed in infancy, contributing to delayed motor milestones. Some patients transition from hypotonia to hypertonia and spasticity.

evidence.snippet: Two had sensorineural deafness. We also identified SLC12A2 variants in three individuals with non-syndromic bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular areflexia.
evidence.explanation: Two of six neurodevelopmental patients plus three DFNA78 patients had sensorineural hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with profound congenital hearing loss and vestibular areflexia with a de novo variant in SLC12A2 located in the splice donor site: NM_001046.2: c.2977+4_2977+7del causing an in-frame skip of exon 21
evidence.explanation: Additional case confirming exon 21 variants cause cochlear-restricted hearing loss.

steps/9.description: Sensorineural deafness occurs in a subset of patients due to impaired endolymph production from NKCC1 dysfunction in the stria vascularis.

evidence.snippet: de novo heterozygous SLC12A2 variants have also been implicated in developmental delay with autistic features.
evidence.explanation: Confirms autistic features are part of the SLC12A2-associated neurodevelopmental phenotype.

steps/10.description: Autistic spectrum features including social communication difficulties and restricted interests are observed in some affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: Through trio exome sequencing we identified de novo mutations in SLC12A2 in six children with neurodevelopmental disorders. All had developmental delay or intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe. Two had sensorineural deafness. We also identified SLC12A2 variants in three individuals with non-syndromic bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular areflexia.
evidence.explanation: Three of nine SLC12A2-variant individuals described in the abstract had vestibular areflexia, which falls in the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with profound congenital hearing loss and vestibular areflexia with a de novo variant in SLC12A2
evidence.explanation: Additional case confirming vestibular areflexia in SLC12A2 mutations.

steps/11.description: Bilateral loss of vestibular function frequently accompanies hearing impairment, contributing to delayed motor development and balance difficulties.

evidence.snippet: brain anomalies (including cortical dysplasia and agenesis of the corpus callosum)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists cortical dysplasia among variable brain anomalies in Delpire-McNeill syndrome.

steps/12.description: Structural brain malformation reflecting disrupted neuronal migration during fetal development, observed on brain MRI in some patients.

evidence.snippet: brain anomalies (including cortical dysplasia and agenesis of the corpus callosum) and spasticity
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists spasticity among variable Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

steps/13.description: Some patients transition from early hypotonia to hypertonia and spasticity.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists global developmental delay among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/4.description: Disrupted neurogenesis and developmental GABA signaling manifest as global developmental delay.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists mild to moderate intellectual disability among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/5.description: Disrupted neurodevelopment manifests as intellectual disability.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists delayed, poor, or absent speech among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/6.description: Neurodevelopmental impairment manifests as delayed, poor, or absent speech.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists hypotonia with delayed or absent walking among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/7.description: Neurodevelopmental motor involvement manifests as hypotonia and delayed walking.

evidence.snippet: bilateral sensorineural deafness, and autistic features
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists autistic features among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/8.description: Disrupted neurodevelopment can manifest as autistic features.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists cortical dysplasia among variable brain anomalies in Delpire-McNeill syndrome.

edges/9.description: Disrupted cortical development can manifest as cortical dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: brain anomalies (including cortical dysplasia and agenesis of the corpus callosum) and spasticity
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists spasticity among variable Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/10.description: Neurodevelopmental motor-system involvement can manifest as spasticity.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists bilateral sensorineural deafness among the defining Delpire-McNeill syndrome features.

edges/11.description: Impaired inner-ear ion transport and endolymph homeostasis manifest as bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with profound congenital hearing loss and vestibular areflexia with a de novo variant in SLC12A2
evidence.explanation: This case report connects de novo SLC12A2 variation to hearing loss with vestibular areflexia.

edges/12.description: Inner-ear SLC12A2 dysfunction can involve vestibular function and manifest as vestibular areflexia.

evidence.snippet: The SLC12A2 de novo mutation rate was demonstrated to be significantly elevated in the deciphering developmental disorders cohort.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates elevated de novo mutation rate in the DDD cohort.

evidence.snippet: All tested variants were shown to reduce co-transporter function in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
evidence.explanation: Functional validation showing all tested variants reduce cotransporter activity.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing revealed a de novo, loss-of-function allele in SLC12A2, the gene encoding the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter-1. The 11-bp deletion in exon 22 results in frameshift (p.Val1026Phefs*2) and truncation of the carboxy-terminal tail of the cotransporter.
evidence.explanation: First characterization of a truncating SLC12A2 variant causing multisystem dysfunction.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous mutations in SLC12A2 on chromosome 5q23.3. All tested variants reduce cotransporter function. The de novo mutation rate shows 9.62-fold enrichment in the DDD cohort (P = 2.71 x 10^-6).

treatments/0.description: Targets communication deficits through speech, sign language, or augmentative alternative communication devices.

treatments/1.description: Stretching, strengthening, and mobility training to address gross motor delay and spasticity.

treatments/2.description: Direct stimulation of the auditory nerve for patients with sensorineural hearing loss.

treatments/3.description: Acoustic amplification for patients with mild to moderate sensorineural hearing loss.

treatments/4.description: Risk assessment and family planning. Recurrence risk is extremely low (<1/200) as cases arise from de novo mutations.

treatments/5.description: Multidisciplinary management including feeding support, respiratory management, and seizure control. No disease-modifying therapies are currently available.

treatments/6.description: Antiseizure medications should be selected based on seizure type and individualized for each patient. Caution is warranted with GABAergic agents (e.g., benzodiazepines, barbiturates), as disruption of the normal GABA excitatory-to-inhibitory developmental switch by NKCC1 haploinsufficiency may alter the pharmacodynamics of drugs that rely on chloride-mediated GABA inhibition.

treatments/7.description: Vestibular rehabilitation therapy, a specialized form of physical therapy, can help patients with vestibular areflexia compensate for balance deficits through central adaptation and gaze-stabilization exercises. Referral is recommended for patients with documented vestibular dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: cardiotoxicity from other cardenolides such as the yellow oleander are also a major problem, with tens of thousands of cases of poisoning each year in South Asia
evidence.explanation: Establishes the scale and geography of the non-pharmaceutical route. BACKGROUND rather than REVIEW_SYNTHESIS because the sentence sits in the review's background section, stating context rather than its own synthesis; the review's synthesis is quoted on the treatments, from its results.

evidence.snippet: The main route of elimination is renal excretion of digoxin, which is closely correlated with the glomerular filtration rate.
evidence.explanation: Establishes renal clearance as the dominant elimination route, which is why declining glomerular filtration is the commonest route to chronic accumulation.

evidence.snippet: High concentrations are found in the heart and kidneys, but the skeletal muscles form the largest digoxin storage.
evidence.explanation: The tissue distribution that makes extracorporeal removal futile: almost none of the body burden is in the blood at any moment.

steps/1.description: Tissue concentrations of digoxin or another cardiac glycoside above what the myocardium tolerates. Reached three ways that behave differently: a single large ingestion in someone not already taking the drug, an extra dose on top of chronic therapy, and slow accumulation at an unchanged dose when renal clearance falls or a P-glycoprotein inhibitor is added. The distinction matters clinically, and the mechanism predicts why: a sudden large inhibition redistributes potassium faster than the kidney can compensate, which is the usual explanation for hyperkalemia being described as an acute-pattern finding.

evidence.snippet: Digoxin's primary mechanism of action is to inhibit the sodium-potassium ATPase pump in the heart's myocardium.
evidence.explanation: Names the molecular lesion. Graded BACKGROUND because the sentence is in the introduction of a case report, restating established pharmacology rather than reporting this paper's own finding.

steps/2.description: Blockade of the sarcolemmal sodium pump. This is simultaneously the therapeutic mechanism and the toxic one - what changes with dose is the fraction of pumps occupied, not the kind of effect - which is the structural reason digitalis has no margin between efficacy and harm.

evidence.snippet: BF and CBG demonstrated a concentration-dependent (0.1 to100 µM) I Ca,L inhibition (maximal ≥50%) without and with the NKA activity blocked by 10 µM Oua
evidence.explanation: The controlled result that makes this node separable from the canonical chain: the calcium-current inhibition is present both with and without the pump already blocked by ouabain, so pump inhibition cannot be producing it. The paper's conclusion sentence states this more directly but quotes a bracketed ion notation that the reference validator strips as a citation marker, so the result sentence is quoted instead.

evidence.snippet: BF and CBG at 100 µM demonstrated a strong inhibition (≥40%) of the rapidly activating component of the delayed rectifier K+ current (I Kr)
evidence.explanation: The measured potassium-current inhibition behind this node. Note the concentration is far above the therapeutic range, which is why the node is grouped under an EMERGING hypothesis rather than the canonical chain.

evidence.snippet: which were more remarkable than that of Oua and PEA (with maximized inhibition ~15% and ~10%, and estimated IC50s of way above 100 µM)
evidence.explanation: Scoped to the claim that this mechanism operates at the digitalis cardenolides. In the same experiment the two cardenolides tested inhibited the current by about 10 to 15 per cent with IC50s above 100 micromolar, so the pump-independent effect is essentially a bufadienolide finding. It does not refute the mechanism, which the bufadienolide arm establishes.

steps/3.description:
Inhibition of the L-type calcium current and of the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current by the glycoside itself, demonstrated with cytosolic calcium chelated and the sodium pump already blocked - so neither the calcium-overload chain nor pump inhibition accounts for it.
The agent caveat is large enough to state plainly: the effect was measured mostly in bufadienolides, which are toad-derived, and the two cardenolides tested - ouabain and pecilocerin A, the class digoxin belongs to - showed around 10 to 15 per cent inhibition with IC50s above 100 micromolar, which is to say essentially none at attainable concentrations. Digoxin itself was not tested. The node is retained because the mechanism is real and this entry covers bufadienolide sources, but it should not be read as operating in ordinary digoxin poisoning.

evidence.snippet: In cardiac myocytes, NKA inhibition causes an accumulation of cytosolic Na+ which in turn activates the reverse-mode of Na+/Ca2+-exchanger.
evidence.explanation: States the pump-to-sodium-to-exchanger step in one sentence. Graded BACKGROUND because it is this paper's framing of established mechanism, not its own result - its own result is the pump-independent one cited elsewhere in this entry.

steps/4.description: Rising cytosolic sodium in the cardiomyocyte, the immediate consequence of a pump that is no longer extruding it.

steps/5.description: Loss of calcium export through NCX1, the exchanger that normally trades three sodium ions inward for one calcium ion outward. Nothing is wrong with the exchanger; its driving gradient has been spent.

evidence.snippet: Inhibition of this pump causes increased intracellular calcium, resulting in increased myocardial contractility and cardiac output while augmenting cardiac vagal tone
evidence.explanation: Links pump inhibition to the calcium rise, and in the same sentence to the vagal limb, which is why it is cited on both nodes. BACKGROUND for the same reason as the pump node.

steps/6.description: Calcium accumulating in the cytosol and, through SERCA, in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. At therapeutic occupancy this is the positive inotropic effect; past a threshold the store holds more than it can retain.

steps/7.description: Unscheduled release of stored calcium through the ryanodine receptor after repolarization is complete - calcium arriving when the cell should be electrically quiet.

evidence.snippet: In quiescent fibers, strophanthidin caused the membrane potential to depolarize and to develop oscillations of progressively larger magnitude which were followed by spontaneous activity.
evidence.explanation: The classical microelectrode experiment behind this node: a cardiac glycoside produces growing diastolic oscillations that end in spontaneous firing, in canine Purkinje fibres. The glycoside here is strophanthidin, not digoxin.
