steps/23.description: Recruited pDCs become a major source of IFN-alpha and IL-33 in induced mouse pancreatitis. Their IFN-alpha sustains T-cell CCL25 production, forming an experimentally supported feedback loop. TLR9 stimulation is required for maximal cytokine output in coculture; human NET-stimulated pDC experiments independently support enhanced IgG4 production.

evidence.snippet: Indications for treatment are symptomatic patients with obstructive jaundice, abdominal pain, posterior pancreatic pain, and involvement of extra-pancreatic digestive organs, including IgG4-related cholangitis.
evidence.explanation: The digestive guideline recognizes pancreatic/biliary manifestations and obstruction.

steps/24.description: Lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and fibrosis affect pancreatic and biliary structures. Duct narrowing and inflammatory enlargement can cause obstructive jaundice; persistent pancreatic injury can leave exocrine or endocrine dysfunction. An IgG4-related pancreatic mass requires distinction from malignancy.

evidence.snippet: tubulointerstitial nephritis with abundant IgG4+ plasma cells was the most common finding (n = 14; 93.3%), and 4 (26.7%) patients had membranous nephropathy.
evidence.explanation: Renal biopsy findings concern the selected 15-biopsy renal cohort, not the prevalence in all IgG4-RD.

steps/25.description: Tubulointerstitial inflammation with IgG4-rich plasma cells and fibrosis can impair intrinsic renal function. Membranous nephropathy occurs in a subset and may coexist. Hypocomplementemia is associated, but the reviewed evidence does not establish a single complement-mediated causal route for all renal injury.

evidence.snippet: Para-aortic or peri-ureteric RPF was evident in 14 patients (50%). This was associated with ureteric obstruction in 6 patients (21.4%)
evidence.explanation: Imaging documents the obstructive mechanism within 28 patients with kidney or retroperitoneal involvement.

steps/26.description: Periaortic and periureteric fibroinflammatory tissue can encase ureters and obstruct drainage, producing hydronephrosis and postrenal dysfunction. This route is distinct from intrinsic IgG4-related tubulointerstitial nephritis.

evidence.snippet: This makes it tempting to speculate that a decreased epithelial barrier function with attraction of immune cells and impaired bicarbonate secretion as a result of dysfunction of laminin 511 by autoantibody binding could potentially be a common systemic pathogenic mechanism in a subset of patients with IgG4-RD.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, IgG4-RD can be classified into four clinical phenotypes based on the distribution of affected organs, with each phenotype showing different dominant immune cell subsets involved in its pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: A review proposes that each organ-distribution phenotype carries its own dominant immune subset. This is the most explicit statement of the mechanism this gap asks about, but it is a synthesis rather than phenotype-matched immunophenotyping, so it motivates the gap instead of closing it.

open_questions/1.rationale: IgG4-RD has a conserved fibroinflammatory histology, but the current model cannot yet explain why particular organs are targeted in individual patients. Organ-restricted antigens, epithelial-barrier functions, chemokine niches, and local stromal repair programs remain plausible but incompletely connected mechanisms.

open_questions/2.rationale: B-cell cocultures establish collagen-promoting activity, but do not reproduce whorled architecture. MMP12 expression in macrophages does not establish a collagen-deposition edge. CTL-associated apoptosis does not by itself explain venous obliteration. The isolated-aortitis comparator is not confirmed IgG4-RD, and human organ distribution cannot be inferred from induced mouse pancreatic initiation. These remain gaps, with clinical and histological findings retained without invented arrows.

This drives abnormal cortical cytoarchitecture (cortical tubers, focal cortical dysplasia, dysmorphic neurons) that seeds the epileptogenic network, and provides the mechanistic rationale for mTOR-inhibitor precision therapy.

steps/2.description: The IESS phenotype reflects abnormal synchronized activity in immature cortical-subcortical networks, producing epileptic spasms and the hypsarrhythmic EEG pattern. A recurrent mechanistic theme is a shift toward net excitation in the developing cortex through impaired GABAergic interneuron development/function (interneuronopathy, exemplified by ARX loss of function), consistent with the conserved epilepsy excitation-inhibition imbalance pattern and with the efficacy of the GABA-augmenting drug vigabatrin.

open_questions/0.rationale: IESS is defined precisely by this convergence: structural, metabolic, and genetic causes producing an indistinguishable spasms/hypsarrhythmia phenotype within a narrow infantile window. The entry currently models the convergence descriptively (diverse etiologies -> abnormal epileptic network activity) but the physiological hub that unifies them is unresolved. Candidate convergent nodes proposed in the literature include CRH/stress-axis hyperactivity, a mistimed GABA developmental switch (NKCC1/KCC2 imbalance), and brainstem/cortical dysmaturation. Identifying the shared hub matters because it would define the syndrome mechanistically rather than by list of causes, and could reveal an etiology-agnostic therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: The stress theory of spasms yielded the corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH)-induced model, which showed the higher proconvulsant potency of CRH in developing rats, although only limbic seizures were observed.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly notes that the CRH model reproduces only limbic (not classic flexion) seizures, the core of the model-to-human mismatch.

evidence.snippet: two genetic mouse models of interneuronopathies with infantile spasms due to loss of function of the aristaless X-linked homeobox-related gene (ARX).

open_questions/1.rationale: The mechanistic case for the excitation-inhibition (ARX interneuronopathy) and stress/CRH arms rests largely on rodent models, yet their fidelity to human IESS is uncertain. The CRH model produces only limbic seizures rather than the classic epileptic (flexion) spasms, and no rodent model convincingly reproduces the human hypsarrhythmic EEG signature or the tightly age-restricted human window. This is a HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than a plain knowledge gap: model-system evidence EXISTS, but its translational validity is the open question. Resolving it matters because the CRH model is the principal mechanistic rationale offered for hormonal (ACTH) therapy, and the ARX model underpins the interneuronopathy account of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Initial control of spasms between days 14 and 42 of treatment was associated with higher mean VABS scores at 18 months

open_questions/2.rationale: Observational data consistently associate shorter lead-time to effective treatment and early spasm control with better developmental outcome, which is often read as evidence that the epileptic encephalopathy itself drives developmental harm and that stopping it early rescues development. But because etiology strongly confounds both treatment response and baseline developmental potential, the association is equally compatible with early responders simply having milder underlying brain disease. Distinguishing a causal disease-modifying effect from a prognostic marker is decision-relevant: it determines whether aggressive early treatment escalation changes long-term outcome or only changes the seizure course.

treatments/3.description: No iNTS vaccine is yet licensed, but O-antigen-based outer-membrane vesicle and Salmonella conjugate vaccines have shown early adult safety and immunogenicity and are advancing through clinical development.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, our genomic and transmission analyses suggest that iNTS infections may involve human-to-human transmission, with diarrheal patients acting as potential intermediaries, deviating from typical zoonotic pathways.
evidence.explanation: The genomic census motivates the open question by supporting non-classic transmission routes for iNTS.

open_questions/0.rationale: African iNTS pathovars deviate from classic zoonotic foodborne Salmonella epidemiology, and recent genomic analyses support a human-to-human component; the environmental reservoir, infectious intermediates, and relative contributions of food, water, and anthroponotic spread remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: This can develop either as a consequence of thrombosis in situ or following embolic occlusion of a cerebral blood vessel
evidence.explanation: This review supports thrombosis and embolic vascular occlusion as proximal ischemic-stroke mechanisms.

steps/0.description: In situ thrombosis, artery-to-artery embolism, cardioembolism, or proximal large-vessel occlusion interrupts cerebral blood flow and initiates the ischemic cascade.

evidence.snippet: In ischemic strokes, severe blood flow deficits in the core rapidly decrease ATP levels and energy stores.
evidence.explanation: This supports energy failure as an early consequence of ischemic core hypoperfusion.

evidence.snippet: The ischemic penumbra then denotes an “at risk” region that is functionally impaired, but potentially salvageable.
evidence.explanation: This supports the penumbra as an at-risk but potentially salvageable tissue compartment.

steps/1.description: Severe flow deficits rapidly deplete ATP in the ischemic core, while residual perfusion in the surrounding penumbra allows slower active cell death and creates a time-sensitive target for reperfusion therapy.

evidence.snippet: autophagy was activated within 7 d of tMCAO induction, and it strengthened at 1 d and then weakened steadily from 3 to 7 d
evidence.explanation: Primary rodent time-course evidence for early activation and subsequent decline of autophagic flux after ischemic stroke.

evidence.snippet: Our results show a time-dependent decrease in CTSD protein levels and activity in the mouse brain after stroke and neurons following OGD, with concurrent defects in lysosomal function.
evidence.explanation: Primary MCAO and oxygen-glucose-deprivation evidence for progressive loss of lysosomal (autophagic-clearance) function after ischemia, distinct from the review (PMID:42419491) that first proposed this axis as a hypothesis.

steps/2.description: Macroautophagy is activated within the ischemic penumbra after arterial occlusion, with autophagosome numbers and autophagy-marker (Beclin-1, LC3B) levels rising early and then declining over the following days as autophagic flux weakens. In parallel, the lysosomal protease cathepsin D (CTSD) is progressively lost, and this lysosomal dysfunction, rather than autophagy induction itself, is the step this node conforms to: loss of CTSD is sufficient to cause lysosomal dysfunction and aggravates neuronal death under oxygen-glucose deprivation, while restoring CTSD activity protects neurons.

evidence.snippet: The treatment of ABT-263 reduced senescence of astrocytes and CECs in MCAO mice.
evidence.explanation: Pharmacologic senolysis directly reducing astrocyte/endothelial senescence markers in the same MCAO model, supporting a causal (druggable) role rather than a bystander correlation.

evidence.snippet: localized removal of senescent cells in the injured brain through the stereotaxical injection of lenti-INK-ATTAC viruses generates neuroprotective effects, protecting against acute ischemic brain injury in mice
evidence.explanation: Independent genetic (non-pharmacologic) senescent-cell clearance approach converging on the same neuroprotective outcome.

evidence.snippet: Patients with poor outcome (mRS > 2) had enriched senescence gene expression compared with those with good outcome (mRS ≤ 2)
evidence.explanation: Independent human clinical evidence linking a senescence-associated gene-expression signature to worse functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke, complementing the rodent mechanistic data above.

steps/3.description: Middle cerebral artery occlusion triggers acute cellular senescence in astrocytes and cerebral endothelial cells within the ischemic hemisphere, marked by p16INK4a upregulation and a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) of MMP-3, IL-1alpha, and IL-6. Senolytic clearance of these senescent cells, whether systemic (ABT-263) or local (targeted lenti-INK-ATTAC), reduces SASP factor levels and improves neurological and locomotor outcomes after occlusion. A senescence-associated blood gene-expression signature is independently associated with worse 90-day functional outcome in acute ischemic stroke patients.

evidence.snippet: Inflammatory signaling is involved in all stages of the ischemic cascade, from the early damaging events triggered by arterial occlusion
evidence.explanation: This supports inflammation as a contributor from early post-occlusion injury through later repair.

evidence.snippet: The BBB homeostasis is remarkably dependent on endothelial-astrocyte-matrix interactions
evidence.explanation: This supports endothelial-astrocyte-matrix interactions as central to blood-brain barrier integrity after stroke.

steps/4.description: Ischemic injury engages endothelial cells, astrocytes, neurons, microglia, and peripheral immune cells; inflammatory signaling, protease activation, and matrix injury can disrupt the blood-brain barrier and amplify tissue damage.

evidence.snippet: significantly elevated expression of TRIM62 was detected in peri-infarct area of wild type (WT) mice
evidence.explanation: Localizes the TRIM62-NLRP3 signaling axis specifically to the peri-infarct (penumbral) region.

evidence.snippet: nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome was dramatically activated in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) conditions, while being ameliorated in TRIM62-KO mice
evidence.explanation: Direct primary evidence of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in ischemia/reperfusion, distinct from the review (PMID:42419491) that first proposed this axis as a hypothesis.

steps/5.description: The NLRP3 inflammasome is dramatically activated in the peri-infarct (penumbral) area after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion, and genetic suppression of its upstream regulator TRIM62 ameliorates NLRP3 activation, reduces neuroinflammation and apoptosis, and attenuates infarct outcomes.

evidence.snippet: accumulated data over the past two decades have implicated excitotoxicity, oxidative stress and in some circumstances, apoptotic-like pathways
evidence.explanation: This supports excitotoxic, oxidative, and apoptotic-like injury processes in acute stroke cell death.

evidence.snippet: Brain injury following stroke results from a complex series of pathophysiological events including excitotoxicity, oxidative and nitrative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: This review independently supports the multi-mechanism cellular injury cascade after ischemic stroke.

steps/6.description: Energy failure and impaired glutamate reuptake promote excitotoxic calcium influx, oxidative and nitrative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptotic-like cell death in neurons and neighboring neurovascular cells.

edges/0.description: Occlusion creates a severely hypoperfused core and a potentially salvageable penumbra with residual perfusion.

edges/1.description: Energy failure disrupts ionic gradients and glutamate handling, triggering calcium overload, oxidative injury, and cell death.

edges/2.description: Ischemic injury activates vascular, glial, and immune responses in the neurovascular unit.

evidence.snippet: Beclin-1, LC3B, ROS, 4-HNE, 8-OHDG, GFAP, TNF-α and IL-6 levels increased (P < 0.01), while p62 and IL-10 levels decreased (P < 0.01) after tMCAO compared to those in the sham group.
evidence.explanation: Directly ties post-occlusion energy/oxidative stress to the induction of autophagy markers (Beclin-1 up, p62 down) in this same tMCAO model.

edges/3.description: Energy failure activates macroautophagy within hours of occlusion, with autophagosome numbers and autophagy-marker levels in the ischemic penumbra rising over the following days.

evidence.snippet: acute senescence is triggered by middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) surgery, particularly in astrocytes and cerebral endothelial cells (CECs)
evidence.explanation: Establishes this specific edge: MCAO-induced ischemia triggers acute senescence in astrocytes and cerebral endothelial cells.

edges/4.description: Astrocytes and cerebral endothelial cells within the ischemic territory undergo acute cellular senescence following arterial occlusion.

edges/5.description: Microglial and vascular inflammatory signaling within the neurovascular unit provides the priming and danger signals for NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in the peri-infarct penumbra.

evidence.snippet: CTSD knockdown further aggravates lysosomal dysfunction and cell death in OGD-exposed neurons.
evidence.explanation: Direct loss-of-function evidence that impaired lysosomal (autophagic-clearance) function worsens ischemic neuronal death. This specific result is from oxygen-glucose-deprived primary cortical neuron culture (the paper's in vitro arm), distinct from the MCAO-mouse evidence cited at the node level.

evidence.snippet: Restoration of CTSD protein levels via lentiviral transduction increases CTSD activity in neurons and, thus, renders resistance to OGD-mediated defects in lysosomal function and cell death.
evidence.explanation: Complementary gain-of-function evidence that restoring the autophagic-lysosomal clearance step is directly protective, supporting a causal (not merely correlative) role for this node. Also from the oxygen-glucose-deprivation cell-culture arm of this study.

edges/6.description: Loss of cathepsin D-dependent lysosomal function aggravates, and its restoration protects against, oxygen-glucose deprivation-induced neuronal cell death, adding a lysosomal-clearance-failure route to excitotoxic and oxidative neuronal injury.

evidence.snippet: The upregulation of p16INK4a and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors including matrix metalloproteinase-3, interleukin-1 alpha and -6 were observed in oxygen-glucose deprivation-treated astrocytes and CECs.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the specific SASP factors (a matrix protease and two proinflammatory cytokines) released by senescent astrocytes/CECs that would be expected to feed forward into neurovascular inflammation and barrier disruption. This measurement is from oxygen-glucose-deprived cell culture, distinct from the MCAO-mouse in vivo evidence cited elsewhere on this node.

edges/7.description: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype (MMP-3, IL-1alpha, IL-6) released by senescent astrocytes and endothelial cells adds to neurovascular inflammatory signaling and blood-brain barrier injury within the ischemic hemisphere.

evidence.snippet: The TRIM62 knockout (KO) mice exhibited alleviated apoptosis and neuroinflammation in the ischemic brain, eventually attenuating the stroke outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Suppressing NLRP3-regulated neuroinflammation (via TRIM62 knockout) directly reduces neuronal apoptosis and improves stroke outcome, supporting a causal contribution to neuronal injury.

edges/8.description: NLRP3-driven neuroinflammatory signaling in the peri-infarct area adds a further, innate-immune route to neuronal injury and apoptosis in the ischemic territory.

evidence.snippet: treatment with intravenous t-PA within three hours of the onset of ischemic stroke improved clinical outcome at three months.
evidence.explanation: This randomized trial established early IV t-PA benefit in acute ischemic stroke.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with this weak recommendation, optimal patient management will likely often include co-treatment with intravenous alteplase, depending on local circumstances and patient presentation.
evidence.explanation: The clinical practice guideline supports co-treatment with intravenous alteplase (t-PA) alongside endovascular thrombectomy in acute large-vessel-occlusion ischemic stroke.

treatments/0.description: Intravenous tissue plasminogen activator can restore perfusion in eligible early-presenting patients, improving 3-month functional outcome while increasing symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage risk.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Thrombolysis aims to dissolve the occluding thrombus and restore cerebral perfusion.

evidence.snippet: Endovascular thrombectomy led to significantly reduced disability at 90 days compared with control
evidence.explanation: This pooled randomized-trial analysis supports thrombectomy for selected large-vessel ischemic stroke.

treatments/1.description: Endovascular clot retrieval improves disability outcomes in selected patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by proximal anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Mechanical clot retrieval removes the proximal occlusion and restores blood flow in large-vessel ischemic stroke.

evidence.snippet: DAPT was more effective than SAPT for prevention of secondary ischemic stroke when initiated early after the onset of minor stroke/high-risk transient ischemic attack and treatment duration was <90 days.
evidence.explanation: This systematic review supports antiplatelet therapy as secondary prevention after selected ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA presentations.

treatments/2.description: Antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrent ischemic events after non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack, with duration and intensity balanced against bleeding risk.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Platelet inhibition reduces recurrent thrombotic arterial occlusion risk after qualifying ischemic stroke presentations.

evidence.snippet: In patients with atrial fibrillation and previous stroke or transient ischemic attack, oral anticoagulants reduce the risk of recurrence over antiplatelets or no antithrombotic treatment.
evidence.explanation: This guideline supports oral anticoagulation for secondary prevention in atrial fibrillation-associated ischemic stroke or TIA.

treatments/3.description: Anticoagulation, particularly direct oral anticoagulant therapy when appropriate, is used after ischemic stroke associated with atrial fibrillation to reduce recurrent embolic events while managing hemorrhage risk.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Anticoagulation reduces cardioembolic clot formation that can occlude cerebral arteries in atrial fibrillation-associated ischemic stroke.

evidence.snippet: These recommendations align with the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 for optimizing cardiovascular and brain health
evidence.explanation: This guideline supports multi-domain vascular risk-factor control for primary stroke prevention.

treatments/4.description: Stroke prevention focuses on cardiovascular and brain-health domains including diet, activity, weight, sleep, glycemic control, blood pressure, lipids, and tobacco avoidance.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Risk-factor control reduces the vascular conditions that promote thrombotic and embolic stroke.

evidence.snippet: Over 40 causative genes have been reported, all encoding for proteins implicated in the structure or functioning of the primary cilium, a subcellular organelle widely present in embryonic and adult tissues.
evidence.explanation: Defines the genetic architecture of JS as variants in genes encoding primary cilium components.

evidence.snippet: The most common variants were in the CPLANE1, CEP290, and TMEM67 genes, and other causative genes were AHI1, ARMC9, CEP41, CSPP1, HYLS1, KATNIP, KIAA0586, KIF7, RPGRIP1L, including some previously unreported variants in these genes.
evidence.explanation: Anchors a representative list of recurrent JS-causative ciliary genes from a clinical cohort.

steps/40.description: Biallelic (or hemizygous, for X-linked OFD1) pathogenic variants in over 40 ciliary genes initiate Joubert syndrome. The encoded proteins localize to distinct primary cilium subcompartments — basal body, transition zone, axoneme/ciliary tip, and intraflagellar transport machinery — and converge on disrupted primary cilium structure and function.

evidence.snippet: Over 40 causative genes have been reported, all encoding for proteins implicated in the structure or functioning of the primary cilium, a subcellular organelle widely present in embryonic and adult tissues.
evidence.explanation: JS genes encode primary cilium components, supporting disrupted cilium assembly.

evidence.snippet: B9 proteins localized to centrioles prior to ciliogenesis, where they facilitated the initiation of ciliogenesis.
evidence.explanation: This supports impaired ciliogenesis initiation as a core ciliary assembly defect.

evidence.snippet: TMEM216 localized to the base of primary cilia, and loss of TMEM216 in mutant fibroblasts or after knockdown caused defective ciliogenesis and centrosomal docking, with concomitant hyperactivation of RhoA and Dishevelled.
evidence.explanation: Places TMEM216 at the ciliary base and shows that its loss produces the cilium-assembly and centrosomal-docking failure this node describes.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that both TMEM138 and TMEM216 are required for ciliogenesis
evidence.explanation: Mutant fibroblasts and IMCD3 knockdown for either gene show failed ciliogenesis, placing TMEM138 alongside TMEM216 at this cilium-assembly node.

steps/41.description: Causative JS genes encode proteins required for primary cilium structure and assembly, disrupting cilium biogenesis in vivo.

evidence.snippet: Our findings implicate a defect in Wnt signaling in the cerebellar midline phenotype seen in Joubert syndrome that can be overcome with Wnt stimulation.
evidence.explanation: Directly links AHI1/Jouberin loss to defective canonical Wnt signaling at the developing cerebellar midline.

evidence.snippet: These mice show cerebellar hypoplasia with a vermis-midline fusion defect early in development.
evidence.explanation: Shows that AHI1 loss in mice produces a cerebellar vermis-midline fusion defect that parallels human JS.

steps/42.description: AHI1 (Jouberin) participates in canonical Wnt signal transduction. In Ahi1-mutant mouse cerebellum, Wnt reporter activity is reduced at the site of cerebellar hemisphere fusion, producing a vermis-midline fusion defect that recapitulates the human cerebellar vermis hypoplasia of JS. The defect is partially rescued by lithium, a Wnt pathway agonist.

evidence.snippet: At early postnatal stages, the Talpid3 mutants exhibit a reduction in proliferation in the dentate gyrus and a disrupted glial scaffold.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates a hippocampal neurogenesis defect in a Talpid3 (KIAA0586) JS model.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest a link between the hippocampal defects and the learning/memory deficits seen in JS patients.
evidence.explanation: Connects the model-organism hippocampal phenotype to human JS cognitive features.

steps/43.description: KIAA0586/Talpid3 is a basal-body protein required for primary cilium assembly. Talpid3 mutant mice show reduced proliferation in the dentate gyrus, a disrupted glial scaffold, and mis-localized progenitors in the granule cell layer — defective hippocampal neurogenesis that links ciliary dysfunction to learning and memory deficits seen in JS patients.

evidence.snippet: Here we reconstituted in vitro the individual and collective activities of the ciliary tip module proteins CEP104, CSPP1, TOGARAM1, ARMC9 and CCDC66, which interact with each other and with microtubules and, when mutated in humans, cause ciliopathies such as Joubert syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Defines the ciliary tip module whose members are JBTS-causative and act together to control axonemal microtubule growth.

steps/44.description: A ciliary tip module composed of CEP104, CSPP1, TOGARAM1, ARMC9 and CCDC66 controls the very slow processive growth of axonemal microtubules. Loss-of-function variants in module members destabilize this assembly and disrupt axonemal microtubule dynamics that are required to build and maintain the primary cilium.

evidence.snippet: In addition, analysis of primary cilium count and morphology showed notable ciliary defects in all differentiating JS patient-derived iPSCs compared to controls.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived cells show abnormal primary cilium structure.

evidence.snippet: Deficiency of the minor spliceosome component U4atac snRNA secondarily results in ciliary defects in human and zebrafish.
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish models demonstrate in vivo ciliary defects consistent with abnormal cilium organization.

evidence.snippet: We found that JBTS mutants have altered primary cilia throughout the brain.
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish JBTS mutants show altered primary cilia in brain tissue.

evidence.snippet: The patient-derived fibroblasts exhibited reduced primary cilia length and altered distribution of PCM1.
evidence.explanation: KIAA0586/TALPID3 variants are associated with reduced cilia length.

evidence.snippet: fibroblasts from a MKS1 c.1476T>G healthy homozygote showed impaired ability to form primary cilia and mildly reduced ciliary length
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived human fibroblasts carrying a recurrent JS-associated MKS1 variant show impaired ciliogenesis and reduced ciliary length, directly supporting abnormal cilium structure and length as a JS cellular defect.

steps/45.description: Primary cilia show abnormal number, morphology, and length in JS models, indicating disrupted cilium organization.

evidence.snippet: We identified biallelic missense and nonsense mutations in the gene encoding the transmembrane protein TMEM218 in unrelated patients with features related to Bardet-Biedl, Joubert and Meckel-Gruber syndrome (MKS) and characterized TMEM218 as a major component of the ciliary TZ module.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that JBTS-spectrum disease arises from variants in genes encoding ciliary transition zone module components.

evidence.snippet: The B9 complex interacted with and anchored TMEM67 to the TZ membrane.
evidence.explanation: Defines a direct molecular interaction at the transition zone whose disruption is a JBTS mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Joubert syndrome-associated B9D2 variants primarily affected axonemal microtubule modifications without disrupting ciliogenesis, whereas the Meckel syndrome-associated B9D2 variant disrupted both ciliogenesis and axonemal microtubule modifications
evidence.explanation: Provides an allele-specific transition-zone mechanism distinguishing Joubert-causing B9D2 variants (selective loss of axonemal microtubule modification with preserved ciliogenesis) from the more severe Meckel-causing variant, refining why the same gene yields different ciliopathies.

evidence.snippet: TMEM231 has been previously shown to localise to the ciliary transition zone, and to interact with several JBTS gene products in a complex involved in the formation of the diffusion barrier between the cilia and plasma membrane.
evidence.explanation: Places TMEM231 in the transition-zone diffusion-barrier complex this node models. The citing paper is the French-Canadian JBTS gene-discovery study, and this sentence restates the prior localization and interaction work rather than reporting its own result.

steps/46.description: The ciliary transition zone (TZ) is a gatekeeper subdomain that controls passage of signaling proteins into and out of the cilium. The TMEM67/MKS module (TMEM67, MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, CC2D2A) and the NPHP module are anchored at the TZ; pathogenic variants in JS genes encoding TZ components reduce TZ gating, anchoring of TMEM67, and posttranslational tubulin modifications.

evidence.snippet: We show that Togaram1 is expressed in the neural tube and Togaram1 knockout mice have abnormal cilia, reduced sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling, abnormal neural tube patterning, and display neural tube closure defects.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that loss of a JBTS gene reduces ciliary Shh signaling and perturbs cilium-dependent patterning.

steps/47.description: Hedgehog signal transduction depends on regulated trafficking of Smoothened and other Hh components through the primary cilium. Disrupted ciliary structure or transition zone gating in JS reduces Hh signaling, perturbing Hh-dependent neural patterning and limb development.

evidence.snippet: Our work demonstrates that before ciliogenesis occurs, B9D2 is crucial for the maturation and maintenance of tight junctions ensuring epithelial barrier tightness and appropriate biliary lumen formation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes a non-ciliary B9D2 function in tight junctions and biliary lumen formation as the mechanism of biliary dysgenesis in JS.

evidence.snippet: For instance, JS individuals harboring pathogenic variants in TMEM67 have a significantly higher risk of liver fibrosis, while pathogenic variants in NPHP1, RPGRIP1L, and TMEM237 are frequently associated to JS with renal involvement, requiring a closer monitoring of liver parameters, or renal functioning.
evidence.explanation: Identifies TMEM67 as the JS genotype most strongly associated with liver fibrosis, downstream of the biliary ductal plate defect.

steps/48.description: TMEM67 variants confer the highest risk of liver fibrosis among JS genotypes. Mechanistically, B9D2 — a TMEM67 partner at the ciliary transition zone — also acts before ciliogenesis to mature and maintain epithelial tight junctions, ensuring biliary lumen formation. Loss of B9D2 function disrupts cholangiocyte tight junctions and biliary lumen formation, producing the ductal plate malformation that underlies congenital hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension in JS.

evidence.snippet: Recently, it has been proposed that CEP290 gene product may also play a role in the microtubule-based ciliary transport, in the vesicle transport, the development and maintenance of the cilium
evidence.explanation: CEP290 dysfunction is linked to impaired intraciliary transport and cilium maintenance.

evidence.snippet: Ciliary defects observed in CCRK-knockout (KO), BROMI-KO, and FAM149B1-KO cells, including abnormally long cilia and accumulation of the IFT machinery and ICK at the ciliary tip, resembled one another
evidence.explanation: Shows that loss of FAM149B1 leaves the intraflagellar transport machinery stranded at the ciliary tip, the transport-turnaround failure this node describes.

evidence.snippet: distinct cilia-related abnormalities were observed in these cells: abnormal accumulation IFT complex at the distal tips of the cilia, which assumed bulbous appearance, increased length of the primary cilium, and dysregulated SHH signaling
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived FAM149B1 mutant fibroblasts show the same distal-tip IFT accumulation, tying the human genotype to this transport node.

steps/49.description: Disruption of ciliary gene products (e.g., CEP290) impairs intraciliary transport and cilium maintenance.

evidence.snippet: All JS patient-derived iPSCs, regardless of the mutant gene, showed a similar impairment to differentiate into mid-hindbrain and cerebellar granule cells when compared to healthy controls.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived cells show impaired neuronal differentiation relevant to neurodevelopmental defects.

evidence.snippet: Classic defects include hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, thickened cerebellar peduncles, and deepened interpeduncular fossa, which is regarded as a "molar tooth" sign.
evidence.explanation: This review describes neurodevelopmental malformations characteristic of JS.

steps/50.description: Disrupted ciliary biology impairs neurodevelopmental programs, contributing to mid-hindbrain and cerebellar developmental abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: Organoids revealed impaired development of outer segment structures, which are modified primary cilia, and mislocalization of visual pigments to photoreceptor cell soma.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived retinal organoids show outer segment defects and visual pigment mislocalization driven by transition zone disruption.

evidence.snippet: All patient-derived cells showed reduced levels of CEP290 protein, a critical cilia transition zone component interacting with NPHP5, providing a plausible mechanism for aberrant ciliary gating and cargo transport.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistically links transition zone (CEP290/NPHP5) dysfunction to photoreceptor cilium failure.

steps/51.description: Photoreceptor outer segments are highly modified primary cilia. Pathogenic JS variants affecting transition zone gating (CEP290) or its interactors (NPHP5/IQCB1) produce aberrantly elongated ciliary axonemes, impaired outer segment development, and mislocalization of visual pigments to photoreceptor cell soma — the cellular basis of JS-associated retinal dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: On the other hand, individuals with causal variants in the CEP290 or AHI1 need a closer surveillance for retinal dystrophy and, in case of CEP290, also for chronic kidney disease.
evidence.explanation: Genotype-phenotype review identifies CEP290 as a JS subtype with elevated chronic kidney disease risk.

evidence.snippet: For instance, JS individuals harboring pathogenic variants in TMEM67 have a significantly higher risk of liver fibrosis, while pathogenic variants in NPHP1, RPGRIP1L, and TMEM237 are frequently associated to JS with renal involvement, requiring a closer monitoring of liver parameters, or renal functioning.
evidence.explanation: Defines the JS gene subset whose variants converge on renal tubular ciliopathy.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, NPHP1 and NPHP6 are major genes of nephronophthisis associated with JS.
evidence.explanation: Identifies NPHP1 as a principal gene behind the nephronophthisis-type tubular disease modeled at this node, from a cohort screened for exactly that combination.

steps/52.description: Renal tubular epithelial cells require functional primary cilia for homeostasis. Variants in JS genes encoding transition zone (CEP290) and NPHP-module components disrupt tubular ciliary signaling and drive nephronophthisis-type tubulointerstitial disease and renal cyst formation. CEP290 variants in particular confer chronic kidney disease risk that warrants surveillance.

evidence.snippet: Classic defects include hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, thickened cerebellar peduncles, and deepened interpeduncular fossa, which is regarded as a "molar tooth" sign.
evidence.explanation: Documents the mid-hindbrain malformation pattern that defines the JS molar tooth sign.

steps/53.description: Disrupted ciliary signaling perturbs morphogenesis of the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, producing the characteristic JS malformation: hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, thickened/elongated superior cerebellar peduncles, and a deepened interpeduncular fossa.

evidence.snippet: JSRD is characterized by lack of decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles, central pontine tracts and corticospinal tracts suggesting defective axon guidance.
evidence.explanation: Establishes failed midline decussation in JS as a defective axon-guidance phenotype at the mid-hindbrain junction.

steps/54.description: A defining feature of JS is failure of axons to cross the midline at the superior cerebellar peduncles, the central pontine tracts, and the corticospinal tracts. This points to a defective axon-guidance program at the mid-hindbrain junction and contributes directly to the molar tooth sign and the cerebellar/motor phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features can be noticed shortly after birth that includes hypotonia episodic tachypnea and apnea that may be followed by developmental delays and speech apraxia.
evidence.explanation: Documents the early-onset brainstem-mediated respiratory dysrhythmias characteristic of JS.

steps/55.description: The same mid-hindbrain malformation that produces the molar tooth sign disrupts brainstem nuclei controlling respiratory rhythm and ocular motor pathways, manifesting in neonates as episodic tachypnea and apnea and as oculomotor apraxia and other abnormal eye movements.

evidence.snippet: Classic defects include hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, thickened cerebellar peduncles, and deepened interpeduncular fossa, which is regarded as a "molar tooth" sign.
evidence.explanation: The molar tooth sign is a classic diagnostic feature of JS.

evidence.snippet: Classic defects include hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, thickened cerebellar peduncles, and deepened interpeduncular fossa, which is regarded as a "molar tooth" sign.
evidence.explanation: This review identifies cerebellar vermis hypoplasia as a classic defect in JS.

evidence.snippet: Other characteristic features are hypotonia with lateral ataxia, intellectual disability/mental retardation, oculomotor apraxia, retinal dystrophy, abnormalities in the respiratory system, renal cysts, hepatic fibrosis, and skeletal changes.
evidence.explanation: Hypotonia is listed as a characteristic feature of JS.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet classifies hypotonia as very frequent (99-80%) in isolated Joubert syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Other characteristic features are hypotonia with lateral ataxia, intellectual disability/mental retardation, oculomotor apraxia, retinal dystrophy, abnormalities in the respiratory system, renal cysts, hepatic fibrosis, and skeletal changes.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet classifies intellectual disability as very frequent (99-80%) in isolated Joubert syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Joubert syndrome (JS) is a recessively inherited congenital ataxia characterized by hypotonia, psychomotor delay, abnormal ocular movements, intellectual disability, and a peculiar cerebellar and brainstem malformation, the "molar tooth sign."
evidence.explanation: Psychomotor delay supports global developmental delay in JS.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001263 | Global developmental delay | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet classifies global developmental delay as very frequent (99-80%) in isolated Joubert syndrome.

evidence.explanation: This case report notes speech apraxia in JS.

evidence.snippet: Joubert syndrome (JS) is a recessively inherited congenital ataxia characterized by hypotonia, psychomotor delay, abnormal ocular movements, intellectual disability, and a peculiar cerebellar and brainstem malformation, the "molar tooth sign."
evidence.explanation: Abnormal ocular movements are a defining neurologic-ophthalmologic feature.

evidence.snippet: Other characteristic features are hypotonia with lateral ataxia, intellectual disability/mental retardation, oculomotor apraxia, retinal dystrophy, abnormalities in the respiratory system, renal cysts, hepatic fibrosis, and skeletal changes.

edges/55.description: Variants in genes encoding basal body, axonemal, and intraflagellar transport components compromise primary cilium biogenesis.

edges/56.description: Variants in transition zone genes (e.g., TMEM67, CC2D2A, MKS1, CEP290, B9D2) disrupt the ciliary gate.

edges/57.description: Variants in ciliary tip module genes (CEP104, CSPP1, TOGARAM1, ARMC9, CCDC66) disrupt axonemal microtubule growth.

edges/58.description: Loss of AHI1/Jouberin (and CEP290) disrupts cilium-coupled canonical Wnt signaling at the cerebellar dorsal midline.

edges/59.description: Failed cilium assembly produces cilia with abnormal number, morphology, and length.

edges/60.description: Defective primary cilium biogenesis disrupts the cilium machinery required for intraciliary transport.

edges/61.description: Loss of basal-body proteins (e.g., KIAA0586/Talpid3) required for cilium assembly disrupts hippocampal progenitor proliferation and migration.

edges/62.description: Abnormal cilium structure compromises the cilium-dependent transduction of Hedgehog signaling.

edges/63.description: Photoreceptor outer segments are modified primary cilia and are particularly sensitive to abnormal cilium structure.

edges/64.description: Renal tubular epithelial cilia mediate cilium-dependent homeostasis that is disrupted by abnormal cilium morphology.

edges/65.description: Defective intraciliary cargo transport mislocalizes outer-segment proteins required for photoreceptor function.

edges/66.description: Impaired ciliary transport disrupts renal tubular cilium-dependent signaling.

edges/67.description: Disrupted ciliary trafficking impairs cilium-dependent neurodevelopmental signaling.

edges/68.description: Disrupted ciliary signaling perturbs mid-hindbrain morphogenesis underlying the JS brain malformation.

edges/69.description: Impaired neurodevelopmental programs lead to vermian hypoplasia, the cardinal cerebellar feature of JS.

edges/70.description: Neurodevelopmental disruption manifests as intellectual disability.

edges/71.description: Neurodevelopmental disruption manifests as global developmental delay.

edges/77.description: Disrupted ciliary tip microtubule dynamics produce cilia of abnormal length and morphology.

edges/78.description: A defective TZ gate compromises selective entry and exit of ciliary cargo.

edges/79.description: TZ gating is required for ciliary localization of Hedgehog pathway components (SMO, GPR161, TULP3).

edges/80.description: B9D2 also functions extra-ciliarly in tight junctions; its loss disrupts biliary epithelial polarity.

edges/84.description: Reduced cilium-dependent Hedgehog signaling disrupts mid-hindbrain morphogenesis.

edges/90.description: Hedgehog signaling drives optic fissure closure during eye morphogenesis; its disruption produces iris coloboma, a developmental morphogenetic defect rather than a degenerative one.

edges/91.description: Reduced Wnt-dependent proliferation at the dorsal midline produces vermis hypoplasia.

edges/92.description: Vermis hypoplasia is the dominant component of the molar tooth sign.

edges/95.description: Mid-hindbrain patterning defects underlie the failure of axonal decussation across the brainstem midline.

edges/96.description: Failed midline morphogenesis produces vermian hypoplasia.

edges/97.description: Mid-hindbrain malformation disrupts brainstem nuclei controlling respiratory rhythm and ocular motor pathways.

edges/100.description: Elongated, non-decussating superior cerebellar peduncles plus deep interpeduncular fossa produce the molar tooth radiographic sign.

edges/101.description: Disrupted brainstem motor pathways contribute to early hypotonia.

edges/102.description: Loss of cerebellar output decussation contributes to ataxia.

edges/105.description: Hippocampal neurogenesis defects contribute to learning/memory impairment.

edges/106.description: Hippocampal and other ciliary neurogenesis defects manifest as global developmental delay.

edges/107.description: Outer segment dystrophy and visual pigment mislocalization produce progressive retinal dystrophy.

edges/108.description: Tubular ciliopathy drives the nephronophthisis-type tubulointerstitial kidney disease in JS.

edges/109.description: Disrupted cilium-dependent tubular signaling produces renal cysts.

edges/110.description: Ductal plate malformation drives congenital hepatic fibrosis.

edges/111.description: Progressive hepatic fibrosis raises portal venous pressure.

edges/112.description: Portal hypertension produces porto-systemic collaterals including esophageal varices.

edges/113.description: Brainstem respiratory control dysfunction drives episodic tachypnea.

edges/114.description: Brainstem respiratory control dysfunction drives apneic episodes.

edges/115.description: Persistent brainstem control dysfunction contributes to sleep apnea later in life.

edges/116.description: Brainstem ocular motor pathway disruption contributes to oculomotor apraxia.

edges/117.description: Brainstem ocular motor pathway disruption produces abnormal eye movements.

evidence.snippet: We now report that MKS2 and CORS2 (JBTS2) loci are allelic and caused by mutations in TMEM216, which encodes an uncharacterized tetraspan transmembrane protein.
evidence.explanation: Assigns the JBTS2 locus to TMEM216, which is the gene-subtype assertion this entry records.

evidence.snippet: we report that mutation of either TMEM138 or TMEM216 causes a phenotypically indistinguishable human ciliopathy, Joubert syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms TMEM216 as a Joubert syndrome gene and states that the TMEM138 phenotype cannot be told apart from it.

genes/35.notes: TMEM216 is the JBTS2 gene. The JBTS2 and MKS2 loci are allelic, so the same gene is curated in this repository under Meckel syndrome and orofaciodigital syndrome as well; the entry here records the Joubert syndrome 2 assertion only.

evidence.snippet: we identified four missense mutations and one splicing homozygous deleterious mutation in evolutionarily conserved residues of the nearby TMEM138 gene of unknown function, thus accounting for all JBTS2-linked families
evidence.explanation: Reports the TMEM138 variants found in the JBTS2-linked families that carried no TMEM216 variant, establishing TMEM138 as a distinct Joubert syndrome gene.

genes/36.notes: TMEM138 sits head-to-tail with TMEM216 at the JBTS2 locus and accounts for the JBTS2-linked families that are TMEM216 mutation-negative. The two genes are not paralogues and share a regulatory element in the intervening noncoding interval, which is why one locus yields two genes and two numbered Joubert subtypes for a phenotype the discovery paper calls indistinguishable.

evidence.snippet: three individuals (two families) were compound heterozygous for the same rare mutations in TMEM231
evidence.explanation: Reports the biallelic TMEM231 genotype found by exome sequencing in a French-Canadian Joubert syndrome cohort.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggest that mutations in TMEM231 cause JBTS, reinforcing the relationship between this condition and the disruption of the barrier at the ciliary transition zone.
evidence.explanation: States the authors' gene-disease conclusion and ties it to the transition-zone barrier mechanism this entry models.

genes/37.notes: TMEM231 encodes a ciliary transition-zone component. As with TMEM216, the same gene also causes Meckel syndrome and is curated under that entry; the assertion recorded here is the Joubert syndrome one.

evidence.snippet: we mapped a ciliopathy phenotype that most closely matches Joubert syndrome (hypotonia, developmental delay, typical facies, oculomotor apraxia, polydactyly, and subtle posterior fossa abnormalities) to a single locus in which a founder homozygous truncating variant in FAM149B1 was identified by exome sequencing

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous chromosomal deletion encompassing the partial or entire ANKRD11 gene, as well as the loss of function mutations, result in haploinsufficiency of the gene, leading to KBG syndrome. This indicates that precise levels of ANKRD11 transcripts or protein are essential for human development.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that both CNV deletions and LoF mutations converge on ANKRD11 haploinsufficiency, and that ANKRD11 dosage is developmentally critical.

steps/1.description: KBG syndrome results predominantly from haploinsufficiency of ANKRD11 (ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 11) at 16q24.3. Heterozygous loss-of-function sequence variants (most frequently frameshift and nonsense), as well as 16q24.3 microdeletions encompassing part or all of ANKRD11 (and even deletions limited to the non-coding exon 1 / upstream region), reduce functional ANKRD11 dosage. Precise levels of ANKRD11 transcript/protein are essential for normal human development, so reduced dosage is the unifying mechanism shared by sequence-variant and CNV cases.

evidence.snippet: Ankyrin repeat domain containing-protein 11 (ANKRD11), a transcriptional factor predominantly localized in the cell nucleus, plays a crucial role in the expression regulation of key genes by recruiting chromatin remodelers and interacting with specific transcriptional repressors or activators during numerous biological processes.
evidence.explanation: Defines ANKRD11's molecular role as a nuclear transcriptional regulator acting through chromatin remodelers and transcriptional repressors/ activators.

evidence.snippet: The ANKRD11 gene encodes the ankyrin repeat-containing protein 11A transcriptional regulator, which is expressed in the brain and implicated in neural development.
evidence.explanation: Supports ANKRD11's role as a transcriptional regulator expressed in brain and implicated in neural development, the basis of the neurodevelopmental phenotype.

evidence.snippet: the truncated protein significantly reduced CDKN1A/P21-promoter luciferase activity in comparison to wild-type ANKRD11 protein, as well as a remarkably decrease in the endogenous CDKN1A/P21 mRNA level in HEK293 cells. These findings suggest a loss of transcriptional activation function and potentially a dominant-negative mechanism.
evidence.explanation: In vitro functional assay demonstrating that a truncating ANKRD11 variant impairs transcriptional activation of CDKN1A/P21, supporting loss of transcriptional regulatory function.

steps/2.description: ANKRD11 is a nuclear transcriptional regulator that controls expression of key developmental genes by recruiting chromatin remodelers and interacting with transcriptional repressors and activators, including HDAC-containing and p160 coactivator complexes. Reduced ANKRD11 function therefore impairs chromatin-linked transcriptional regulation, placing KBG syndrome among the "chromatinopathies." Functional studies of truncating variants show escape from nonsense-mediated decay, aberrant nuclear accumulation of truncated protein, and reduced transactivation of target promoters such as CDKN1A/P21, implicating impaired transcriptional regulatory function and, for some alleles, a possible dominant-negative effect.

evidence.snippet: Our molecular analysis showed that this deletion leads to reduction in the ANKRD11 transcript and global transcriptome alterations similar to those seen in KBG syndrome patients.
evidence.explanation: Shows that reduced ANKRD11 dosage from a non-coding deletion drives global transcriptome alterations resembling KBG syndrome.

steps/3.description: Reduced ANKRD11 dosage produces broad downstream transcriptional changes. Patient-derived cells carrying ANKRD11-involving deletions (including microdeletions limited to the non-coding exon 1 and upstream region) show reduced ANKRD11 transcript levels together with global transcriptome alterations resembling those seen in classic KBG syndrome, linking the primary chromatin-regulatory defect to systems-level developmental dysregulation.

steps/4.description: Postnatal short stature, a hallmark feature, is hypothesized to arise from ANKRD11 deficiency disrupting the orderly differentiation of growth plate chondrocytes and thereby impairing longitudinal endochondral bone growth.
