evidence.snippet: Although the combined presence of ataxia and pyramidal features has a long differential, the presence of a true spastic-ataxia as the predominant clinical syndrome has a rather limited differential diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports the syndrome as a recognizable spastic-ataxia clinical entity.

steps/3.description: The syndrome represents a clinically coherent but genetically diverse neurodegenerative phenotype in which ataxia and pyramidal-spastic features co-occur.

evidence.snippet: In ARSACS, but not SPG7 patients, we observed a complex and multi-faced involvement of brain WM, with a clinically meaningful widespread loss of axonal and dendritic integrity, secondary demyelination and, overall, a reduction in cellularity and volume.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports white-matter degeneration and secondary demyelination as a mechanistic branch in spastic ataxia.

steps/4.description: In paradigmatic SPAX disorders, especially ARSACS, widespread white matter damage with secondary demyelination contributes to the spastic-ataxic phenotype. Only SACS is bound here: the PROSPAX comparison cited below found this pattern in ARSACS but explicitly not in SPG7 patients, so binding SPG7 to this node would contradict the entry's own evidence.

evidence.snippet: In this work, we demonstrated that mitochondrial proteotoxicity in the absence/mutation of AFG3L2 activates the OMA1-DELE1-HRI pathway eliciting the integrated stress response.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports a subtype-specific mitochondrial stress mechanism within the spastic-ataxia syndrome family.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the m-AAA subunits AFG3L2 and paraplegin are associated with autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA28) and autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG7), respectively.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that AFG3L2 and SPG7 encode subunits of the same m-AAA protease, which is the basis for binding both genes to this node.

steps/5.description: Mitochondrial protein quality control in the inner membrane is carried out by the m-AAA protease, whose subunits are AFG3L2 and paraplegin (SPG7). Both of this entry's mitochondrial subtypes are defects of that one complex, which is why they are modelled at a single node: in the SPAX5 subtype, biallelic AFG3L2 dysfunction causes mitochondrial proteotoxic stress and activates the OMA1-DELE1-HRI integrated stress response pathway, and SPG7-associated disease is the paraplegin-subunit counterpart. The integrated-stress-response detail below is established for the AFG3L2 arm specifically.

evidence.snippet: Although the combined presence of ataxia and pyramidal features has a long differential, the presence of a true spastic-ataxia as the predominant clinical syndrome has a rather limited differential diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports ataxia as one of the two defining syndrome elements.

steps/6.description: Cerebellar ataxia is a defining feature of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Although the combined presence of ataxia and pyramidal features has a long differential, the presence of a true spastic-ataxia as the predominant clinical syndrome has a rather limited differential diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports pyramidal or spastic features as a defining syndrome component.

steps/7.description: Pyramidal or spastic motor features are the other defining clinical component of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Spastic ataxias are a group of diseases causing symptoms such as walking difficulties and balance impairments that lead to a high risk of falls.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports gait and balance impairment as a major functional phenotype across spastic ataxias.

steps/8.description: Gait impairment is a major functional manifestation of the combined ataxic and spastic syndrome.

edges/3.description: Several paradigmatic subtypes share white-matter injury and neurodegenerative propagation.

edges/4.description: Some subtypes, especially SPAX5, are driven by mitochondrial proteostasis failure.

edges/5.description: White-matter and cerebellar system injury contribute to the core ataxic phenotype.

edges/6.description: Pyramidal tract dysfunction contributes to spastic clinical features.

edges/7.description: Combined cerebellar and pyramidal-system injury produces gait impairment.

edges/8.description: Purkinje neuron and cerebellar dysfunction produce ataxia.

edges/9.description: Mitochondrial neurodegeneration in SPAX5 includes spastic features.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous AFG3L2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 28 (SCA28) or dominant optic atrophy type 12 (DOA12), while biallelic AFG3L2 mutations result in the rare and severe spastic ataxia type 5 (SPAX5).
evidence.explanation: This directly supports AFG3L2 as a causal gene within the syndrome spectrum.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic AFG3L2 variants define the SPAX5 subtype within the broader spastic-ataxia syndrome family.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal recessive ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay, late-onset Friedreich ataxia, and hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 are examples of genetic diseases with such a prominent spastic-ataxic syndrome as the clinical hallmark.
evidence.explanation: This supports ARSACS, the SACS-related disease, as a genetic cause of the spastic-ataxia syndrome.

genes/1.notes: SACS variants cause autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay, a paradigmatic spastic-ataxia subtype.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal recessive ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay, late-onset Friedreich ataxia, and hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 are examples of genetic diseases with such a prominent spastic-ataxic syndrome as the clinical hallmark.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 as a genetic disease with a prominent spastic-ataxic syndrome.

genes/2.notes: SPG7 variants cause hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7, a common genetic spastic-ataxia differential and subtype.

evidence.snippet: The three objectives of this project are: 1) to determine the effect of a 12-week rehabilitation program on disease severity as compared with usual care for individuals with spastic ataxias;
evidence.explanation: This directly supports rehabilitation as a disease-relevant intervention under formal study.

treatments/0.description: Disease-specific rehabilitation is under active clinical evaluation for spastic ataxias.

evidence.snippet: The team has developed the program to specifically target symptoms present in these patients and was previously pilot-tested.
evidence.explanation: This supports structured exercise-oriented rehabilitation for the symptomatic treatment of spastic ataxias.

treatments/1.description: The IMPACT program is a structured exercise-based rehabilitation approach targeting gait, balance, and disease severity.

evidence.snippet: In SCA2 patients, the repeat was perfect and expanded to 36-52 repeats.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the expanded, uninterrupted CAG tract in ATXN2 as the initiating molecular lesion.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion is a CAG repeat in exon 1 of ATXN2 expanded beyond the pathogenic threshold of approximately 35 copies, within the translated reading frame, so the tract is expressed as an elongated polyglutamine domain in ataxin-2. Normal alleles are 14-30 copies and carry CAA interruptions; pathogenic alleles are typically pure CAG, and loss of the interruption is itself part of the lesion rather than an incidental detail. Repeat length is inversely correlated with age of onset.

evidence.snippet: In SCA2 brains, we found cytoplasmic, but not nuclear, microaggregates.
evidence.explanation: Direct human neuropathological evidence that SCA2 aggregation is cytoplasmic, unlike the intranuclear inclusions of other polyQ diseases.

evidence.snippet: Mice expressing ataxin-2 with Q58 showed progressive functional deficits accompanied by loss of the Purkinje cell dendritic arbor and finally loss of Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: A cytoplasmic, non-ubiquitinated polyQ-ataxin-2 species is sufficient to produce progressive dendritic-arbor loss and Purkinje cell death, so nuclear inclusion formation is not required for the degenerative phenotype.

steps/2.description: PolyQ-expanded ataxin-2 misfolds and forms microaggregates. This is the node at which SCA2 departs from the polyglutamine stereotype set by Huntington disease and SCA3: in SCA2 brains the aggregates are cytoplasmic, not nuclear, and transgenic ataxin-2[Q58] remains cytoplasmic without detectable ubiquitination while still producing progressive Purkinje cell loss. Neither nuclear localization nor inclusion-body formation is necessary for pathogenesis. Curators extending this entry should not "correct" it toward the nuclear-inclusion pattern; the cytoplasmic localization is the experimentally supported claim and is what differentiates SCA2 within the Polyglutamine Disorders grouping.

evidence.snippet: We discovered that altered ataxin-2 levels interfere with the assembly of stress granules and cellular P-body structures.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ataxin-2's normal role in RNA-triage compartment assembly, the function lost on expansion.

evidence.snippet: Using RNA immunoprecipitation we showed that ATXN2 interacted selectively with RGS8 mRNA. This interaction was impaired when ATXN2 harbored an expanded polyglutamine.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that polyQ expansion impairs a specific, identified mRNA-binding function of ataxin-2, linking the translational lesion to mGluR1 signalling.

steps/3.description: Normal ataxin-2 is an RNA-binding translational regulator: it interacts with the DEAD/H-box helicase DDX6 and with poly(A)-binding protein, and its concentration governs assembly of stress granules and P-bodies. PolyQ expansion impairs selective mRNA binding - shown directly for RGS8 mRNA, whose protein product attenuates mGluR1 signalling. This node is curated as a disease-specific translational lesion rather than as conformance to the module's "Transcriptional Dysregulation" node, because ataxin-2 is an RNA and translation regulator, not a transcription factor; asserting transcriptional conformance here would import a claim from the HD/SCA17 pattern that SCA2's own evidence does not make.

evidence.snippet: We found that intermediate-length polyQ expansions (27-33 glutamines) in ATXN2 were significantly associated with ALS. These data establish ATXN2 as a relatively common ALS susceptibility gene.
evidence.explanation: The landmark association study establishing intermediate ATXN2 alleles as an ALS susceptibility factor, with the length band as the authors report it.

evidence.snippet: The decrease in ataxin-2 reduced aggregation of TDP-43, markedly increased survival and improved motor function.
evidence.explanation: Supports the mechanism of the ALS arm as ataxin-2 dose-dependent modification of TDP-43 toxicity, distinct from SCA2's own polyQ cascade.

steps/4.description: This node is deliberately kept off the main SCA2 chain. Intermediate-length ATXN2 polyglutamine expansions are an established risk factor for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, acting by modifying TDP-43 toxicity rather than through the cytoplasmic polyQ aggregation route that drives SCA2 itself. It is a susceptibility claim about a different disease, not a step in SCA2 pathogenesis, and is curated here because the same locus carries both. Reported length bands differ by source and are not reconciled: Elden et al. report 27-33 glutamines for ALS association, while STRchive's intermediate band is 31-34. Note the boundary is not absolute - FTLD-ALS with TDP-43 pathology has been described in a family carrying a full ataxin-2 expansion - so full-expansion carriers should not be described as categorically free of motor neuron disease.

evidence.snippet: Association with Atx2-58Q increased the sensitivity of InsP(3)R1 to activation by InsP(3) in planar lipid bilayer reconstitution experiments.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the direct molecular interaction by which mutant ataxin-2 destabilizes Purkinje cell calcium handling.

evidence.snippet: Glutamate-induced cell death of 58Q PC cultures was attenuated by dantrolene, a clinically relevant RyanR inhibitor and Ca(2+) stabilizer.
evidence.explanation: Pharmacological rescue supports the calcium lesion as causal rather than merely correlated with degeneration.

steps/5.description: Mutant ataxin-2 binds the cytosolic C-terminal region of the type 1 inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor and increases its sensitivity to activation, producing exaggerated calcium release in Purkinje cells and increased vulnerability to glutamate. The pharmacological arm of this claim is unusually strong for a mechanism node: the ryanodine-receptor inhibitor and calcium stabilizer dantrolene both attenuates glutamate-induced death in culture and reduces Purkinje cell loss in the SCA2-58Q mouse.

evidence.snippet: Although motor performance began to deteriorate at 8 weeks of age, reductions in PC number were not seen until after 12 weeks. Decreases in the PC firing frequency first showed at 6 weeks and paralleled deterioration of motor performance with progression of disease.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the temporal ordering: firing decline precedes both motor signs and Purkinje cell loss.

steps/6.description: Purkinje cells lose intrinsic firing frequency well before they are lost. In the ATXN2-Q127 mouse, firing frequency falls from 6 weeks and tracks motor deterioration, while Purkinje cell number is preserved until after 12 weeks. This ordering is the mechanistic rationale for ATXN2-lowering therapy: the treatable lesion is an electrophysiological one that precedes irreversible cell loss, and ASO treatment restores firing even when started after motor onset.

evidence.snippet: The degeneration of the olivopontocerebellar regions as in classical olivopontocerebellar atrophy occurred early and severely in SCA2.
evidence.explanation: Quantitative autopsy series establishing the olivopontocerebellar distribution and its early, severe onset.

evidence.snippet: The neuropathological progression soon included neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, striatum, pallidum and later even the neocortex, while the dentate nucleus was consistently spared.
evidence.explanation: Records both the extracerebellar spread and the consistently spared dentate nucleus, which distinguishes SCA2 from SCA3.

steps/7.description: SCA2 produces early and severe degeneration of the olivopontocerebellar system - cerebellar cortex, pontine nuclei and inferior olives - extending with progression to substantia nigra, striatum, pallidum and eventually neocortex, while the dentate nucleus is consistently spared. This distribution is broader than the purely cerebellar SCAs and overlaps regions affected in Huntington disease, and it accounts for the parkinsonian and cognitive features that appear later in the course.

evidence.snippet: Then an acceleration was detected after 10 years of disease duration: SARA scores progressed 0.35 before and 2.45 points/year after this deadline (p = 0.013).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies stage-dependent, non-linear progression in a prospective SCA2 cohort.

evidence.snippet: Age at onset, mutation severity, and presence of amyotrophy, parkinsonism, dystonic manifestations and cognitive decline at baseline did not influence the rate of disease progression.
evidence.explanation: A negative result worth preserving: baseline clinical features do not predict progression rate, so disease duration is the operative variable.

steps/8.description: Age of onset is inversely correlated with repeat length, and intergenerational instability produces anticipation. Progression is not linear: in a prospective cohort, SARA scores advanced 0.35 points per year before 10 years of disease duration and 2.45 points per year after it, which matters directly for trial design because disease duration, not baseline severity, sets the expected rate.

edges/4.description: The elongated polyglutamine domain drives misfolding and aggregation of ataxin-2.

edges/5.description: The same expansion impairs ataxin-2's normal selective mRNA-binding function, so toxic gain and partial loss of function arise from one lesion.

edges/6.description: Mutant ataxin-2 associates with and sensitizes the type 1 inositol trisphosphate receptor.

edges/7.description: Reduced RGS8 removes attenuation of mGluR1 signalling, converging on the same hyperexcitable mGluR1-ITPR1 axis.

edges/8.description: Disturbed calcium handling degrades the intrinsic pacemaking that sets Purkinje cell output.

edges/9.description: Sustained Purkinje dysfunction proceeds to frank neuronal loss across the olivopontocerebellar system.

edges/10.description: Progressive loss of cerebellar and brainstem neurons produces the clinical syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In SCA2 patients, the repeat was perfect and expanded to 36-52 repeats. The most common disease allele contained (CAG)37, one of the shortest expansions seen in a CAG expansion syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The identifying paper reports both the expansion range and the loss of CAA interruptions ("perfect" repeat) that distinguishes disease alleles.

evidence.snippet: Using this contig, we identified a CAG trinucleotide repeat with CAA interruptions that was expanded in patients with SCA2.
evidence.explanation: Localises the expansion to ATXN2 and records the CAA interruption structure.

evidence.snippet: | Pathogenic | 35 | 500 |
evidence.explanation: STRchive gives the pathogenic ATXN2 CAG repeat range (35-500 copies) as a structured, snippet-validatable source for a threshold that would otherwise be uncited prose.

evidence.snippet: | Benign | 14 | 30 |
evidence.explanation: STRchive gives the benign ATXN2 CAG repeat range.

evidence.snippet: | Intermediate | 31 | 34 |
evidence.explanation: STRchive's intermediate band. Note this does not coincide with the 27-33 band Elden et al. report for ALS risk; the two numbers come from different sources and are curated separately rather than reconciled.

genes/0.notes: Repeat-length thresholds in SCA2 are source-dependent and must not be silently harmonised. STRchive gives intermediate = 31-34; Elden et al. (PMID:20740007) report ALS association for 27-33 glutamines; the ARO-ATXN2 trial enrols at 33 or more repeats. Each number is attributed to its source where it is used.

evidence.snippet: The primary endpoint, SARA score improvement of at least 1 point after 12 months, was observed in seven patients (32%) in the treated group versus nine patients (39%) in the placebo group
evidence.explanation: The SCA2-specific randomised trial did not meet its primary endpoint; numerically fewer treated than placebo patients improved.

treatments/0.description: Tested specifically in SCA2 in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled ATRIL trial and found not to be effective. Curated as a refuted treatment claim rather than omitted, because the negative result is what a curator or clinician needs to know about a drug with positive reports in mixed-aetiology ataxia cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Notably, the firing frequency of Purkinje cells returned to normal even when treatment was initiated more than 12 weeks after the onset of the motor phenotype in BAC-Q72 mice.
evidence.explanation: Supports reversibility of the Purkinje firing lesion after symptom onset, the central preclinical rationale for ATXN2 lowering.

treatments/1.description: Reducing ATXN2 expression addresses the initiating lesion rather than a downstream consequence. In two SCA2 mouse models the lead oligonucleotide ASO7 delayed phenotype onset and restored Purkinje cell firing frequency even when started more than 12 weeks after motor onset, which is the strongest available argument that the electrophysiological lesion is reversible. This is preclinical; no ASO is approved for SCA2.

evidence.snippet: The most promising oligonucleotide, ASO7, downregulated ATXN2 mRNA and protein, which resulted in delayed onset of the SCA2 phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that lowering ATXN2 at the initiating node delays the downstream phenotype.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Lowers expression of the mutant transcript at the initiating node, upstream of aggregation and calcium dysregulation.

evidence.snippet: For treatment, levodopa is temporarily useful for rigidity/bradykinesia and for tremor, magnesium for muscle cramps, but neuroprotective therapy will depend on the elucidation of pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Supports symptomatic levodopa benefit and the explicit absence of neuroprotective therapy.

treatments/2.description: Symptomatic only; temporarily useful for rigidity, bradykinesia and tremor in patients with the parkinsonian presentation. Does not modify the underlying degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Speech therapy and communication devices such as writing pads and computer-based devices may benefit those with dysarthria.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews management step for the curated dysarthria phenotype.

treatments/3.description: Symptomatic management of dysarthria. Included because the entry curates dysarthria as a phenotype and GeneReviews specifies the corresponding intervention, so leaving it out would model the problem without the response.

evidence.snippet: Management is supportive. Affected individuals should maintain activity. Canes and walkers help prevent falls; grab bars, raised toilet seats, and ramps to accommodate motorized chairs may be necessary.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews supportive-care standard, including the instruction to maintain activity.

treatments/4.description: Canes, walkers, grab bars, raised toilet seats and ramps. Supportive rather than disease-modifying, and GeneReviews is explicit that patients should maintain activity rather than be immobilised.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol and medications known to affect cerebellar function.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews' agents-to-avoid list.

treatments/5.description: An agents-to-avoid instruction rather than an intervention. Curated because it is actionable and because the mechanism is coherent with the entry: the cerebellum is already operating on reduced Purkinje output, so agents that further depress cerebellar function subtract from a diminished reserve.

evidence.snippet: A recent genome-wide association study (GWAS) in HD found association between age at onset and genetic variants in DNA repair pathways, and we therefore tested whether the modifying effects of variants in DNA repair genes have wider effects in the polyglutamine diseases.
evidence.explanation: Shows the DNA-repair modifier signal is established across pooled polyglutamine diseases, which is suggestive for SCA2 but does not isolate it - the precise reason this is a gap rather than a curated edge.

open_questions/0.rationale: This entry deliberately does NOT declare conformance to mismatch_repair_driven_repeat_instability#Somatic Repeat Expansion in Post-Mitotic Cells, although SCA2 is a CAG-repeat disease and the module's other conformers do. The reason is evidential, not conceptual. The best available support is Bettencourt et al., which pools Huntington disease with multiple polyglutamine SCAs and finds DNA-repair variants modifying age at onset across the pooled set; it does not isolate SCA2, and no study measuring somatic ATXN2 CAG mosaicism in human SCA2 tissue was identified. Conformance is therefore withheld rather than asserted from analogy, which keeps the module's flagship conformers - all of which have direct measurements - honest. Conformance to the threshold and repeat-length-dependence nodes IS declared, because those are directly evidenced.

open_questions/1.rationale: The aggregation node is curated as part of the causal chain because the aggregates track the distribution of degeneration, but the direction of that relationship is not settled. Evidence exists that smaller soluble oligomers are the more toxic species and that inclusions act as reservoirs. The node's downstream edge is therefore best read as "accompanies and marks" rather than as a demonstrated toxic mechanism at the level of the inclusion itself.

evidence.snippet: Genome sequencing of the deletion breakpoints showed that the DLX5 and DLX6 genes are disomic but the putative DYNC1I1 exon 15 and 17 enhancers are deleted.
evidence.explanation: Establishes enhancer deletion with retention of both target genes in family 2.

evidence.snippet: partially encompassing exons 11–18 of the SLC25A13 gene and exons 14–17 of the DYNC1I1 gene
evidence.explanation: Defines the coding overlap of the larger deletion containing the named enhancers.

evidence.snippet: These results demonstrate that the exonic sequences are necessary but not sufficient for full enhancer activity.
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish deletion-series assays of DYNC1I1 eExon 15 show that the exon and its 5-prime intronic flank cooperate, so the named enhancer is not asserted to be only the coding exon.

evidence.snippet: DYNC1I1 eExon 17 drove specific LacZ expression in the anterior limb mesenchyme
evidence.explanation: Establishes the limb activity of the human exon 17-associated fragment in E11.5 mouse reporter assays.

steps/1.description: The family 2 deletion reported by Lango Allen et al. removes the DYNC1I1 exon 15- and exon 17-associated limb enhancers together with additional DYNC1I1 and SLC25A13 exons. DLX5 and DLX6 remain disomic. The physical loss includes protein-coding sequence, but the proposed limb mechanism is loss of regulation of the intact DLX5/DLX6 genes. DYNC1I1 and SLC25A13 are annotated here for sequence overlap, without attributing all effects of the multigene deletion to either protein.

evidence.snippet: These results show that Dync1i1 eExon 15 is in close proximity with Dlx5/6 promoter regions in the developing AER at E11.5, supporting its proposed role as an enhancer during limb development.
evidence.explanation: Mouse embryonic chromatin-contact assays support the distal targets, independently of coding overlap.

evidence.snippet: However, Dync1i1 and Hdac9 were not detected in mouse E11.5 limbs but expressed in the mouse adult cortex and heart, respectively
evidence.explanation: The assayed limb enhancer activity is distinct from expression of its DYNC1I1 host gene.

evidence.snippet: This result suggests that DYNC1I1 exons 15 and 17 act as tissue-specific enhancers of DLX5/6 expression in humans as well as in mouse and zebrafish.
evidence.explanation: Human deletion mapping supports the proposed regulatory mechanism without directly measuring limb expression.

steps/2.description: Loss of the DYNC1I1 exonic enhancer region is proposed to impair DLX5/DLX6 expression during limb development. Human enhancer fragments drive limb reporters in mice, and the endogenous mouse exon 15-associated region contacts Dlx5/Dlx6 promoters in the E11.5 apical ectodermal ridge. These experiments support enhancer function and candidate targets; they do not measure the expression change in the human deletion carriers. DYNC1I1 is the enhancer host and is not itself expressed in the assayed mouse embryonic limb.

evidence.snippet: Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) is caused by mutations in TP63, DLX5, DLX6, FGF8, FGFR1, WNT10B, and BHLHA9.
evidence.explanation: Lists the convergent set of SHFM-causing genes that act on a shared AER regulatory pathway.

evidence.snippet: The mutations in SHFM-related genes lead to dysregulation of Fgf8 in the central portion of the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) and subsequently lead to misexpression of a number of downstream target genes, failure of stratification of the AER, and thus SHFM.
evidence.explanation: States the core mechanism: central-AER FGF8 dysregulation and failed AER stratification produce SHFM.

evidence.snippet: SHFM is caused by failure to maintain normal apical ectodermal ridge function during limb development.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that the unifying defect is failed AER maintenance.

evidence.snippet: This leads to ectopic activation of the Lbx1 and Btrc genes in the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) in an Fgf8-like pattern induced by AER-specific enhancers of Fgf8.
evidence.explanation: Places the SHFM3 10q24 duplication genes (BTRC, FBXW4) on this node: the rearrangement acts through ectopic AER gene activation driven by the AER-specific FGF8 enhancers.

evidence.snippet: Through whole-exome and targeted sequencing, we detected three novel variants in a gene encoding a transcription factor, PRDM1, that arose de novo in families with SHFM or segregated with the phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Supports PRDM1 as an SHFM gene acting on limb development, so it belongs on the shared AER node rather than outside the pathograph.

steps/3.description: The unifying mechanism across SHFM loci is failure to maintain normal apical ectodermal ridge (AER) function during limb development. The AER is the epithelial signaling center at the distal tip of the limb bud that sustains outgrowth of the underlying mesenchyme. SHFM-associated mutations converge on dysregulation of FGF8 in the central portion of the AER, failure of AER stratification, and disruption of reciprocal Wnt-BMP-FGF signaling between the AER and progress-zone mesenchyme. The central-ray defect reflects loss of this signaling specifically in the median AER.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling is involved in the pathogenesis of SHFM.
evidence.explanation: Implicates disrupted canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling in SHFM pathogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Syndactyly of the remaining digits is most likely the effects of dysregulation of Fgf-Bmp-Msx signaling on apoptotic cell death.
evidence.explanation: Links syndactyly of remaining digits to dysregulated FGF-BMP-MSX signaling and altered apoptosis.

evidence.snippet: Loss of digit identity in SHFM is hypothesized to be the effects of misexpression of HOX genes, abnormal SHH gradient, or the loss of balance between GLI3A and GLI3R.
evidence.explanation: Attributes loss of digit identity to HOX misexpression, abnormal SHH gradient, and disturbed GLI3A/GLI3R balance.

evidence.snippet: The absence of hand/foot anomalies in any of the individuals with deletions of DLX1/DLX2 but not the HOXD cluster supports the hypothesis that haploinsufficiency of the HOXD cluster, rather than DLX1/DLX2, accounts for the skeletal abnormalities in subjects with 2q31.1 microdeletions.
evidence.explanation: Supports wiring HOXD13 rather than DLX1/DLX2 to this node: the 2q31.1 limb phenotype tracks HOXD-cluster haploinsufficiency, consistent with this node's loss of digit identity from HOX misexpression.

steps/4.description: Loss of central-AER FGF8 dysregulates the reciprocal Wnt-BMP-FGF signaling loop. Disruption of canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling, together with altered FGF-BMP-MSX signaling, drives the phenotype: median clefts with absent or hypoplastic central rays, syndactyly of the remaining digits (from dysregulated apoptotic cell death), and loss of digit identity (from misexpression of HOX genes and an abnormal SHH gradient or loss of GLI3A/GLI3R balance).

evidence.snippet: This implies that in normal situations these SHFM-associated genes share an underlying regulatory pathway that is involved in the development of the central parts of the hands and feet.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the central hand/foot rays as the developmental territory affected, the basis of the split-hand phenotype.

evidence.snippet: One-third of the mutations are dominant-negative mutations that affect the glycine residue in the G-X-Y repeats of the alpha 1 chain. These mutations disrupt the collagen triple helix and are common in achondrogenesis type II and hypochondrogenesis.

steps/1.description: Glycine-to-amino-acid substitutions in the Gly-X-Y repeats of the COL2A1 triple-helical domain destabilize the type II collagen triple helix through a dominant-negative mechanism. Because glycine is the only amino acid small enough to fit in the center of the triple helix, its substitution prevents proper chain folding. Even a single mutant alpha-1(II) chain incorporated into a trimeric molecule disrupts the entire structure, causing altered electrophoretic mobility, reduced thermostability, and slow secretion.

evidence.snippet: Our studies demonstrated that chondrocytes expressing the thermolabile R992C mutant collagen II molecules endured endoplasmic reticulum stress, had atypical polarization, and had reduced proliferation.
evidence.explanation: Conditional transgenic mouse model of SED demonstrates ER stress, atypical chondrocyte polarization, and reduced proliferation as direct consequences of mutant collagen II expression.

evidence.snippet: The COL2pathy-iChon cells showed suppressed expression of COL2A1 and significant apoptosis. A distended endoplasmic reticulum (ER) was detected, thus suggesting the adaptation of gene expression and cell death caused by excess ER stress.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived iPSC chondrocytes demonstrate ER distension, suppressed COL2A1 expression, and apoptosis, directly modeling the ER stress pathomechanism.

evidence.snippet: Arg719Cys procollagen-II was excessively post-translationally modified and partially retained within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), leading to ER distention. Notably, despite introduction of an aberrant cysteine residue-expected to engage redox-sensitive folding and quality control pathways-Arg719Cys procollagen-II was not detectably recognized by the ER proteostasis network.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that certain COL2A1 substitutions cause ER retention and matrix deficiency without canonical UPR activation, revealing a failed surveillance mechanism.

steps/2.description: Misfolded type II procollagen molecules accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum of chondrocytes, causing ER distention and an ER storage disorder phenotype. The cellular response to this accumulation is variant-dependent: some mutations activate canonical ER stress and the unfolded protein response (UPR), leading to chondrocyte apoptosis and growth plate disorganization. However, recent iPSC-derived cartilage models demonstrate that certain COL2A1 substitutions cause ER retention and defective matrix deposition without robust UPR activation, indicating a failure in cellular surveillance where misfolded procollagen evades ER quality control. Both pathways converge on reduced chondrocyte proliferation and compromised cartilage matrix.

evidence.snippet: we analyzed the pathomechanisms responsible for growth alterations in transgenic mice with conditional expression of the R992C collagen II mutation. Specifically, we studied the alterations of the growth plates of mutant mice in which chondrocytes lacked their typical columnar arrangement.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that mutant collagen II expression disrupts growth plate columnar organization, a hallmark of impaired endochondral ossification.

evidence.snippet: Individuals affected with these disorders exhibit abnormalities of the growth plate, nucleus pulposus, and vitreous humor, which are tissues that contain type II collagen.
evidence.explanation: Growth plate abnormalities in SEMD Strudwick patients confirm disrupted endochondral ossification in human disease.

steps/3.description: The combined effects of ER stress-induced chondrocyte dysfunction, reduced proliferation, and premature apoptosis in the growth plate disrupt the normal sequence of endochondral ossification. Chondrocytes fail to organize into proper columns, and the progression from proliferative to hypertrophic zones is impaired. The resulting disorganized growth plate architecture underlies the characteristic skeletal abnormalities including short-trunk dwarfism, platyspondyly, and metaphyseal dysplasia.

evidence.explanation: Extends the directly observed cortical phenotype to a pachygyria-polymicrogyria complex.

steps/6.description: The cortical phenotype spans pachygyria, agyria, subcortical band heterotopia, and a reported pachygyria-polymicrogyria complex. Pachygyria was present in all eight people summarized in the 2025 review. Cystic leukomalacia is kept separate as a non-cortical radiological extension.

evidence.snippet: All eight patients had abnormal brain MRI findings, including pachygyria in eight (100%); thin corpus callosum in six (75%); cerebellar volume loss in three (37.5%); SBH, subependymal cyst, thin brainstem, and cystic foci in white matter in two each (25%); delayed myelination in one (12.5%); and periventricular leukomalacia in one (12.5%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the non-cortical MRI findings in the eight-person review set.

evidence.snippet: we identified a rare case of TUBGCP2-related tubulinopathy presenting with cystic leukomalacia, expanding the known radiological spectrum.
evidence.explanation: Supports cystic leukomalacia as a later non-cortical radiological extension, not as evidence for the cortical-malformation mechanism.

steps/7.description: Callosal, cerebellar, brainstem, white-matter, cystic, and visual-system abnormalities expand the structural spectrum beyond the cortex. Their developmental links to TUBGCP2 and to each other are not established.

evidence.snippet: All eight patients had abnormal brain MRI findings, including pachygyria in eight (100%)

steps/8.description: Pachygyria was present in 8/8 people in the 2025 cumulative review set. A later case report described a pachygyria-polymicrogyria complex; that later report is not included in this frequency denominator.

evidence.explanation: Direct case-report support for polymicrogyria in the cortical spectrum.

steps/13.description: Present in 7/8 people in the 2025 review set, with onset from 5 months to 4 years and a median of 21.5 months.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI revealed cortical malformations consistent with the pachygyria-polymicrogyria complex, as well as a thickened corpus callosum.

steps/20.description: A later case with a homozygous frameshift variant had a thick corpus callosum. No frequency is assigned because this report is outside the 8-person denominator.

evidence.snippet: She presented with severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and intractable epilepsy at age 6 months and lost all motor and cognitive abilities gradually by 4 years of age.
evidence.explanation: Exact patient-level evidence for hypotonia; it also documents regression, which is curated separately.

steps/21.description: Severe hypotonia was documented in one p.Glu311Lys sibling. No frequency is assigned because the cited case sentence does not define a cumulative denominator.

evidence.snippet: Neurological examination revealed microcephaly, atrophy, and contractures of the extremities with brisk deep tendon reflexes and spasticity.
evidence.explanation: Exact patient-examination evidence for spasticity.

steps/22.description: Spasticity with brisk reflexes and limb contractures was documented in a p.Glu311Lys sibling. No cumulative frequency is assigned.

evidence.snippet: She presented with severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and intractable epilepsy at age 6 months and lost all motor and cognitive abilities gradually by 4 years of age.
evidence.explanation: Exact patient-level evidence for loss of acquired abilities.

steps/23.description: One severely affected p.Glu311Lys sibling lost previously acquired motor and cognitive abilities by four years. No cumulative frequency is assigned.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, a few patients present with visual system abnormalities, including optic atrophy and cortical blindness.
evidence.explanation: Supports optic atrophy without a count-based frequency.

steps/24.description: Optic atrophy has been reported in a few patients, but the review did not provide a denominator suitable for frequency assignment.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, a few patients present with visual system abnormalities, including optic atrophy and cortical blindness.
evidence.explanation: Supports a central visual-system phenotype without a count-based frequency.

steps/25.description: The review reports cortical blindness in a few patients. This is mapped to cerebral visual impairment without assigning a frequency.

edges/1.description: The p.Glu311Lys allele has computational and patient-fibroblast evidence; whether the same proximal effect applies to every reported allele is not established.

edges/2.description: The developmental route from TUBGCP2 variation to facial dysmorphism is unknown.

edges/3.description: A mitotic-state abnormality is seen in a depletion model, but its route from the human variant-dependent fibroblast state is not established.

edges/4.description: Migration is inferred from human cortical imaging; it has not been assayed in patient neural cells or either animal model.

edges/5.description: The developmental route to the non-cortical MRI findings is unresolved.

edges/6.description: The model links altered mitotic-cell abundance with reduced brain size, but the intervening cell-fate and population dynamics remain unresolved.

edges/7.description: The tissue-level reduced-brain-growth state is expressed clinically as microcephaly.

edges/8.description: The neurodevelopmental intermediates producing global delay are unresolved.

edges/9.description: The epileptogenic circuit intermediates are unresolved.

edges/10.description: The mechanism of regression in the severely affected patient is unresolved.

edges/11.description: The neural and motor-system intermediates producing hypotonia are unresolved.

edges/12.description: The corticospinal intermediates producing spasticity are unresolved.

edges/13.description: A migration defect is a plausible route to the cortical phenotype, but direct cellular validation and relevant intermediates are lacking.

edges/14.description: Pachygyria is the constant cortical imaging manifestation in the review set.

edges/15.description: Subcortical band heterotopia is a less frequent cortical manifestation.

edges/16.description: Polymicrogyria was reported as part of a pachygyria-polymicrogyria complex.

evidence.snippet: Our data demonstrate that pathogenic variants in TUBGCP2 cause an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental trait consisting of a neuronal migration disorder
evidence.explanation: The founding gene-disease observation.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we reported a 6-year-old patient with LIS caused by a hemizygous variant in TUBGCP2 (two paternal missense variants: c.178 C>T, c.538T>C and one maternal exon variant: 2–14 deletion).
evidence.explanation: Documents the later mixed missense/deletion configuration.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing identified a homozygous NM_006659.4:c.2647dupC p.(Gln883Profs*62) variant in the TUBGCP2 gene, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
evidence.explanation: Documents the later homozygous frameshift allele.

genes/0.notes: TUBGCP2 encodes GCP2, a core gamma-tubulin ring-complex component. The founding families carried homozygous p.Arg333Cys or p.Ala615Pro, or compound-heterozygous p.Arg297Cys and c.2025-2A>G alleles. Subsequent reports added homozygous p.Glu311Lys; a Chinese configuration with paternal c.178C>T and c.538T>C/p.Trp180Arg variants opposite a maternal exons 2-14 deletion; and homozygous c.2647dupC/p.Gln883Profs*62. Functional consequences cannot be generalized across this mixed allele series.

evidence.snippet: Seizures are treated with anti-seizure medications based on the specific seizure type.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL because this GeneReviews overview does not discuss TUBGCP2 and is used only as phenotype-based management extrapolation.

treatments/0.description: Anti-seizure medication is selected according to seizure type. This is phenotype-based management extrapolated from general tubulinopathy guidance; no TUBGCP2-specific comparative treatment evidence is available.

evidence.snippet: Supportive management, including an individualized therapy plan that includes physical therapy to manage the complications of spasticity, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and vision therapy for oculomotor deficits and/or strabismus should begin at the time of diagnosis to ensure the best possible functionality and developmental outcome.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL because this general tubulinopathy guidance does not mention TUBGCP2 and supplies no disorder-specific outcome data.

treatments/1.description: An individualized plan may include physical, occupational, speech, and vision therapy, with physical therapy addressing complications of spasticity. This is general tubulinopathy guidance rather than a measured TUBGCP2-specific outcome.

evidence.snippet: Our data demonstrate that pathogenic variants in TUBGCP2 cause an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental trait consisting of a neuronal migration disorder
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL support: the source establishes recessive inheritance but does not report a counseling intervention or outcome.

treatments/2.description: Counseling should communicate autosomal recessive inheritance and interpret recurrence in light of confirmed familial variants and parental phase. The cited disease paper does not directly support a numerical recurrence-risk or carrier-testing outcome claim.

open_questions/0.rationale: The mixed allele series includes missense, splice-altering, frameshift, and multi-exon deletion variants, but no common assay establishes their effects. For p.Glu311Lys, GCP2 abundance is preserved while gamma-tubulin, HAUS6, and NEDD1 localization changes. That allele-specific result does not classify the truncating, splice, or deletion alleles and does not demonstrate a dominant-negative mechanism. Functional impact therefore remains UNKNOWN.

evidence.snippet: Currently, functional and proteomic studies on TUBGCP2 gene variants in human neurons are lacking.
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly identifies the human-neural evidence gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: Current functional evidence comes from p.Glu311Lys skin fibroblasts and low-fidelity depletion/null animal models. The human cortical imaging suggests a migration disorder, but no patient-derived neural system measures migration, mitosis, or nucleation. This missing bridge prevents a causal assignment from the fibroblast localization phenotype to cortical malformation.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI revealed cortical malformations consistent with the pachygyria-polymicrogyria complex, as well as a thickened corpus callosum.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence for the later opposite-direction callosal finding.

open_questions/2.rationale: Thin corpus callosum occurred in 6/8 people in the 2025 review, while a later patient with homozygous c.2647dupC/p.Gln883Profs*62 had a thick corpus callosum. With one thick-callosum report, it is unknown whether direction tracks genotype, age, a modifier, or measurement differences.

evidence.snippet: L-serine treatment in cultured skin fibroblasts revealed an 8% increased proliferation in both TUBGCP2-patient and control, while a 26% reduction of cytotoxicity was detected in patient-derived cells compared to 14% in controls. These changes did not reach statistical significance.
evidence.explanation: The exact nonsignificant in-vitro result that motivates, but does not answer, the question.

open_questions/3.rationale: A patient-fibroblast experiment found an 8% proliferation increase in both patient and control cells and a larger numerical reduction in cytotoxicity in patient cells, but neither result reached statistical significance. There is no animal or human treatment evidence, so L-serine remains a model-only observation rather than a treatment.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the peroxisome targeting signal (PTS) 1 receptor gene, PEX5, are responsible for complementation group (CG) 2 of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders (PBD).
evidence.explanation: Identifies PEX5 as the peroxisomal targeting signal type 1 receptor and as the gene of complementation group 2 of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders.

evidence.snippet: cells from PBD005 (homozygous for the nonsense mutation R390ter) are defective in the import of both PTS1 and PTS2 proteins, suggesting that the PTS1 receptor also mediates PTS2-targeted protein import
evidence.explanation: Shows that a patient PEX5 nonsense allele removes import of both type 1 and type 2 matrix cargo, so loss of this receptor blocks recognition of both matrix protein classes.

evidence.snippet: the PEX7 gene, which codes for the peroxin 7 receptor protein required for peroxisomal import of proteins containing a peroxisomal targeting signal type 2.
evidence.explanation: States the function of PEX7 as the receptor for peroxisomal targeting signal type 2 cargo, the step this subtype disables.

steps/14.description: Peroxisomal matrix proteins are recognised in the cytosol by shuttling receptors before they ever reach the organelle: PEX5 is the receptor for peroxisomal targeting signal type 1 cargo and is also required for import of type 2 cargo, which PEX7 recognises. Biallelic loss of either receptor removes cargo recognition at the first step of import, so matrix enzymes are never delivered even when the peroxisomal membrane and its translocation machinery are intact.

evidence.snippet: Import of proteins into peroxisomes depends on PEX5, PEX13 and PEX14.
evidence.explanation: States that peroxisomal matrix protein import depends on PEX13 and PEX14 alongside the import receptor PEX5.

evidence.snippet: The SH3 domain also binds WxxxF peptide motifs in the import receptor PEX5, demonstrating evolutionary conservation of such interactions from yeast to human.
evidence.explanation: Shows the PEX13 SH3 domain binding the import receptor PEX5 directly, the receptor-engagement step at the peroxisomal membrane that this record describes.

steps/15.description: Peroxisomal matrix protein import depends on PEX13 and PEX14 alongside the import receptor PEX5, which the PEX13 SH3 domain binds directly. Biallelic loss of either peroxin leaves the cargo-loaded receptor unable to engage the membrane, so folded matrix proteins are not translocated into the organelle.

evidence.snippet: Recycling requires receptor monoubiquitination by a membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligase complex composed of three RING finger (RF) domain-containing proteins: PEX2, PEX10, and PEX12.
evidence.explanation: Names PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 as the three RING finger proteins of the membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligase complex that monoubiquitinates the import receptor, the step this subtype disables.

evidence.snippet: A recent cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the complex reveals its function as a retro-translocation channel for peroxisomal import receptors.
evidence.explanation: Supports the RING complex doubling as the retrotranslocation channel for the import receptor, not only as a ligase.

steps/16.description: PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 are the three RING finger peroxins of a membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligase complex. The complex monoubiquitinates the import receptor after cargo release and forms the channel through which the receptor is retrotranslocated back to the cytosol; when recycling is compromised the receptor is instead polyubiquitinated and degraded. Biallelic loss of any of the three therefore exhausts the receptor pool and stops further import.

evidence.snippet: The ATP-dependent protein complex in charge of resetting this machinery-the Receptor Export Module (REM)-comprises two members of the "ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities" (AAA+) family, PEX1 and PEX6, and a membrane protein that anchors the ATPases to the organelle membrane.
evidence.explanation: Supports the receptor export module resetting the import machinery and comprising PEX1, PEX6 and a membrane anchor, and that ATP hydrolysis is used only for that reset.

evidence.snippet: Peroxisomal biogenesis factor PEX26 is a membrane anchor for the multi-subunit PEX1-PEX6 protein complex that controls ubiquitination and dislocation of PEX5 cargo receptors for peroxisomal matrix protein import.
evidence.explanation: States that PEX26 anchors the PEX1-PEX6 complex to the peroxisomal membrane, the step this subtype disables.

steps/17.description: The receptor export module resets the import machinery. PEX1 and PEX6 are its two AAA+ ATPases and PEX26 the membrane protein that anchors them to the organelle. Unlike most translocases, peroxisomal matrix import does not use ATP hydrolysis to move cargo; it uses it only to extract the receptor afterwards, which is why losing this module stalls the cycle rather than the individual translocation event. PEX1 variants are among the most prevalent reported in this spectrum.

evidence.snippet: it is generally accepted that peroxisomes employ three proteins - Pex3, Pex19 and Pex16 in mammals - for the insertion of peroxisomal membrane proteins into the peroxisomal membrane.
evidence.explanation: Names PEX3, PEX19 and PEX16 as the three mammalian peroxins required for insertion of peroxisomal membrane proteins, the step this subtype disables.

evidence.snippet: In the absence of any of these, no peroxisomal structures can be identified and PMPs are mistargeted or become degraded
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that losing any one of the three membrane-biogenesis peroxins leaves no identifiable peroxisomal structures and mistargeted membrane proteins.

evidence.snippet: peroxins including Pex3p, Pex16p and Pex19p, are responsible for peroxisome membrane biogenesis via Pex19p- and Pex3p-dependent class I and Pex19p- and Pex16p-dependent class II pathways
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the PEX19- and PEX3-dependent class I route from the PEX19- and PEX16-dependent class II route of peroxisomal membrane biogenesis.

steps/18.description: PEX3, PEX16 and PEX19 are the three mammalian peroxins dedicated to inserting peroxisomal membrane proteins into the peroxisomal membrane, by a PEX19- and PEX3-dependent class I route and a PEX19- and PEX16-dependent class II route. Their loss is categorically different from a matrix import defect: in the absence of any of the three no peroxisomal structures can be identified at all, and peroxisomal membrane proteins are mistargeted or degraded, so there is no membrane compartment left for the import machinery to act on.

evidence.snippet: The peroxisomal membrane is elongated by Pex11β and then divided by the dynamin-like GTPase, DLP1 (also known as DRP1 encoded by DNM1L gene), which also functions as a fission factor for mitochondria.
evidence.explanation: States that PEX11B elongates the peroxisomal membrane ahead of DLP1-mediated division, the step this subtype disables.

evidence.snippet: The PEX11β gene contains four exons and encodes peroxisomal membrane protein 11β, which is involved in peroxisome proliferation and division.
evidence.explanation: States the molecular function of the PEX11B product in peroxisome proliferation and division.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in this gene result in a rare genetic disorder with autosomal recessive inheritance called peroxisome biogenesis disorder 14B
evidence.explanation: States the human gene-disease relationship: biallelic PEX11B variants cause peroxisome biogenesis disorder 14B.

steps/19.description: PEX11B elongates the peroxisomal membrane ahead of scission by the dynamin-like GTPase DLP1, so peroxisome number is set by division of pre-existing organelles rather than by assembly. Biallelic PEX11B loss therefore disables the proliferation and division step rather than the matrix import or membrane assembly steps that account for the rest of this spectrum, and the resulting disorder is peroxisome biogenesis disorder 14B.

evidence.snippet: Defects in PEX genes impair peroxisome assembly and multiple metabolic pathways confined to this organelle, thus providing the biochemical and molecular bases of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders (PBD).
evidence.explanation: This review directly supports PEX-gene-mediated peroxisome assembly failure as the molecular basis of ZSD.

evidence.snippet: Peroxisome is a single-membrane-bounded ubiquitous organelle containing a hundred different enzymes that catalyze various metabolic pathways
evidence.explanation: Fujiki's CHO cell-mutant complementation review supports the role of peroxisomes as multifunctional metabolic organelles whose biogenesis failure underlies ZSD.

steps/20.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PEX genes (peroxins) disrupt peroxisome assembly, matrix protein import, membrane biogenesis, or peroxisome division. The result is absent or empty "ghost" peroxisomes incapable of carrying out peroxisomal metabolism. The individual genes are not listed on this node: each is wired to the specific biogenesis step its peroxin serves, on the six upstream nodes that feed this one.

evidence.snippet: We generated Pex19 Drosophila mutants, which recapitulate the hallmarks of PBDs, like absence of peroxisomes, reduced viability, neurodegeneration, mitochondrial abnormalities, and accumulation of VLCFAs.
evidence.explanation: Drosophila Pex19 model recapitulates VLCFA accumulation, the defining biochemical signature of ZSD.

evidence.snippet: PDs are characterized by abnormal elevations of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA).
evidence.explanation: Clinical case series confirms VLCFA elevation as the defining biochemical feature of peroxisomal disorders including ZSD.

steps/21.description: Defective peroxisomal beta-oxidation causes pathologic elevations of saturated very long-chain fatty acids (C26:0) and the branched-chain fatty acids phytanic and pristanic acid in plasma, fibroblasts, and tissues, providing the principal biochemical diagnostic signature.

evidence.snippet: it is worth investigating the level of long-chain fatty acids, plasmalogen of erythrocytes, intermediate metabolites of bile acid synthesis, or carrying out genetic sequencing.
evidence.explanation: Clinical case report supports erythrocyte plasmalogen depletion and bile acid intermediate accumulation as biochemical hallmarks of ZSD.

steps/22.description: Loss of peroxisomal ether-phospholipid synthesis depletes red blood cell and tissue plasmalogens, while blocked bile acid side-chain shortening produces accumulation of dihydroxycholestanoic acid (DHCA) and trihydroxycholestanoic acid (THCA). Plasmalogen deficiency is implicated in CNS myelin instability.

evidence.snippet: Affected newborns are hypotonic and feed poorly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports the early multi-system clinical presentation of severe ZSD.

evidence.snippet: Peroxisome biogenesis disorders, of which Zellweger syndrome is the most severe, result in severe neurological dysfunction associated with abnormal CNS neuronal migrations due to the lack of functional peroxisomes.
evidence.explanation: PEX2 mouse model supports neuronal migration defects as a core neurodevelopmental consequence of peroxisome deficiency.

steps/23.description: Combined toxic accumulation and product deficiency produce the characteristic Zellweger phenotype: profound hypotonia, intractable seizures, craniofacial dysmorphism, leukodystrophy, hepatic dysfunction, renal cortical cysts, and progressive sensory loss.

evidence.snippet: Affected newborns are hypotonic and feed poorly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports neonatal hypotonia as a defining presenting feature of ZSD.

steps/24.description: Profound generalized hypotonia is one of the earliest and most consistent presenting features of severe Zellweger spectrum disorders.

evidence.snippet: Affected newborns are hypotonic and feed poorly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports poor feeding in affected newborns.

steps/25.description: Poor feeding is an early neonatal manifestation that often contributes to nutritional compromise and the need for supportive feeding care.

evidence.snippet: neuronal migration defects associated with neonatal-onset seizures
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports neonatal-onset seizures as a characteristic congenital malformation phenotype of severe ZSD.

steps/26.description: Neonatal-onset seizures, often intractable, are characteristic of classic Zellweger syndrome.

evidence.snippet: liver disease that can be severe
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports hepatic disease as a major organ-system phenotype of severe ZSD.

steps/27.description: Hepatomegaly is a specific hepatic manifestation within the severe liver disease seen in Zellweger spectrum disorders.

evidence.snippet: sensory loss (secondary to retinal dystrophy and sensorineural hearing loss)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports sensorineural hearing loss as a recognized progressive sensory phenotype of milder ZSD.

steps/28.description: Progressive sensorineural hearing loss is a frequent feature, particularly in the milder NALD and IRD forms.

evidence.snippet: sensory loss (secondary to retinal dystrophy and sensorineural hearing loss)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports retinal dystrophy as a key sensory phenotype in milder ZSD.

steps/29.description: Progressive retinal degeneration with retinitis pigmentosa is a hallmark of the milder NALD and IRD phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: They have distinctive facies
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports distinctive facial features as a hallmark of severe ZSD.

steps/30.description: Craniofacial features including high forehead, large fontanelles, flat occiput, and broad nasal bridge are characteristic of classic Zellweger syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Primary adrenal insufficiency was found in 7/24 patients examined, with 4/7 being asymptomatic.
evidence.explanation: Clinical cohort study supports adrenal insufficiency as a frequent and often asymptomatic phenotype in ZSD.

steps/31.description: Primary adrenal insufficiency is common in ZSD, frequently asymptomatic in milder forms, and associated with specific PEX1 variants.

evidence.snippet: neuronal migration defects associated with neonatal-onset seizures, renal cysts, and bony stippling
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports renal cortical cysts as a characteristic congenital malformation of severe ZSD.

steps/32.description: Renal cortical cysts are a near-universal congenital malformation of severe Zellweger syndrome.

evidence.snippet: renal cysts, and bony stippling
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports chondrodysplasia punctata (epiphyseal stippling) as a characteristic congenital skeletal malformation of severe ZSD.

steps/33.description: Punctate epiphyseal calcifications (chondrodysplasia punctata) of the patellae and long bones are a characteristic congenital skeletal feature of severe Zellweger syndrome.

evidence.snippet: neurologic involvement (ataxia, polyneuropathy, and leukodystrophy)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports leukodystrophy as a major progressive neurologic phenotype of milder ZSD.

steps/34.description: Progressive white matter disease (leukodystrophy) is a major neurologic feature of the intermediate (NALD) and milder (IRD) ZSD phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: While hypotonia and developmental delays are typical, intellect can be normal.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports developmental delay as a typical neurodevelopmental phenotype across the ZSD spectrum.

steps/35.description: Global developmental delay is a typical feature across the Zellweger spectrum, although intellect can be normal in the mildest cases.

evidence.snippet: neurologic involvement (ataxia, polyneuropathy, and leukodystrophy)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly lists ataxia in intermediate/milder ZSD.

steps/36.description: Ataxia occurs in intermediate and milder ZSD as part of progressive neurologic involvement.

evidence.snippet: neurologic involvement (ataxia, polyneuropathy, and leukodystrophy)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly lists polyneuropathy in intermediate/milder ZSD.

steps/37.description: Polyneuropathy occurs in intermediate and milder ZSD as part of progressive neurologic involvement.

evidence.snippet: liver dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency, and renal oxalate stones.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly lists renal oxalate stones in ZSD.

steps/38.description: Renal oxalate stones occur in intermediate and milder ZSD and require renal surveillance and supportive management.

evidence.snippet: Some have osteopenia; almost all have ameleogenesis imperfecta in the secondary teeth.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports osteopenia in some individuals with ZSD.

steps/39.description: Reduced bone mineral density is reported in a subset of individuals with ZSD.

evidence.snippet: Some have osteopenia; almost all have ameleogenesis imperfecta in the secondary teeth.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports amelogenesis imperfecta of secondary teeth.

steps/40.description: Dental enamel dysplasia of the secondary teeth is a common manifestation in ZSD survivors.

evidence.snippet: the absence of peroxisomes results in an impairment of metabolic processes in which peroxisomes are normally involved
